13.7 Tangent Planes and Normal Lines

Larson & Edwards 7e & Dr. Alhumaidy Notes — Gradient Normal Vectors $\nabla F(P_0)$, Tangent Planes, Normal Lines, Surface Intersection Curves, Angle of Inclination & Parallel/Perpendicular Plane Conditions.

What You Already Know

In Calculus I, a differentiable curve $y = f(x)$ has tangent line $y - y_0 = f'(x_0)(x - x_0)$ built from a single slope $f'(x_0)$. In 3D space, any plane through $P_0(x_0, y_0, z_0)$ with normal vector $\mathbf{n} = \langle A, B, C \rangle$ satisfies:

$$A(x - x_0) + B(y - y_0) + C(z - z_0) = 0$$

Similarly, any line through $P_0$ in direction $\mathbf{v}$ uses $\mathbf{v}$ as its direction numbers, and the 2D gradient $\nabla f(x_0, y_0)$ is always orthogonal to the level curve $f(x, y) = k$. Section 13.7 lifts that exact orthogonality idea one dimension higher into 3D space.

Core Concept • §1

1. Tangent Plane & Normal Line via $\nabla F(x_0, y_0, z_0)$

Intuition: Imagine resting a rigid flat pane of glass against a smooth billiard ball at a point $P_0(x_0, y_0, z_0)$, while driving a straight pin through $P_0$ perpendicular to that glass pane. The flat glass is the tangent plane, and the perpendicular line of impact is the normal line.

Writing a surface in general 3-variable level-surface form $F(x, y, z) = 0$ puts $x$, $y$, and $z$ on equal footing. Its 3D gradient $\nabla F(P_0)$ supplies that perpendicular direction vector in one step.

Note (Instructor Notes vs. Book): Larson writes gradients with unit vectors $\mathbf{i}, \mathbf{j}, \mathbf{k}$, whereas Dr. Alhumaidy’s notes use component brackets: $$\nabla F(x_0, y_0, z_0) = \langle F_x(P_0), F_y(P_0), F_z(P_0) \rangle \neq \langle 0, 0, 0 \rangle$$

For explicit surfaces $z = f(x, y)$, Dr. Alhumaidy recommends memorizing the direct solved-$z$ form rather than leaving $-(z - z_0)$ on the left:

$$z = f(x_0, y_0) + f_x(x_0, y_0)(x - x_0) + f_y(x_0, y_0)(y - y_0)$$ Textbook p. 934; Instructor Notes pp. 932, 934
Level surface $F(x,y,z)=0$ Tangent plane through $P_0$ Normal vector $\nabla F(P_0)$ & normal line Tangent vectors $\mathbf{r}'(t_0)$ in the plane

The surface gradient at the point of tangency makes a 90-degree angle with every curve tangent vector lying in the tangent plane.

Theorem 13.13: Equation of Tangent Plane

If $F$ is differentiable at $P_0(x_0, y_0, z_0)$ with $\nabla F(P_0) \neq \mathbf{0}$, then an equation of the tangent plane to the surface given by $F(x, y, z) = 0$ at $(x_0, y_0, z_0)$ is:

$$F_x(x_0, y_0, z_0)(x - x_0) + F_y(x_0, y_0, z_0)(y - y_0) + F_z(x_0, y_0, z_0)(z - z_0) = 0$$ Textbook p. 932, Theorem 13.13
Definitions: Tangent Plane, Normal Line & Explicit Form

Let $F$ be differentiable at $P_0(x_0, y_0, z_0)$ on the surface $F(x, y, z) = 0$ with $\nabla F(P_0) \neq \mathbf{0}$. The tangent plane at $P_0$ is the plane through $P_0$ normal to $\nabla F(P_0)$, and the normal line at $P_0$ is the line through $P_0$ in the direction of $\nabla F(P_0)$.

Symmetric equations of the normal line (provided $F_x(P_0), F_y(P_0), F_z(P_0) \neq 0$):

$$\frac{x - x_0}{F_x(P_0)} = \frac{y - y_0}{F_y(P_0)} = \frac{z - z_0}{F_z(P_0)}$$

Special explicit case $z = f(x, y)$: setting $F(x, y, z) = f(x, y) - z = 0$ gives the normal vector:

$$\nabla F(P_0) = \langle f_x(x_0, y_0), f_y(x_0, y_0), -1 \rangle$$

This produces the solved explicit tangent plane equation:

$$z = f(x_0, y_0) + f_x(x_0, y_0)(x - x_0) + f_y(x_0, y_0)(y - y_0)$$ Textbook pp. 932–934; Instructor Notes p. 934
Example: Tangent Plane and Normal Line to a Sphere
Find an equation of the tangent plane and symmetric equations of the normal line to the sphere at $P_0(1, 2, 2)$: $$x^2 + y^2 + z^2 = 9$$
Step 1: Rewrite as $F(x, y, z) = 0$ and compute $\nabla F$. Move $9$ to the left to define $F(x, y, z) = x^2 + y^2 + z^2 - 9 = 0$, and differentiate: $$\nabla F(x, y, z) = \langle 2x, 2y, 2z \rangle$$
Step 2: Evaluate the gradient at $P_0(1, 2, 2)$. Substituting $(1, 2, 2)$ gives a normal vector parallel to $\mathbf{n} = \langle 1, 2, 2 \rangle$: $$\nabla F(1, 2, 2) = \langle 2, 4, 4 \rangle = 2\langle 1, 2, 2 \rangle$$
Step 3: Write the tangent plane and normal line. Using $\mathbf{n} = \langle 1, 2, 2 \rangle$ at $(1, 2, 2)$ gives the tangent plane: $$\begin{aligned} 1(x - 1) + 2(y - 2) + 2(z - 2) &= 0 \\ x + 2y + 2z &= 9 \end{aligned}$$

Symmetric equations of the normal line are:

$$\frac{x - 1}{1} = \frac{y - 2}{2} = \frac{z - 2}{2}$$
Step 4: Verify at $P_0(1, 2, 2)$. Both $1^2 + 2^2 + 2^2 = 9$ and $1 + 2(2) + 2(2) = 9$ hold, and substituting $(1, 2, 2)$ into the normal line yields $0 = 0 = 0$.
Answer: Tangent plane $x + 2y + 2z = 9$ and symmetric normal line: $$\frac{x - 1}{1} = \frac{y - 2}{2} = \frac{z - 2}{2}$$
Textbook p. 937, Ex. 18
Why It Works: Chain Rule Proof of Gradient Orthogonality

Let a differentiable curve on the surface $S$ passing through $P_0 = \mathbf{r}(t_0)$ be parametrized by:

$$\mathbf{r}(t) = \langle x(t), y(t), z(t) \rangle$$

Because every point of the curve lies on $S$, we have $F(x(t), y(t), z(t)) = 0$ for all $t$. Differentiating both sides by the Chain Rule and evaluating at $t = t_0$ produces:

$$\begin{aligned} \frac{d}{dt}\big[F(\mathbf{r}(t))\big] &= F_x x'(t) + F_y y'(t) + F_z z'(t) = 0 \\ \nabla F(P_0) \cdot \mathbf{r}'(t_0) &= 0 \end{aligned}$$

Thus $\nabla F(P_0)$ is orthogonal to the tangent vector of every curve on $S$ through $P_0$, so all tangent lines to $S$ at $P_0$ lie in the single plane normal to $\nabla F(P_0)$.

Textbook p. 932
Theorem 13.14: Gradient Is Normal to Level Surfaces

If $F$ is differentiable at $(x_0, y_0, z_0)$ and

$$\nabla F(x_0, y_0, z_0) \neq \mathbf{0}$$

then $\nabla F(x_0, y_0, z_0)$ is normal to the level surface through $(x_0, y_0, z_0)$.

Compare the dimensions: $\nabla f(x, y)$ is a vector in the $xy$-plane normal to level curves, whereas $\nabla F(x, y, z)$ is a vector in 3D space normal to level surfaces.

Textbook p. 936, Theorem 13.14
Quick Check 1

Which vector is normal to the surface $z = x^2 - 3y$ at the point $P_0(2, 1, 1)$?

(A) $\langle 4, -3, 1 \rangle$
(B) $\langle 4, -3, -1 \rangle$
(C) $\langle 4, -3, 0 \rangle$
(D) $\langle 2, -3, -1 \rangle$
Check Answer & Reason

Answer: (B) $\langle 4, -3, -1 \rangle$. Move $z$ to the same side to write $F(x, y, z) = x^2 - 3y - z = 0$, then compute the gradient at $P_0(2, 1, 1)$:

$$\begin{aligned} \nabla F(x, y, z) &= \langle 2x, -3, -1 \rangle \\ \nabla F(2, 1, 1) &= \langle 4, -3, -1 \rangle \end{aligned}$$
Core Concept • §2

2. Tangent Line to the Intersection Curve of Two Surfaces

Intuition: When two smooth surfaces $F(x, y, z) = 0$ and $G(x, y, z) = 0$ slice through each other, their seam forms a 3D space curve $C$. At any shared point $P_0$ on $C$, the tangent line to $C$ is the intersection of the two tangent planes, so its direction vector $\mathbf{v}$ must be perpendicular to both $\nabla F(P_0)$ and $\nabla G(P_0)$.

$\nabla F(P_0)$ normal to $F=0$ $\nabla G(P_0)$ normal to $G=0$ Cross product $\mathbf{v} = \nabla F \times \nabla G$

Because the intersection curve lies on both surfaces simultaneously, its tangent direction vector is orthogonal to both surface gradients, matching their cross product.

Formula: Tangent Line to an Intersection Curve

If the cross product direction vector is nonzero:

$$\mathbf{v} = \nabla F(P_0) \times \nabla G(P_0) = \langle a, b, c \rangle \neq \langle 0, 0, 0 \rangle$$

then parametric equations of the tangent line to the intersection curve at $P_0(x_0, y_0, z_0)$ are:

$$\begin{aligned} x &= x_0 + at \\ y &= y_0 + bt \\ z &= z_0 + ct \end{aligned}$$ Textbook p. 935; Instructor Notes p. 937
Example: Tangent Line to an Intersection Curve
Find parametric equations for the tangent line to the curve of intersection of the ellipsoid and the paraboloid at $(0, 1, 3)$: $$x^2 + 2y^2 + 2z^2 = 20$$ $$x^2 + y^2 + z = 4$$
Step 1: Define $F = 0$ and $G = 0$ and evaluate both gradients at $(0, 1, 3)$. Set $F(x, y, z) = x^2 + 2y^2 + 2z^2 - 20$ and $G(x, y, z) = x^2 + y^2 + z - 4$: $$\begin{aligned} \nabla F(x, y, z) &= \langle 2x, 4y, 4z \rangle \implies \nabla F(0, 1, 3) = \langle 0, 4, 12 \rangle \\ \nabla G(x, y, z) &= \langle 2x, 2y, 1 \rangle \implies \nabla G(0, 1, 3) = \langle 0, 2, 1 \rangle \end{aligned}$$
Step 2: Compute the cross product $\nabla F \times \nabla G$ at $(0, 1, 3)$. $$\mathbf{v} = \begin{vmatrix} \mathbf{i} & \mathbf{j} & \mathbf{k} \\ 0 & 4 & 12 \\ 0 & 2 & 1 \end{vmatrix} = \langle 4(1) - 12(2),\; 0,\; 0 \rangle = \langle -20, 0, 0 \rangle$$
Step 3: Write the parametric tangent line. Dividing $\langle -20, 0, 0 \rangle$ by $-20$ gives simplified direction numbers $1, 0, 0$ through $(0, 1, 3)$: $$\begin{aligned} x &= t \\ y &= 1 \\ z &= 3 \end{aligned}$$
Step 4: Verify point membership and orthogonality. At $(0, 1, 3)$, $0 + 2(1) + 2(9) = 20$ and $0 + 1 + 3 = 4$, and both dot products vanish: $$\begin{aligned} \langle 1, 0, 0 \rangle \cdot \langle 0, 4, 12 \rangle &= 0 \\ \langle 1, 0, 0 \rangle \cdot \langle 0, 2, 1 \rangle &= 0 \end{aligned}$$
Answer: Parametric equations of the tangent line: $$\begin{aligned} x &= t \\ y &= 1 \\ z &= 3 \end{aligned}$$
Textbook p. 935, Example 5
Why It Works: Orthogonal to Both Surface Normals

Any curve $C$ shared by $F = 0$ and $G = 0$ has its tangent vector $\mathbf{v}$ at $P_0$ lying inside both tangent planes simultaneously. This forces both dot products to vanish:

$$\begin{aligned} \mathbf{v} \cdot \nabla F(P_0) &= 0 \\ \mathbf{v} \cdot \nabla G(P_0) &= 0 \end{aligned}$$

Because the cross product $\nabla F(P_0) \times \nabla G(P_0)$ is orthogonal to both $\nabla F(P_0)$ and $\nabla G(P_0)$, it gives the exact direction of the intersection tangent line.

Textbook p. 935
Quick Check 2

Which vector is parallel to the tangent line to the intersection curve of $x^2 + y^2 = 2$ and $z = x$ at $(1, 1, 1)$?

(A) $\langle 1, 1, 1 \rangle$
(B) $\langle 1, -1, 1 \rangle$
(C) $\langle 1, -1, 0 \rangle$
(D) $\langle 2, 2, -1 \rangle$
Check Answer & Reason

Answer: (B) $\langle 1, -1, 1 \rangle$. Using $F = x^2 + y^2 - 2$ and $G = x - z$, compute both gradients at $(1, 1, 1)$:

$$\begin{aligned} \nabla F(1, 1, 1) &= \langle 2, 2, 0 \rangle \\ \nabla G(1, 1, 1) &= \langle 1, 0, -1 \rangle \end{aligned}$$

Their cross product simplifies to:

$$\nabla F(1, 1, 1) \times \nabla G(1, 1, 1) = \langle -2, 2, -2 \rangle = -2\langle 1, -1, 1 \rangle$$
Textbook p. 937, Ex. 27
Core Concept • §3

3. Angle of Inclination of a Tangent Plane

Intuition: The angle of inclination $\theta$ ($0 \le \theta \le \tfrac{\pi}{2}$) of a tangent plane is the acute tilt angle between the tangent plane and the horizontal $xy$-plane. Imagine resting a flat board on the floor and tilting it up by $\theta$: a perpendicular pole attached to the board tilts away from the vertical vector $\mathbf{k} = \langle 0, 0, 1 \rangle$ by that exact same angle $\theta$.

Tangent plane tilted by $\theta$ Vertical normal $\mathbf{k} = \langle 0,0,1\rangle$ Surface normal $\mathbf{n} = \nabla F(P_0)$ Equal acute angles $\theta \approx 35.3^\circ$

Side cross-section drawn to exact scale for an angle of inclination of about 35.3 degrees: tilting the tangent plane away from the horizontal xy-plane tilts its normal vector away from the vertical unit vector k by the same angle.

Formulas: Angle of Inclination of a Plane

Because $\mathbf{k} = \langle 0, 0, 1 \rangle$ has length $\|\mathbf{k}\| = 1$, the acute angle $\theta$ ($0 \le \theta \le \tfrac{\pi}{2}$) between a plane with normal $\mathbf{n} = \nabla F(P_0)$ and the $xy$-plane satisfies:

$$\cos\theta = \frac{|\mathbf{n} \cdot \mathbf{k}|}{\|\mathbf{n}\|\,\|\mathbf{k}\|} = \frac{|F_z(P_0)|}{\sqrt{F_x(P_0)^2 + F_y(P_0)^2 + F_z(P_0)^2}}$$

For an explicit surface $z = f(x, y)$ at $(x_0, y_0, z_0)$, setting $F(x, y, z) = f(x, y) - z$ gives $|F_z(P_0)| = 1$, so the formula simplifies to:

$$\cos\theta = \frac{1}{\sqrt{[f_x(x_0, y_0)]^2 + [f_y(x_0, y_0)]^2 + 1}}$$ Textbook pp. 935–936
Example: Angle of Inclination of an Ellipsoid Tangent Plane
Find the angle of inclination of the tangent plane to the ellipsoid at $(2, 2, 1)$: $$\frac{x^2}{12} + \frac{y^2}{12} + \frac{z^2}{3} = 1$$
Step 1: Define $F(x, y, z) = 0$ and compute $\nabla F(2, 2, 1)$. Let $F(x, y, z)$ be the level function: $$F(x, y, z) = \frac{x^2}{12} + \frac{y^2}{12} + \frac{z^2}{3} - 1$$

Taking partial derivatives and evaluating at $(2, 2, 1)$ yields:

$$\begin{aligned} \nabla F(x, y, z) &= \left\langle \frac{x}{6},\; \frac{y}{6},\; \frac{2z}{3} \right\rangle \\ \nabla F(2, 2, 1) &= \left\langle \frac{1}{3},\; \frac{1}{3},\; \frac{2}{3} \right\rangle \end{aligned}$$
Step 2: Apply the angle of inclination formula. Compute $\cos\theta$ using $\mathbf{n} = \nabla F(2, 2, 1)$: $$\cos\theta = \frac{|2/3|}{\sqrt{(1/3)^2 + (1/3)^2 + (2/3)^2}} = \frac{2/3}{\sqrt{6}/3} = \sqrt{\frac{2}{3}}$$
Step 3: Solve for $\theta$ and verify bounds. Taking the inverse cosine gives: $$\theta = \arccos\sqrt{\frac{2}{3}} \approx 35.3^\circ$$

Since $0 < \cos\theta < 1$, the angle $\theta$ is strictly acute in $[0, \tfrac{\pi}{2}]$, matching the diagram above.

Answer: $$\theta = \arccos\sqrt{\frac{2}{3}} \approx 35.3^\circ$$
Textbook p. 936, Example 6
Why It Works: Dihedral Angle Between Plane Normals

The acute dihedral angle between two intersecting planes equals the acute angle between their normal vectors. Here the tangent plane has normal $\mathbf{n} = \nabla F(P_0)$ and the horizontal $xy$-plane has unit normal $\mathbf{k} = \langle 0, 0, 1 \rangle$.

Taking the absolute value guarantees $\cos\theta \ge 0$, keeping $\theta$ in $[0, \tfrac{\pi}{2}]$ regardless of whether $\nabla F$ points upward or downward:

$$|\mathbf{n} \cdot \mathbf{k}| = |F_z(P_0)|$$ Textbook p. 935
Quick Check 3

What is the angle of inclination $\theta$ of the tangent plane to $x^2 - y^2 + z = 0$ at $(1, 2, 3)$?

(A) $$\arccos\left(\frac{1}{\sqrt{21}}\right)$$
(B) $$\arcsin\left(\frac{1}{\sqrt{21}}\right)$$
(C) $$\arccos\left(\frac{4}{\sqrt{21}}\right)$$
(D) $$0$$
Check Answer & Reason

Answer: (A). Let $F(x, y, z) = x^2 - y^2 + z$, then evaluate the gradient and its magnitude at $(1, 2, 3)$:

$$\begin{aligned} \nabla F(1, 2, 3) &= \langle 2, -4, 1 \rangle \\ \|\nabla F(1, 2, 3)\| &= \sqrt{2^2 + (-4)^2 + 1^2} = \sqrt{21} \end{aligned}$$

Thus:

$$\cos\theta = \frac{|1|}{\sqrt{21}} \implies \theta = \arccos\left(\frac{1}{\sqrt{21}}\right)$$
Textbook p. 937, Ex. 35
Core Concept • §4

4. Locating Horizontal, Parallel, or Perpendicular Tangent Planes

Intuition: Instead of being handed $P_0$ directly, exam problems frequently ask you to find the unknown point $(a, b, c)$ on a surface where its tangent plane satisfies a geometric condition. Every such condition — horizontal, parallel to a given plane, or perpendicular to a line or another surface — translates directly into an algebraic equation on $\nabla F(x, y, z)$.

Surface gradient $\nabla F(P_0)$ Target plane normal $\mathbf{n}$ Second surface gradient $\nabla G(P_0)$

Every geometric condition on tangent planes translates into an algebraic condition on the surface gradient, followed by substituting back into the surface equation.

Conditions: Horizontal, Parallel, Tangent & Perpendicular Planes

1. Horizontal tangent plane on $z = f(x, y)$: Set $f_x(x, y) = 0$ and $f_y(x, y) = 0$, solve for $(x_0, y_0)$, and substitute back into $z = f(x_0, y_0)$ to find $z_0$.

2. Tangent plane parallel to $Ax + By + Cz = D$ (or perpendicular to a line with direction $\mathbf{v}$): Solve $\nabla F(P_0) = \alpha\,\mathbf{n}$ for $(x_0, y_0, z_0)$ in terms of $\alpha \neq 0$, then plug into the surface equation to find $\alpha$.

3. Tangent or perpendicular surfaces at $P_0$: First verify $P_0$ lies on both surfaces; then the surfaces are tangent if $\nabla F(P_0) \parallel \nabla G(P_0)$, and perpendicular if $\nabla F(P_0) \cdot \nabla G(P_0) = 0$.

Textbook pp. 937–938; Instructor Notes pp. 937–938
Example: Finding a Horizontal Tangent Plane
Find the point on the surface where the tangent plane is horizontal: $$z = 3 - x^2 - y^2 + 6y$$
Step 1: Set both partial derivatives equal to zero. Compute $f_x$ and $f_y$ and equate each to $0$: $$\begin{aligned} f_x &= -2x = 0 \implies x = 0 \\ f_y &= -2y + 6 = 0 \implies y = 3 \end{aligned}$$
Step 2: Substitute $(x, y) = (0, 3)$ back into $z$. $$z = 3 - 0^2 - 3^2 + 6(3) = 3 - 9 + 18 = 12$$
Step 3: Verify the normal vector at $(0, 3, 12)$. At $(0, 3)$, $f_x(0, 3) = 0$ and $f_y(0, 3) = 0$, so the tangent plane is $z = 12$, which is horizontal.
Answer: $(0, 3, 12)$
Textbook p. 937, Ex. 37; Instructor Notes p. 937
Why It Works: Gradient Proportionality and Scalar $\alpha$

Two planes are parallel if and only if their normal vectors are parallel, meaning one is a nonzero scalar multiple $\alpha$ of the other. Setting $\nabla F(a, b, c) = \mathbf{n}$ without $\alpha$ artificially forces $\alpha = 1$ and misses the true point on the surface.

Including $\alpha$ generates three equations in four unknowns ($a, b, c, \alpha$), and the surface equation $F(a, b, c) = 0$ supplies the fourth equation needed to pin down $\alpha$.

Instructor Notes p. 938
Quick Check 4

If $(a, b, c)$ with $a < 0$ is the point on $4x^2 + 2y^2 - z^2 = 100$ where the tangent plane is parallel to the $yz$-plane ($x = 0$), what is $a^2 + b^2 + c^2$?

(A) $16$
(B) $25$
(C) $100$
(D) $225$
Check Answer & Reason

Answer: (B) $25$. The $yz$-plane has normal $\langle 1, 0, 0 \rangle$, so parallel normals require:

$$\nabla F(a, b, c) = \langle 8a, 4b, -2c \rangle = \alpha\langle 1, 0, 0 \rangle$$

This gives $b = 0$ and $c = 0$. Substituting into the surface gives $4a^2 = 100 \implies a = -5$ (since $a < 0$), so $(-5)^2 + 0 + 0 = 25$.

KFUPM Final Term 251, Q9
Master Formulas

Section 13.7 Formula Reference & Edge Cases

Tangent Planes & Normal Lines (Summary)

Assume $F$ is differentiable at $P_0(x_0, y_0, z_0)$ and $\nabla F(P_0) \neq \mathbf{0}$.

Level surface $F(x, y, z) = 0$ tangent plane:

$$F_x(P_0)(x - x_0) + F_y(P_0)(y - y_0) + F_z(P_0)(z - z_0) = 0$$

Explicit surface $z = f(x, y)$ tangent plane:

$$z = f(x_0, y_0) + f_x(x_0, y_0)(x - x_0) + f_y(x_0, y_0)(y - y_0)$$

Parametric equations of the normal line at $P_0$:

$$\begin{aligned} x &= x_0 + F_x(P_0)t \\ y &= y_0 + F_y(P_0)t \\ z &= z_0 + F_z(P_0)t \end{aligned}$$

Symmetric equations of the normal line (when $F_x(P_0), F_y(P_0), F_z(P_0) \neq 0$):

$$\frac{x - x_0}{F_x(P_0)} = \frac{y - y_0}{F_y(P_0)} = \frac{z - z_0}{F_z(P_0)}$$

Edge case: if any component vanishes (say $F_x(P_0) = 0$), write $x = x_0$ separately and keep the symmetric fraction form only for nonzero components:

$$x = x_0, \quad \frac{y - y_0}{F_y(P_0)} = \frac{z - z_0}{F_z(P_0)}$$ Textbook pp. 932–934; Instructor Notes p. 934
Intersection Curves & Angle of Inclination

Tangent line to the intersection curve of $F(x, y, z) = 0$ and $G(x, y, z) = 0$ at $P_0$ uses direction $\mathbf{v} = \nabla F \times \nabla G$ evaluated at $P_0$ (requiring $\mathbf{v} \neq \mathbf{0}$).

Angle of inclination $\theta \in [0, \tfrac{\pi}{2}]$ for an implicit surface $F(x, y, z) = 0$:

$$\cos\theta = \frac{|F_z(P_0)|}{\|\nabla F(P_0)\|}$$

Angle of inclination $\theta \in [0, \tfrac{\pi}{2}]$ for an explicit surface $z = f(x, y)$:

$$\cos\theta = \frac{1}{\sqrt{[f_x(x_0, y_0)]^2 + [f_y(x_0, y_0)]^2 + 1}}$$

Edge cases: a horizontal tangent plane has $\theta = 0$, whereas a vertical tangent plane ($F_z(P_0) = 0$) has $\theta = \tfrac{\pi}{2}$.

Textbook pp. 935–936
Quadric Surface & Cone Tangent Shortcuts

At any point $(x_0, y_0, z_0)$ on an ellipsoid or hyperboloid of one sheet, replace squares by products:

$$\frac{x^2}{a^2} + \frac{y^2}{b^2} \pm \frac{z^2}{c^2} = 1 \implies \frac{x_0 x}{a^2} + \frac{y_0 y}{b^2} \pm \frac{z_0 z}{c^2} = 1$$

Any tangent plane to the cone $z^2 = a^2 x^2 + b^2 y^2$ (away from the vertex) passes through the origin $(0, 0, 0)$.

Textbook pp. 938–939, Ex. 57–59; Instructor Notes p. 939
Exam Traps

5 Classic Mistakes (WRONG vs. RIGHT)

Trap 1 — Wrong sign on $z$ when converting $z = f(x, y)$ to $F(x, y, z) = 0$:

WrongUsing $+1$ as the third component for $z = x^2 + y^2$: $$\nabla F = \langle f_x, f_y, +1 \rangle$$
RightMove everything to one side first so $F = f(x, y) - z = 0$, giving: $$\nabla F = \langle f_x, f_y, -1 \rangle$$

Trap 2 — Leaving variables $(x, y, z)$ inside the normal coefficients:

WrongWriting a quadratic expression instead of a linear plane: $$2x(x - 1) + 4y(y - 2) + 6z(z - 1) = 0$$
RightEvaluate $F_x, F_y, F_z$ at $(x_0, y_0, z_0)$ first to get numbers before writing the plane.

Trap 3 — Ignoring the fixed coefficient or constant in KFUPM MCQs:

WrongGetting $4x - 4y + 2z + 2 = 0$ and reading $(a, b, c) = (4, -4, 2)$ when the prompt specifies $ax + by + cz + 1 = 0$.
RightDivide the entire equation by $2$ first to match $+1$: $2x - 2y + z + 1 = 0$, so $(a, b, c) = (2, -2, 1)$.

Trap 4 — Forgetting scalar $\alpha$ in parallel-plane problems or dividing by zero in symmetric equations:

WrongSetting $\nabla F(a, b, c) = \mathbf{n}$ without a scalar $\alpha$, or writing a zero denominator: $$\frac{z - 3}{0}$$
RightAlways solve $\nabla F(a, b, c) = \alpha\,\mathbf{n}$, and separate any zero-component coordinate: $$z = 3, \quad \frac{x - x_0}{a} = \frac{y - y_0}{b}$$

Trap 5 — Using $\sin\theta$ or forgetting absolute value in angle of inclination:

WrongUsing sine or leaving a negative dot product from $F_z = -1$: $$\sin\theta = \frac{F_z}{\|\nabla F\|}$$
RightThe acute angle between two planes uses cosine and absolute value so $0 \le \theta \le \tfrac{\pi}{2}$: $$\cos\theta = \frac{|F_z(P_0)|}{\|\nabla F(P_0)\|} \ge 0$$
Worked Examples

From Textbook Basics to KFUPM Final Level

Example 1: Tangent Plane & Normal Line to a Hyperboloid
Find an equation of the tangent plane and symmetric equations of the normal line to the hyperboloid at $P_0(1, -1, 4)$: $$z^2 - 2x^2 - 2y^2 = 12$$
Step 1: Define $F(x, y, z) = 0$ and compute $\nabla F$. Move $12$ to the left-hand side and differentiate with respect to $x$, $y$, and $z$: $$\begin{aligned} F(x, y, z) &= z^2 - 2x^2 - 2y^2 - 12 = 0 \\ \nabla F(x, y, z) &= \langle -4x,\; -4y,\; 2z \rangle \end{aligned}$$
Step 2: Evaluate $\nabla F$ at $P_0(1, -1, 4)$. Plug $(1, -1, 4)$ into the gradient to obtain the numerical normal vector: $$\nabla F(1, -1, 4) = \langle -4(1),\; -4(-1),\; 2(4) \rangle = \langle -4,\; 4,\; 8 \rangle = 4\langle -1,\; 1,\; 2 \rangle$$
Step 3: Write the tangent plane and symmetric normal line equations. Using $\langle -4, 4, 8 \rangle$ at $(1, -1, 4)$ gives the tangent plane: $$\begin{aligned} -4(x - 1) + 4(y + 1) + 8(z - 4) &= 0 \\ -4x + 4 + 4y + 4 + 8z - 32 &= 0 \\ -4x + 4y + 8z - 24 &= 0 \\ x - y - 2z + 6 &= 0 \end{aligned}$$

Using simplified direction $\langle -1, 1, 2 \rangle$ gives the symmetric normal line:

$$\frac{x - 1}{-1} = \frac{y + 1}{1} = \frac{z - 4}{2}$$
Step 4: Verify the result. Both equations contain $P_0(1, -1, 4)$: the surface gives $4^2 - 2(1)^2 - 2(-1)^2 = 12$, and the plane gives $1 - (-1) - 2(4) + 6 = 0$.
Answer: Tangent plane $x - y - 2z + 6 = 0$ and symmetric normal line: $$\frac{x - 1}{-1} = \frac{y + 1}{1} = \frac{z - 4}{2}$$
Textbook p. 933, Example 2; Instructor Notes p. 933
Example 2: Matching Standard Form $ax + by + cz + 1 = 0$
If $ax + by + cz + 1 = 0$ is an equation for the tangent plane to the surface $z = (x - y)^2$ at the point $(1, 2, 1)$, find $a + b + c$.
Step 1: Compute the partial derivatives at $(1, 2)$. For $f(x, y) = (x - y)^2$, find $f_x$ and $f_y$ and evaluate at $(1, 2)$: $$\begin{aligned} f_x(x, y) &= 2(x - y) \implies f_x(1, 2) = 2(1 - 2) = -2 \\ f_y(x, y) &= -2(x - y) \implies f_y(1, 2) = -2(1 - 2) = 2 \end{aligned}$$
Step 2: Assemble the explicit tangent plane and match the $+1$ constant. Substitute $f(1, 2) = 1$, $f_x(1, 2) = -2$, and $f_y(1, 2) = 2$ into the explicit tangent plane formula: $$\begin{aligned} z &= 1 - 2(x - 1) + 2(y - 2) \\ z &= 1 - 2x + 2 + 2y - 4 \\ z &= -2x + 2y - 1 \\ 2x - 2y + z + 1 &= 0 \end{aligned}$$

Comparing directly with $ax + by + cz + 1 = 0$ gives $a = 2$, $b = -2$, and $c = 1$, so $a + b + c = 2 - 2 + 1 = 1$.

Step 3: Verify the result. Point $(1, 2, 1)$ satisfies $2(1) - 2(2) + 1 + 1 = 0$, and the normal vector matches $-\nabla(f - z)$ at $(1, 2, 1)$: $$-\nabla(f - z)|_{(1, 2, 1)} = -\langle -2, 2, -1 \rangle = \langle 2, -2, 1 \rangle$$
Answer: $a + b + c = 1$ (from $2x - 2y + z + 1 = 0$).
KFUPM Final Term 253, Q11
Example 3: Tangent Line Where a Sphere Meets a Plane
Find parametric equations for the tangent line to the curve of intersection of the sphere and the plane at $P_0(3, 1, 2)$: $$x^2 + y^2 + z^2 = 14$$ $$x - y - z = 0$$
Step 1: Find both gradients at $P_0(3, 1, 2)$. Write $F(x, y, z) = x^2 + y^2 + z^2 - 14$ and $G(x, y, z) = x - y - z$: $$\begin{aligned} \nabla F(x, y, z) &= \langle 2x, 2y, 2z \rangle \implies \nabla F(3, 1, 2) = \langle 6, 2, 4 \rangle \\ \nabla G(x, y, z) &= \langle 1, -1, -1 \rangle \implies \nabla G(3, 1, 2) = \langle 1, -1, -1 \rangle \end{aligned}$$
Step 2: Compute the cross product $\nabla F(P_0) \times \nabla G(P_0)$. $$\begin{aligned} \nabla F \times \nabla G &= \begin{vmatrix} \mathbf{i} & \mathbf{j} & \mathbf{k} \\ 6 & 2 & 4 \\ 1 & -1 & -1 \end{vmatrix} \\ &= \big(2(-1) - 4(-1)\big)\mathbf{i} - \big(6(-1) - 4(1)\big)\mathbf{j} + \big(6(-1) - 2(1)\big)\mathbf{k} \\ &= \langle 2,\; 10,\; -8 \rangle = 2\langle 1,\; 5,\; -4 \rangle \end{aligned}$$

Using the simplified direction vector $\langle 1, 5, -4 \rangle$ through $(3, 1, 2)$ gives the parametric tangent line.

Step 3: Verify orthogonality and point membership. At $(3, 1, 2)$, $3^2 + 1^2 + 2^2 = 14$ and $3 - 1 - 2 = 0$, while both dot products vanish: $$\begin{aligned} \langle 1, 5, -4 \rangle \cdot \langle 6, 2, 4 \rangle &= 6 + 10 - 16 = 0 \\ \langle 1, 5, -4 \rangle \cdot \langle 1, -1, -1 \rangle &= 1 - 5 + 4 = 0 \end{aligned}$$
Answer: Parametric equations ($-\infty < t < \infty$): $$\begin{aligned} x &= 3 + t \\ y &= 1 + 5t \\ z &= 2 - 4t \end{aligned}$$
Textbook p. 937, Ex. 31; Instructor Notes p. 937
Example 4: Coupled System for a Horizontal Tangent Plane
Find the point $(x_0, y_0, z_0)$ on the surface at which the tangent plane is horizontal: $$z = 4x^2 + 4xy - 2y^2 + 8x - 5y - 4$$
Step 1: Set $z_x = 0$ and $z_y = 0$ simultaneously. $$\begin{cases} z_x = 8x + 4y + 8 = 0 & (1) \\ z_y = 4x - 4y - 5 = 0 & (2) \end{cases}$$
Step 2: Solve the linear system for $x_0$ and $y_0$. Add equations $(1)$ and $(2)$ directly to eliminate $y$: $$\begin{aligned} (8x + 4y + 8) + (4x - 4y - 5) &= 0 \\ 12x + 3 &= 0 \\ x_0 &= -\frac{1}{4} \end{aligned}$$

Substitute $x_0 = -\tfrac{1}{4}$ into $(1)$ to solve for $y_0$:

$$\begin{aligned} 8\left(-\frac{1}{4}\right) + 4y + 8 &= 0 \\ 4y + 6 &= 0 \\ y_0 &= -\frac{3}{2} \end{aligned}$$
Step 3: Substitute $(x_0, y_0)$ back into $z$ to find $z_0$. $$\begin{aligned} z_0 &= 4\left(\frac{1}{16}\right) + 4\left(-\frac{1}{4}\right)\left(-\frac{3}{2}\right) - 2\left(\frac{9}{4}\right) + 8\left(-\frac{1}{4}\right) - 5\left(-\frac{3}{2}\right) - 4 \\ &= \frac{1}{4} + \frac{3}{2} - \frac{9}{2} - 2 + \frac{15}{2} - 4 \\ &= \frac{1}{4} + \frac{9}{2} - 6 = -\frac{5}{4} \end{aligned}$$
Step 4: Verify the result. Checking both partial derivatives at $(-\tfrac{1}{4}, -\tfrac{3}{2})$ confirms $z_x = -2 - 6 + 8 = 0$ and $z_y = -1 + 6 - 5 = 0$.
Answer: $$P_0\left(-\frac{1}{4},\; -\frac{3}{2},\; -\frac{5}{4}\right)$$
Textbook p. 937, Ex. 40; Instructor Notes p. 937; KFUPM Final Term 241, Q5
Example 5: Finding $(a, b, c)$ with $a < 0$ Using $\nabla F = \alpha\,\mathbf{n}$
If $(a, b, c)$ with $a < 0$ is the point on the hyperboloid $x^2 + 4y^2 - z^2 = -4$ where the tangent plane is parallel to the plane $2x - 4y + 3z = 1$, find $a + b + c$.
Step 1: Equate $\nabla F(a, b, c) = \alpha\,\mathbf{n}$. With $F(x, y, z) = x^2 + 4y^2 - z^2 + 4$ and target normal $\mathbf{n} = \langle 2, -4, 3 \rangle$, equate $\nabla F(a, b, c) = \alpha\,\mathbf{n}$ for some scalar $\alpha \neq 0$: $$\langle 2a, 8b, -2c \rangle = \alpha\langle 2, -4, 3 \rangle$$ $$\begin{cases} 2a = 2\alpha \implies a = \alpha \\ 8b = -4\alpha \implies b = -\dfrac{\alpha}{2} \\ -2c = 3\alpha \implies c = -\dfrac{3\alpha}{2} \end{cases}$$
Step 2: Substitute into the surface equation and enforce $a < 0$. $$\begin{aligned} \alpha^2 + 4\left(-\frac{\alpha}{2}\right)^2 - \left(-\frac{3\alpha}{2}\right)^2 &= -4 \\ \alpha^2 + \alpha^2 - \frac{9}{4}\alpha^2 &= -4 \\ -\frac{1}{4}\alpha^2 &= -4 \\ \alpha^2 &= 16 \implies \alpha = \pm 4 \end{aligned}$$

Because $a = \alpha$ and $a < 0$, choose $\alpha = -4$, giving $a = -4$, $b = 2$, $c = 6$, and $a + b + c = 4$.

Step 3: Verify the point and gradient alignment. Plug $(-4, 2, 6)$ into the surface equation and gradient: $$\begin{aligned} (-4)^2 + 4(2)^2 - 6^2 &= 16 + 16 - 36 = -4 \\ \nabla F(-4, 2, 6) &= \langle -8, 16, -12 \rangle = -4\langle 2, -4, 3 \rangle \end{aligned}$$
$y=2$ cross-section $z^2 - x^2 = 20$ Exact tangent $2x + 3z = 10$ at $x=-4, z=6$ Gradient $\langle -8, 16, -12 \rangle$ parallel to $\langle 2, -4, 3 \rangle$

Cross-section at y equals 2 showing the negative-x point (-4, 2, 6) on the upper hyperbola branch, where the tangent line has an exact slope of negative two-thirds matching the target plane.

Answer: $(a, b, c) = (-4, 2, 6)$, so $a + b + c = 4$.
KFUPM Final Term 242, Q9
One-Screen Summary

The 5 Things to Know for the Exam

  1. Move all terms to one side ($F(x, y, z) = 0$) before taking $\nabla F$: The normal to $z = f(x, y)$ at $(x_0, y_0, z_0)$ is $\langle f_x, f_y, -1 \rangle$ — never $+1$ — and you must plug in $(x_0, y_0, z_0)$ so your plane equation has numerical coefficients.
  2. Match the exact constant or coefficient requested: If a KFUPM question gives $ax + by + cz + 1 = 0$, rescale your entire tangent plane equation until the constant term matches $+1$ before summing $a, b, c$.
  3. Surface intersection tangent line = cross product of both gradients: Write both surfaces as $F=0$ and $G=0$, evaluate at $P_0$, and take $\mathbf{v} = \nabla F \times \nabla G$ (scaling out common factors is always legal).
  4. Angle of inclination $\theta \in [0, \tfrac{\pi}{2}]$ uses $\cos\theta$ and $|F_z|$: Check $F_z = 0$ (vertical wall, $\theta = \tfrac{\pi}{2}$) and $F_x = F_y = 0$ (horizontal plane, $\theta = 0$), and compute: $$\cos\theta = \frac{|F_z(P_0)|}{\|\nabla F(P_0)\|}$$
  5. Finding an unknown point $(a, b, c)$ for horizontal, parallel, or perpendicular planes: Solve $\nabla F = \alpha\,\mathbf{n}$ (never omit $\alpha$), plug into the surface equation to find $\alpha$, and apply any sign constraint ($a < 0$ or $a > 0$).

What You Already Know

In Calculus I, a function $y = f(x)$ can have a relative extremum only at a critical number where $f'(c) = 0$ or $f'(c)$ does not exist, and the Second Derivative Test uses the sign of $f''(c)$ to tell peaks from valleys. On a closed interval $[a, b]$, the Extreme Value Theorem guarantees an absolute maximum and minimum found by comparing critical values with endpoints.

In Section 13.7, you saw that a smooth surface $z = f(x, y)$ has a horizontal tangent plane precisely when $f_x(x_0, y_0) = 0$ and $f_y(x_0, y_0) = 0$. Section 13.8 turns those ideas into a complete toolkit for optimizing surfaces in 3D.

Core Concept • §1

1. Relative Extrema & Critical Points ($f_x = f_y = 0$ or DNE)

Intuition: Think of standing on a hilly terrain $z = f(x, y)$. A relative maximum is a hilltop higher than every point in a small circular disk around your feet, while a relative minimum is the bottom of a bowl lower than all nearby points.

At any hilltop or bowl bottom, either the ground flattens completely (a horizontal tangent plane, $f_x = 0$ and $f_y = 0$) or the surface comes to a sharp tip or ridge where at least one slope fails to exist.

Note (Instructor Notes vs. Book): Dr. Alhumaidy’s notes write $= 0$ or $\text{DNE}$ right next to the partial derivatives so you never forget undefined points, and highlight a sharp warning (?!!) on cusp problems: having only one partial equal to zero (like $f_x = 0$ along the $y$-axis) does not create a critical point unless the other partial is also zero or one of them does not exist. Always distinguish the critical point $(x_0, y_0)$ from the extreme value $f(x_0, y_0)$. Textbook p. 942 & Instructor Notes
Smooth slice $y=3$ of paraboloid Cusp slice $y=0$ of radial cusp Horizontal tangent vs. vertical cusp Critical point $(x_0, y_0, z_0)$

Cross-sections comparing two critical point types: a smooth valley with a horizontal tangent plane where both first partial derivatives are zero, and a sharp radial cusp where the partial derivatives fail to exist.

Definition: Relative Extrema

Let $f$ be a function defined on a region $R$ containing $(x_0, y_0)$.

1. The function $f$ has a relative minimum at $(x_0, y_0)$ if for all $(x, y)$ in an open disk containing $(x_0, y_0)$:

$$f(x, y) \ge f(x_0, y_0)$$

2. The function $f$ has a relative maximum at $(x_0, y_0)$ if for all $(x, y)$ in an open disk containing $(x_0, y_0)$:

$$f(x, y) \le f(x_0, y_0)$$ Textbook p. 940, Definition of Relative Extrema
Definition: Critical Point

Let $f$ be defined on an open region $R$ containing $(x_0, y_0)$. The point $(x_0, y_0)$ is a critical point of $f$ if one of the following is true:

Condition 1 (both first partials vanish):

$$\begin{aligned} f_x(x_0, y_0) &= 0 \\ f_y(x_0, y_0) &= 0 \end{aligned}$$

Condition 2 (at least one first partial fails to exist):

$f_x(x_0, y_0)$ does not exist, or $f_y(x_0, y_0)$ does not exist.

Textbook p. 941, Definition of Critical Point
Theorem 13.16: Relative Extrema Occur Only at Critical Points

If $f$ has a relative extremum at $(x_0, y_0)$ on an open region $R$, then $(x_0, y_0)$ is a critical point of $f$.

Textbook p. 941, Theorem 13.16
Example: Relative Extremum at an Undefined-Partial Cusp
Find the relative extrema of $$f(x, y) = 1 - (x^2 + y^2)^{1/3}.$$
Step 1: Compute both first partial derivatives. Differentiate with respect to $x$ and $y$ using the Chain Rule: $$\begin{aligned} f_x(x, y) &= -\frac{2x}{3(x^2 + y^2)^{2/3}} \\ f_y(x, y) &= -\frac{2y}{3(x^2 + y^2)^{2/3}} \end{aligned}$$
Step 2: Locate all critical points. Both partial derivatives exist everywhere except at $(0, 0)$, where the denominator is $0$ (DNE), so $(0, 0)$ is a critical point. Note that along the $y$-axis ($x = 0, y \neq 0$), $f_x = 0$ but $f_y \neq 0$, so those points are not critical points; thus $(0, 0)$ is the only critical point.
Step 3: Verify the result by direct inequality comparison. Since $x^2 + y^2 > 0$ for every $(x, y) \neq (0, 0)$, the cube root satisfies $(x^2 + y^2)^{1/3} > 0$, giving: $$f(x, y) = 1 - (x^2 + y^2)^{1/3} < 1 = f(0, 0)$$ This confirms $f$ achieves a relative (and absolute) maximum at $(0, 0)$.
Answer: $$\text{Relative maximum at } (0, 0) \text{ with value } f(0, 0) = 1.$$
Textbook p. 942, Example 2 & Instructor Notes
Why It Works: Slicing Along Coordinate Lines Forces Critical Points

Suppose $f$ has a relative extremum at $(x_0, y_0)$ on an open disk. Fixing $y = y_0$ gives a 1-variable function $g(x) = f(x, y_0)$ with a relative extremum at $x_0$, so by Calculus I either $g'(x_0) = f_x(x_0, y_0) = 0$ or $f_x(x_0, y_0)$ does not exist.

Repeating the same slice along $x = x_0$ requires $f_y(x_0, y_0) = 0$ or DNE, which makes $(x_0, y_0)$ a critical point:

$$\begin{aligned} f_x(x_0, y_0) &= 0 \text{ (or DNE)} \\ f_y(x_0, y_0) &= 0 \text{ (or DNE)} \end{aligned}$$
Quick Check 1

Consider the function defined by:

$$f(x, y) = \sqrt[3]{x^2 + y^2} + 2$$

Which statement describes the extrema of $f$?

(A) a saddle point at $(0, 0)$
(B) no critical points and no extrema
(C) a relative maximum at $(0, 0)$
(D) a relative minimum at $(0, 0)$
Check Answer & Reason

Answer: (D). Both first partial derivatives fail to exist at $(0, 0)$:

$$\begin{aligned} f_x(x, y) &= \frac{2x}{3(x^2 + y^2)^{2/3}} \\ f_y(x, y) &= \frac{2y}{3(x^2 + y^2)^{2/3}} \end{aligned}$$

Thus $(0, 0)$ is a critical point. Since $x^2 + y^2 \ge 0$ everywhere, we have:

$$f(x, y) = \sqrt[3]{x^2 + y^2} + 2 \ge 2 = f(0, 0)$$

Therefore, $f$ has a relative minimum at $(0, 0)$.

KFUPM Final Term 241, Q9 & Textbook p. 946, Exercise 20
Core Concept • §2

2. Saddle Points & The Second Partials Test

Intuition: Finding $\nabla f = \mathbf{0}$ only hands you suspects — not every flat point is a peak or valley. On the hyperbolic paraboloid $f(x, y) = y^2 - x^2$, moving along the $y$-axis goes uphill ($f_{yy} = 2 > 0$), while moving along the $x$-axis goes downhill ($f_{xx} = -2 < 0$), creating a saddle point at $(0, 0, 0)$.

Even more subtly, if $f_{xx}$ and $f_{yy}$ have the same sign, a strong mixed cross-twist $f_{xy}$ can still bend a diagonal slice the opposite way. The discriminant $D = f_{xx}f_{yy} - [f_{xy}]^2$ compares pure curvature ($f_{xx}f_{yy}$) against squared diagonal twist ($[f_{xy}]^2$).

Note (Instructor Notes vs. Book): Larson writes lowercase $d$ for the Second Partials Test discriminant, whereas Dr. Alhumaidy’s notes consistently write uppercase $D$ and organize every problem in a structured table: Critical Point | $f_{xx}$ | $f_{yy}$ | $f_{xy}$ | $D$. Dr. Alhumaidy also classifies quadratic polynomials such as $2x^2+y^2+8x-6y+20$ directly with this $D$-table rather than completing the square. Textbook p. 943 & Instructor Notes
Increasing / $+$ level contours Decreasing outward contours Negative saddle branches ($-$) Critical point $(a, b)$

Contour behavior around a smooth critical point: a positive discriminant forces closed elliptical contours around a bowl or dome, whereas a negative discriminant forces hyperbolic cross-contours of opposite signs.

Theorem 13.17: Second Partials Test

Let $f$ have continuous second partial derivatives on an open region containing a point $(a, b)$ for which $f_x(a, b) = 0$ and $f_y(a, b) = 0$. Define the discriminant:

$$D = f_{xx}(a, b)\,f_{yy}(a, b) - \big[f_{xy}(a, b)\big]^2 = \begin{vmatrix} f_{xx}(a, b) & f_{xy}(a, b) \\ f_{yx}(a, b) & f_{yy}(a, b) \end{vmatrix}$$
  • Case 1: If $D > 0$ and $f_{xx}(a, b) > 0$, then $f$ has a relative minimum at $(a, b)$.
  • Case 2: If $D > 0$ and $f_{xx}(a, b) < 0$, then $f$ has a relative maximum at $(a, b)$.
  • Case 3: If $D < 0$, then $\big(a, b, f(a, b)\big)$ is a saddle point.
  • Case 4: If $D = 0$, the test is inconclusive.

Remark: Whenever $D > 0$, the second partials must satisfy:

$$f_{xx}(a, b)\,f_{yy}(a, b) > \big[f_{xy}(a, b)\big]^2 \ge 0$$

Hence $f_{xx}(a, b)$ and $f_{yy}(a, b)$ have the same sign, so either one can be checked in Cases 1 and 2.

Textbook p. 943, Theorem 13.17
Example: Classifying a Saddle Point Where Pure Second Partials Vanish
Classify all critical points of $$z = f(x, y) = e^{xy}.$$
Step 1: Set both first partial derivatives equal to zero. Compute the first partials: $$\begin{aligned} f_x(x, y) &= y e^{xy} = 0 \\ f_y(x, y) &= x e^{xy} = 0 \end{aligned}$$ Since $e^{xy} > 0$ for all $(x, y)$, the unique critical point is $(0, 0)$.
Step 2: Compute second partials and evaluate $D(0, 0)$. Differentiate again to find the three second partial derivatives: $$\begin{aligned} f_{xx}(x, y) &= y^2 e^{xy} \\ f_{yy}(x, y) &= x^2 e^{xy} \\ f_{xy}(x, y) &= (1 + xy)e^{xy} \end{aligned}$$ At $(0, 0)$, we have $f_{xx}(0, 0) = 0$, $f_{yy}(0, 0) = 0$, and $f_{xy}(0, 0) = 1$, giving: $$D(0, 0) = (0)(0) - 1^2 = -1 < 0$$
Step 3: Verify the result along two diagonal slices. Along $y = x$, $f(x, x) = e^{x^2} > 1$ for $x \neq 0$; along $y = -x$, $f(x, -x) = e^{-x^2} < 1$ for $x \neq 0$, confirming that $f$ both rises above and falls below $f(0, 0) = 1$ near $(0, 0)$.
Answer: $$\text{Saddle point at } (0, 0, 1) \text{ (no relative extrema).}$$
Textbook p. 946, Exercise 28 & Instructor Notes
Why It Works: Completing the Square in the Quadratic Taylor Form

Near $(a, b)$ where $f_x = f_y = 0$, the second-degree Taylor change for small steps $(h, k)$ is:

$$\Delta f \approx \frac{1}{2}\big(f_{xx}h^2 + 2f_{xy}hk + f_{yy}k^2\big)$$

Completing the square in $h$ (assuming $f_{xx} \neq 0$) rewrites this change in terms of $D = f_{xx}f_{yy} - [f_{xy}]^2$:

$$\Delta f \approx \frac{1}{2f_{xx}}\Big[\big(f_{xx}h + f_{xy}k\big)^2 + D\,k^2\Big]$$

When $D > 0$, the bracket is strictly positive for all $(h, k) \neq (0, 0)$, so $\Delta f$ always keeps the sign of $f_{xx}$. When $D < 0$, moving along $k = 0$ gives the sign of $f_{xx}$ while moving along $f_{xx}h + f_{xy}k = 0$ gives the opposite sign, producing a saddle.

Quick Check 2

Suppose $f$ has continuous second partials near critical point $(3, 7)$, where $f_{xx}(3, 7) = 2$ and $f_{yy}(3, 7) = 8$. If $f$ has a relative minimum at $(3, 7)$ with $D > 0$, what is the interval of possible values for $f_{xy}(3, 7)$?

(A) $(-4, 4)$
(B) $(-\infty, -4) \cup (4, \infty)$
(C) $(-16, 16)$
(D) $(0, 4)$
Check Answer & Reason

Answer: (A). For $D > 0$ at $(3, 7)$, we require:

$$\begin{aligned} D &= f_{xx}(3, 7)\,f_{yy}(3, 7) - \big[f_{xy}(3, 7)\big]^2 > 0 \\ 2(8) - \big[f_{xy}(3, 7)\big]^2 &> 0 \\ \big[f_{xy}(3, 7)\big]^2 &< 16 \\ -4 &< f_{xy}(3, 7) < 4 \end{aligned}$$
Textbook p. 947, Exercise 49
Core Concept • §3

3. When the Second Partials Test Fails ($D = 0$ or Partials DNE)

Intuition: The Second Partials Test fails in two exact situations: (1) either first partial derivative does not exist at $(a, b)$, or (2) $D(a, b) = 0$. When $D = 0$, the surface could still be a bowl, a dome, or a saddle — you must return to the definition of relative extrema and test the sign of $f(x, y) - f(a, b)$ directly around $(a, b)$.

Region where $f(x,y) - f(a,b) > 0$ Region where $f(x,y) - f(a,b) < 0$ Zero-level boundary $y = -x$

Sign charts for two critical cases where the discriminant equals zero: a product of squares stays nonnegative around the coordinate axes to form an absolute minimum, while a sum of cubes changes sign across a diagonal line and has no extremum.

Direct Analysis Rules When $D = 0$ or Partials DNE:

  • Prove an extremum: Rewrite $f(x, y) - f(a, b)$ as a sum of squares, even powers, or clearly nonnegative terms (such as $x^2 y^2 \ge 0$, $(x^2+y^2)^{1/3} \ge 0$, or $x^{2/3}+y^{2/3} \ge 0$) to prove $f(x, y) \ge f(a, b)$ or $f(x, y) \le f(a, b)$ on an open disk.
  • Disprove an extremum: Find two paths through $(a, b)$ (such as $y = x$ and $y = -x$, or positive vs. negative values of a parameter) on which $f(x, y) - f(a, b)$ takes opposite signs arbitrarily close to $(a, b)$.
Example: Resolving an Inconclusive Discriminant $D = 0$
Find the relative extrema of $$f(x, y) = x^2 y^2.$$
Step 1: Find all critical points. Set both first partial derivatives equal to zero: $$\begin{aligned} f_x(x, y) &= 2xy^2 = 0 \\ f_y(x, y) &= 2x^2y = 0 \end{aligned}$$ Both equations hold whenever $x = 0$ or $y = 0$, so every point on the $x$-axis or $y$-axis is a critical point.
Step 2: Apply the Second Partials Test. Compute the second partials ($f_{xx} = 2y^2$, $f_{yy} = 2x^2$, $f_{xy} = 4xy$) and evaluate the discriminant: $$D(x, y) = (2y^2)(2x^2) - (4xy)^2 = -12x^2y^2$$ Whenever $x = 0$ or $y = 0$, we get $D(x, y) = 0$, so the Second Partials Test fails at every critical point.
Step 3: Verify the result by direct sign comparison. At any point $(x_0, y_0)$ on either axis, $f(x_0, y_0) = 0$. Off the axes, squares are strictly positive so $f(x, y) = x^2y^2 > 0$, confirming $f(x, y) \ge 0$ everywhere.
Answer: $$\text{Every point on the } x\text{- and } y\text{-axes yields a relative (and absolute) minimum of } 0.$$
Textbook p. 944, Example 4
Why It Works: Higher-Order Terms Govern $D = 0$ Behavior

The Second Partials Test only examines quadratic (degree-2) curvature around $(a, b)$. When $D = 0$, quadratic curvature vanishes along at least one direction, so higher-order terms control the surface shape:

$$\Delta f = f(x, y) - f(a, b)$$

Direct inequality comparison checks the exact definition of relative extrema using those higher-degree terms without relying on second derivatives.

Quick Check 3

For $f(x, y) = x^3 + y^3$, the only critical point is $(0, 0)$, where $D(0, 0) = 0$. What is true at $(0, 0)$?

(A) $f$ has a relative minimum at $(0, 0)$
(B) $f$ has a relative maximum at $(0, 0)$
(C) $f$ has neither a relative maximum nor a relative minimum at $(0, 0)$
(D) $(0, 0)$ is not a critical point because $D = 0$
Check Answer & Reason

Answer: (C). Along the line $y = x$, we get:

$$f(x, x) = 2x^3$$

This is positive for $x > 0$ and negative for $x < 0$, so every open disk centered at $(0, 0)$ contains points above and below $f(0, 0) = 0$.

Textbook p. 947, Exercise 35
Core Concept • §4

4. Absolute Extrema on Closed Bounded Regions

Intuition: Suppose you fence off a finite closed patch $R$ of the $xy$-plane (such as a rectangle, triangle, or parabolic lens containing all its border curves). By the Extreme Value Theorem, any continuous function $f(x, y)$ must reach an absolute maximum $M$ and an absolute minimum $m$ somewhere on $R$.

Just like Calculus I on $[a, b]$, those extreme values can happen at an interior critical point, along a boundary curve (found by 1D calculus after plugging in the curve’s equation), or at a corner vertex where two boundary curves meet.

Note (Instructor Notes vs. Book): In handwritten solutions for rectangular, triangular, and parabolic regions, Dr. Alhumaidy enforces a strict 3-step exam routine: (1) always sketch $R$ and mark its corners; (2) cross out (outside $\times$) any critical point of $f$ or of a boundary edge that falls outside $R$; and (3) collect all surviving interior, boundary, and corner points in a single candidate table $(x_0, y_0) \mid f(x_0, y_0)$ to read off $M$ and $m$ without using $D$. Instructor Notes
Interior critical point $(0, 1)$ Top edge $y=4$ & critical point $(0, 4)$ Parabolic edge $y=x^2$ & $(\pm\tfrac{1}{2}, \tfrac{1}{4})$ Corners $(\pm 2, 4)$ attaining $M = 28$

Closed bounded region between the upward parabola and the horizontal top line: testing the interior critical point, both boundary curves, and the corner vertices guarantees that no absolute extremum is missed.

Theorem 13.15: Extreme Value Theorem

Let $f$ be a continuous function of two variables $x$ and $y$ defined on a closed bounded region $R$ in the $xy$-plane (meaning $R$ contains all its boundary points and is a subregion of a closed disk).

1. There is at least one point $(a, b) \in R$ at which $f$ takes on a minimum value.

2. There is at least one point $(c, d) \in R$ at which $f$ takes on a maximum value.

$$f(a, b) \le f(x, y) \le f(c, d) \quad \text{for all } (x, y) \in R$$ Textbook p. 940, Theorem 13.15

3-Step Candidate Procedure: For a continuous function $f(x, y)$ on a closed bounded region $R$:

  1. Interior Critical Points: Solve $f_x = 0, f_y = 0$ (and check where partials DNE). Keep only points strictly inside $R$; discard any point outside $R$.
  2. Boundary Curve Critical Points: For each piece of the boundary (horizontal/vertical lines, slanted segments, or curves like $y = x^2$), substitute the boundary equation into $f(x, y)$ to obtain a 1-variable function $g(t)$ on a closed interval, then solve $g'(t) = 0$ (or DNE) inside that interval.
  3. Corners & Candidate Table: Collect all boundary intersection corners/endpoints together with the surviving points from Steps 1–2, evaluate $f(x, y)$ at every candidate, and read off the largest value (absolute maximum) and smallest value (absolute minimum).
Example: Absolute Extrema on a Closed Rectangle
Find the absolute extrema of $$f(x, y) = \sin(xy)$$ on the closed rectangular region $$R = \{(x, y) : 0 \le x \le \pi,\; 0 \le y \le 1\}.$$
Step 1: Find interior critical points of $f$. Set both first partial derivatives equal to zero: $$\begin{aligned} f_x(x, y) &= y\cos(xy) = 0 \\ f_y(x, y) &= x\cos(xy) = 0 \end{aligned}$$ This yields the corner point $(0, 0)$ and every point along the hyperbola $xy = \tfrac{\pi}{2}$ inside $R$, where: $$f(x, y) = \sin\frac{\pi}{2} = 1$$
Step 2: Check all four boundary edges and corners.
  • Along $x = 0$ or $y = 0$, $f(x, y) = \sin(0) = 0$.
  • Along $y = 1$ ($0 \le x \le \pi$), $g_1(x) = \sin x$ has $g_1'(x) = \cos x = 0$ at $x = \tfrac{\pi}{2}$, giving $f(\tfrac{\pi}{2}, 1) = 1$, and endpoints $(0, 1)$ and $(\pi, 1)$ give $0$.
  • Along $x = \pi$ ($0 \le y \le 1$), $g_2(y) = \sin(\pi y)$ has $g_2'(y) = \pi\cos(\pi y) = 0$ at $y = \tfrac{1}{2}$, giving $f(\pi, \tfrac{1}{2}) = 1$, and endpoints $(\pi, 0)$ and $(\pi, 1)$ give $0$.
Step 3: Verify the result using global range bounds on $R$. Because $0 \le x \le \pi$ and $0 \le y \le 1$, their product satisfies $0 \le xy \le \pi$, which guarantees $0 \le \sin(xy) \le 1$ throughout $R$.
Answer:

The absolute maximum is $M = 1$ along the curve:

$$xy = \frac{\pi}{2} \quad (0 \le x \le \pi,\; 0 \le y \le 1)$$

The absolute minimum is $m = 0$ along the $x$- and $y$-axes and at the corner $(\pi, 1)$.

Textbook p. 945, Example 5
Why It Works: Interior Critical Points Plus 1D Boundary Calculus Cover Every Possibility

A closed bounded region $R$ contains its boundary and fits inside a closed disk, so Theorem 13.15 guarantees $f$ attains both $M$ and $m$ on $R$. Any extremum in the open interior must satisfy Theorem 13.16 ($f_x = f_y = 0$ or DNE).

Any extremum on a boundary arc is a 1D extremum on a closed interval, which occurs either at an endpoint (corner) or where the 1D derivative along that curve vanishes.

Quick Check 4

When finding the absolute extrema of $f(x, y) = x^2 - 4xy + 5$ on the closed rectangle:

$$R = \{(x, y) : 1 \le x \le 4,\; 0 \le y \le 2\}$$

What should you do with the critical point $(0, 0)$ obtained from $f_x = 0$ and $f_y = 0$?

(A) Test $(0, 0)$ with the Second Partials Test $D$
(B) Discard $(0, 0)$ because $(0, 0) \notin R$
(C) Include $(0, 0)$ in the candidate table because $f(0, 0) = 5$
(D) Replace $(0, 0)$ with $(1, 0)$ automatically
Check Answer & Reason

Answer: (B). Since $R$ requires $1 \le x \le 4$, the point $(0, 0)$ lies outside the region $R$ and cannot be an extremum of $f$ on $R$.

Textbook p. 947, Exercise 39; Instructor Notes & KFUPM Final Term 232, Q14
Master Formulas

Section 13.8 Formula Reference & Edge Cases

Master Reference: Critical Points, Classification & Shortcuts
  • Critical Points on an Open Region $R$: $(x_0, y_0) \in R$ is critical if $f_x(x_0, y_0) = 0$ and $f_y(x_0, y_0) = 0$, or if $f_x(x_0, y_0)$ or $f_y(x_0, y_0)$ does not exist.
  • Second Partials Test Discriminant (at smooth critical point $(a, b)$): $$D = f_{xx}(a, b)\,f_{yy}(a, b) - \big[f_{xy}(a, b)\big]^2$$
    • $D > 0$ and $f_{xx}(a, b) > 0$ (equivalently $f_{yy} > 0$) $\implies$ Relative Minimum at $(a, b)$.
    • $D > 0$ and $f_{xx}(a, b) < 0$ (equivalently $f_{yy} < 0$) $\implies$ Relative Maximum at $(a, b)$.
    • $D < 0$ $\implies$ Saddle Point at $\big(a, b, f(a, b)\big)$.
    • $D = 0$ $\implies$ Inconclusive (use direct inequality, completing the square, or 2-path test).
  • Absolute Extrema on Closed & Bounded $R$: Evaluate $f$ at all interior critical points inside $R$, all 1D boundary curve critical points inside each edge interval, and all corners/vertices.
  • Functions of $n$ Variables: When all first partials of $w = f(x_1, \dots, x_n)$ exist, critical points satisfy: $$f_{x_1} = f_{x_2} = \dots = f_{x_n} = 0$$
  • Quick Saddle Shortcut: If $f_{xx}(a, b)$ and $f_{yy}(a, b)$ have opposite signs at a critical point (or $f_{xx} = f_{yy} = 0$ with $f_{xy} \neq 0$), then $D < 0$ automatically — guaranteed saddle point!
Textbook pp. 940–947
Exam Traps

5 Classic Mistakes (WRONG vs. RIGHT)

Trap 1 — Calling a point critical when only ONE partial is zero:

WrongSetting $f_x = 0$ alone and listing all points on the $y$-axis for $1 - (x^2+y^2)^{1/3}$ as critical points.
RightRequire both $f_x = 0$ AND $f_y = 0$ simultaneously (or at least one partial DNE).

Trap 2 — Ignoring points where $f_x$ or $f_y$ does not exist (or plugging them into $D$):

WrongSaying $f(x, y) = (x^2 + y^2)^{1/3} + 2$ has no extrema because $f_x = 0, f_y = 0$ has no solution.
RightCheck where denominators vanish: $(0, 0)$ is critical (partials DNE), and $(x^2+y^2)^{1/3} \ge 0$ gives a rel. min directly.

Trap 3 — Confusing $D > 0$ signs or ignoring $-[f_{xy}]^2$:

WrongConcluding $f_{xx} > 0, f_{yy} > 0 \implies$ relative minimum without computing $D$, or thinking $f_{xx} > 0$ means maximum.
RightAlways compute $D = f_{xx}f_{yy} - [f_{xy}]^2$: $D > 0, f_{xx} > 0 \implies$ min (cup up); $D > 0, f_{xx} < 0 \implies$ max (cup down); $D < 0 \implies$ saddle.

Trap 4 — Including interior critical points that lie outside $R$:

WrongEvaluating $f(0, 0) = 5$ in the absolute extrema table for $1 \le x \le 4$ and $0 \le y \le 2$.
RightVerify every critical point against ALL inequalities defining $R$ (here $x = 0 < 1$, so $(0, 0) \notin R$ and must be rejected).

Trap 5 — Only checking corners of $R$ and skipping boundary interior critical points:

WrongPlugging only the 4 rectangle corners into $f(x, y) = x^2 + xy$ on $|x| \le 2, |y| \le 1$ (missing $m = -\tfrac{1}{4}$!).
RightSubstitute each edge equation into $f$ (e.g., $y=1 \implies x^2+x$), solve $g'(t) = 0$, and add those edge points to the candidate table.
Worked Examples

From Textbook Basics to KFUPM Final Level

Example: Finding Relative Extrema and Saddle Points via the $D$-Table
Find all relative extrema and saddle points of $$f(x, y) = -x^3 + 4xy - 2y^2 + 1.$$
Step 1: Solve $f_x = 0$ and $f_y = 0$ for critical points. Because $f$ is a polynomial, $f_x$ and $f_y$ exist everywhere: $$\begin{cases} f_x(x, y) = -3x^2 + 4y = 0 & (1) \\ f_y(x, y) = 4x - 4y = 0 & (2) \end{cases}$$ From $(2)$, $4(x - y) = 0 \implies y = x$. Substitute $y = x$ into $(1)$: $$\begin{aligned} -3x^2 + 4x &= 0 \\ x(4 - 3x) &= 0 \end{aligned}$$ This gives $x = 0$ or $x = \tfrac{4}{3}$. Since $y = x$, the two critical points are $(0, 0)$ and $(\tfrac{4}{3}, \tfrac{4}{3})$.
Step 2: Compute second partials and evaluate the discriminant $D$. Differentiate $f_x$ and $f_y$ to form $D(x, y) = f_{xx}f_{yy} - (f_{xy})^2$: $$\begin{aligned} f_{xx}(x, y) &= -6x \\ f_{yy}(x, y) &= -4 \\ f_{xy}(x, y) &= 4 \\ D(x, y) &= (-6x)(-4) - 4^2 = 24x - 16 \end{aligned}$$
  • At $(0, 0)$: $f_{xx} = 0$, $f_{yy} = -4$, $f_{xy} = 4$, so $D = 0(-4) - 16 = -16 < 0$, giving a saddle point at $(0, 0, 1)$.
  • At $(\tfrac{4}{3}, \tfrac{4}{3})$: $f_{xx} = -8$, $f_{yy} = -4$, $f_{xy} = 4$, so $D = (-8)(-4) - 16 = 16 > 0$. Since $D > 0$ and $f_{xx} = -8 < 0$, this is a relative maximum.
Evaluate the maximum value: $$f\!\left(\frac{4}{3}, \frac{4}{3}\right) = -\left(\frac{4}{3}\right)^3 + 4\left(\frac{4}{3}\right)^2 - 2\left(\frac{4}{3}\right)^2 + 1 = -\frac{64}{27} + \frac{32}{9} + 1 = \frac{59}{27}$$
Step 3: Verify the result along the diagonal slice $y = x$. Let $g(x) = f(x, x) = -x^3 + 2x^2 + 1$, so $g'(x) = -3x^2 + 4x$ and $g''(x) = -6x + 4$. At $x = \tfrac{4}{3}$, $g''(\tfrac{4}{3}) = -4 < 0$ (concave down at the maximum), whereas at $x = 0$, $g''(0) = 4 > 0$ (concave up along $y = x$, opposite to $f_{yy} = -4 < 0$ along $x = 0$, confirming the saddle at $(0, 0)$).
Answer:

Saddle point at $(0, 0, 1)$, and relative maximum at:

$$f\!\left(\frac{4}{3}, \frac{4}{3}\right) = \frac{59}{27}$$
Textbook p. 944, Example 3 & Instructor Notes
Example: Eliminating Cross Terms to Find Two Saddle Points
Determine the number and type of relative extrema and saddle points of the function $$f(x, y) = 4 + x - y - x^2 y + x y^2.$$
Step 1: Set first partial derivatives to zero and add equations. Because $f$ is a polynomial, critical points occur where both first partials vanish: $$\begin{cases} f_x(x, y) = 1 - 2xy + y^2 = 0 & (1) \\ f_y(x, y) = -1 - x^2 + 2xy = 0 & (2) \end{cases}$$ Adding $(1)$ and $(2)$ cancels both the constants and $\pm 2xy$: $$\begin{aligned} (1 - 2xy + y^2) + (-1 - x^2 + 2xy) &= 0 \\ y^2 - x^2 &= 0 \\ (y - x)(y + x) &= 0 \end{aligned}$$
Step 2: Solve both branches $y = x$ and $y = -x$.
  • Case 1 ($y = x$): Substitute into $(1)$ to get $1 - 2x^2 + x^2 = 1 - x^2 = 0$, so $x = \pm 1$. This gives $(1, 1)$ and $(-1, -1)$ (both satisfy $(2)$).
  • Case 2 ($y = -x$): Substitute into $(1)$ to get $1 - 2x(-x) + (-x)^2 = 1 + 3x^2 = 0$, which has no real solution since $1 + 3x^2 \ge 1 > 0$.
Step 3: Apply the Second Partials Test. Compute the second partial derivatives and discriminant: $$\begin{aligned} f_{xx}(x, y) &= -2y \\ f_{yy}(x, y) &= 2x \\ f_{xy}(x, y) &= -2x + 2y \\ D(x, y) &= (-2y)(2x) - (-2x + 2y)^2 = -4xy - 4(y - x)^2 \end{aligned}$$ At $(1, 1)$: $D(1, 1) = -4(1)(1) - 0 = -4 < 0$ (saddle point). At $(-1, -1)$: $D(-1, -1) = -4(-1)(-1) - 0 = -4 < 0$ (saddle point).
Step 4: Verify the result using opposite signs of pure curvature. At $(1, 1)$, $f_{xx} = -2 < 0$ and $f_{yy} = 2 > 0$; at $(-1, -1)$, $f_{xx} = 2 > 0$ and $f_{yy} = -2 < 0$. Because $f_{xx}$ and $f_{yy}$ have opposite signs at both critical points, $D = f_{xx}f_{yy} - [f_{xy}]^2$ is guaranteed negative.
Answer:

Two saddle points at $(1, 1)$ and $(-1, -1)$, and no relative extrema:

$$D(1, 1) = D(-1, -1) = -4 < 0$$
KFUPM Final Term 253, Q12
Example: Factored Partial Derivatives Yielding Mixed Critical Points
Classify all critical points of $$f(x, y) = \frac{1}{3}x^3 - x^2 + (x - 1)y^2.$$
Step 1: Factor $f_y = 0$ carefully to avoid missing branches. Compute the first partial derivatives and set both to zero: $$\begin{aligned} f_x(x, y) &= x^2 - 2x + y^2 = 0 \\ f_y(x, y) &= 2(x - 1)y = 0 \end{aligned}$$ From $2(x - 1)y = 0$, either $y = 0$ or $x = 1$:
  • If $y = 0$: $$f_x = x^2 - 2x = x(x - 2) = 0$$ This gives $x = 0$ or $x = 2$, yielding $(0, 0)$ and $(2, 0)$.
  • If $x = 1$: $$f_x = 1 - 2 + y^2 = 0 \implies y^2 = 1$$ This gives $y = \pm 1$, yielding $(1, 1)$ and $(1, -1)$.
Step 2: Classify all four critical points via $D$. Compute the second partials and discriminant: $$\begin{aligned} f_{xx}(x, y) &= 2(x - 1) \\ f_{yy}(x, y) &= 2(x - 1) \\ f_{xy}(x, y) &= 2y \\ D(x, y) &= 4(x - 1)^2 - 4y^2 \end{aligned}$$
  • At $(0, 0)$: $D = 4(-1)^2 - 0 = 4 > 0$ and $f_{xx}(0, 0) = -2 < 0 \implies$ Relative maximum.
  • At $(2, 0)$: $D = 4(1)^2 - 0 = 4 > 0$ and $f_{xx}(2, 0) = 2 > 0 \implies$ Relative minimum.
  • At $(1, 1)$: $D = 0 - 4(1)^2 = -4 < 0 \implies$ Saddle point.
  • At $(1, -1)$: $D = 0 - 4(-1)^2 = -4 < 0 \implies$ Saddle point.
Step 3: Verify the result along $y = 0$ and at $(1, \pm 1)$. Along $y = 0$, $f(x, 0) = \tfrac{1}{3}x^3 - x^2$ indeed has a local maximum at $x = 0$ and local minimum at $x = 2$. At $(1, \pm 1)$, $f_{xx} = f_{yy} = 0$ while $f_{xy} = \pm 2 \neq 0$, ensuring $D = -[f_{xy}]^2 = -4 < 0$.
Answer:
  • Two saddle points at $(1, 1)$ and $(1, -1)$
  • One relative maximum at $(0, 0)$
  • One relative minimum at $(2, 0)$
$$\text{Total: } 2 \text{ saddles, } 1 \text{ relative max, } 1 \text{ relative min.}$$
KFUPM Final Term 252, Q10
Example: Absolute Extrema on the Parabolic Region $y = x^2$ to $y = 4$
Find the absolute maximum and absolute minimum values of $$f(x, y) = 3x^2 + 2y^2 - 4y$$ over the closed region $R$ in the $xy$-plane bounded by the graphs of $y = x^2$ and $y = 4$.
Step 1: Describe region $R$ and check interior critical points. Setting $x^2 = 4$ gives corners $(-2, 4)$ and $(2, 4)$, so the closed region is: $$R = \{(x, y) : -2 \le x \le 2,\; x^2 \le y \le 4\}$$ Solve $\nabla f = \mathbf{0}$ inside $R$: $$\begin{aligned} f_x &= 6x = 0 \implies x = 0 \\ f_y &= 4y - 4 = 0 \implies y = 1 \end{aligned}$$ Since $0^2 = 0 < 1 < 4$, $(0, 1)$ lies strictly inside $R$ with $f(0, 1) = 0 + 2 - 4 = -2$.
Step 2: Optimize $f$ along both boundary curves.

On the top segment ($y = 4$, $-2 \le x \le 2$):

$$g_1(x) = f(x, 4) = 3x^2 + 2(16) - 4(4) = 3x^2 + 16$$

Setting $g_1'(x) = 6x = 0$ gives $x = 0$, so $(0, 4)$ yields $f(0, 4) = 16$, while endpoints $x = \pm 2$ yield $f(\pm 2, 4) = 3(4) + 16 = 28$.

On the parabolic arc ($y = x^2$, $-2 \le x \le 2$):

$$\begin{aligned} g_2(x) = f(x, x^2) &= 3x^2 + 2x^4 - 4x^2 = 2x^4 - x^2 \\ g_2'(x) &= 8x^3 - 2x = 2x(4x^2 - 1) = 0 \end{aligned}$$

This gives $x = 0$ with $f(0, 0) = 0$, and $x = \pm\tfrac{1}{2}$ (both in $[-2, 2]$) where:

$$f\!\left(\pm\frac{1}{2}, \frac{1}{4}\right) = 2\left(\frac{1}{16}\right) - \frac{1}{4} = -\frac{1}{8}$$
Step 3: Compare all candidates in one list.

The candidate values are $f(0, 1) = -2$, $f(0, 0) = 0$, $f(0, 4) = 16$, $f(\pm 2, 4) = 28$, and at the parabolic critical points:

$$f\!\left(\pm\frac{1}{2}, \frac{1}{4}\right) = -\frac{1}{8}$$
Step 4: Verify the result by completing the square. Rewrite $f$ as: $$f(x, y) = 3x^2 + 2(y - 1)^2 - 2$$ Thus $f(x, y) \ge -2$ everywhere (confirming $m = -2$ at $(0, 1)$), while on $R$ we have $|x| \le 2$ and $|y - 1| \le 3$, bounding $f(x, y) \le 3(4) + 2(9) - 2 = 28$, achieved at $(\pm 2, 4)$.
Answer:

Absolute maximum at $(-2, 4)$ and $(2, 4)$:

$$M = 28$$

Absolute minimum at $(0, 1)$:

$$m = -2$$
Textbook p. 947, Exercise 43; Instructor Notes & KFUPM Final Term 242, Q11
Example: Absolute Extrema of $f(x, y) = (2x - y)^2$ on a Triangle
Let $T$ be the closed triangular region in the $xy$-plane with vertices $(2, 0)$, $(0, 1)$, and $(1, 2)$. If $M$ and $m$ are the absolute maximum and absolute minimum values of $$f(x, y) = (2x - y)^2$$ over $T$, find $M + m$.
Step 1: Find the interior critical line $y = 2x$. Compute both first partial derivatives: $$\begin{aligned} f_x &= 4(2x - y) = 0 \\ f_y &= -2(2x - y) = 0 \end{aligned}$$ Both equations reduce to $y = 2x$, where $f(x, 2x) = 0$. The vertex $(1, 2)$ lies on this line, and $y = 2x$ slices right through the interior of $T$.
Step 2: Parameterize all three triangle edges ($S_1, S_2, S_3$).

On edge $S_1$ from $(2, 0)$ to $(1, 2)$, the slope is $-2$, giving $y = -2x + 4$ ($1 \le x \le 2$):

$$\begin{aligned} g_1(x) &= \big(2x - (-2x + 4)\big)^2 = (4x - 4)^2 \\ g_1'(x) &= 32x - 32 = 0 \implies x = 1,\; y = 2 \end{aligned}$$

On edge $S_2$ from $(0, 1)$ to $(1, 2)$, the slope is $1$, giving $y = x + 1$ ($0 \le x \le 1$):

$$\begin{aligned} g_2(x) &= \big(2x - (x + 1)\big)^2 = (x - 1)^2 \\ g_2'(x) &= 2(x - 1) = 0 \implies x = 1,\; y = 2 \end{aligned}$$

On edge $S_3$ from $(2, 0)$ to $(0, 1)$, the slope is $-\tfrac{1}{2}$, giving $y = -\tfrac{1}{2}x + 1$ ($0 \le x \le 2$):

$$\begin{aligned} g_3(x) &= \left(2x - \left(-\frac{1}{2}x + 1\right)\right)^2 = \left(\frac{5}{2}x - 1\right)^2 \\ g_3'(x) &= 2\left(\frac{5}{2}x - 1\right)\left(\frac{5}{2}\right) = \frac{25}{2}x - 5 = 0 \implies x = \frac{2}{5},\; y = \frac{4}{5} \end{aligned}$$

At $(\tfrac{2}{5}, \tfrac{4}{5})$, we have $y = 2x$, so $f(\tfrac{2}{5}, \tfrac{4}{5}) = 0$.

Step 3: Compare all candidates and compute $M + m$. Evaluating at all vertices and critical points gives $f(1, 2) = 0$, $f(0, 1) = 1$, $f(2, 0) = 16$, $f(\tfrac{2}{5}, \tfrac{4}{5}) = 0$, and $f(x, 2x) = 0$ along $y = 2x$ inside $T$. Thus $M = 16$, $m = 0$, and $M + m = 16$.
Triangular region $T$ and edges $S_1, S_2, S_3$ Critical line $y = 2x$ (attains $m = 0$) Vertex $(2, 0)$ (attains $M = 16$)

Triangular region sliced by a critical line of zero values: the line enters along the bottom edge and exits at the top vertex to achieve the absolute minimum of zero, while the farthest right corner achieves the absolute maximum.

Step 4: Verify the result using linearity of $2x - y$. Since $f(x, y) = (2x - y)^2 \ge 0$ everywhere and $y = 2x$ intersects $T$, $m = 0$ is immediate. On any line segment, $2x - y$ is linear, so $|2x - y|$ is maximized at one of the three vertices: $|4 - 0| = 4$, $|0 - 1| = 1$, and $|2 - 2| = 0$, confirming $M = 4^2 = 16$.
Answer: $$M + m = 16 + 0 = 16$$
Textbook p. 947, Exercise 42; Instructor Notes & KFUPM Final Term 241, Q10
One-Screen Summary

The 5 Things to Know for the Exam

  1. Critical points require BOTH partials $= 0$ OR at least one partial DNE: Never stop after solving $f_x = 0$ alone, and always inspect denominators and fractional powers like $(x^2+y^2)^{1/3}$ where partials fail to exist.
  2. Use Dr. Alhumaidy’s $D$-table ($D = f_{xx}f_{yy} - [f_{xy}]^2$): At every smooth critical point, $D > 0$ and $f_{xx} > 0$ gives a relative minimum; $D > 0$ and $f_{xx} < 0$ gives a relative maximum; $D < 0$ gives a saddle point.
  3. When $D = 0$ or partials DNE, switch immediately to direct comparison: Check whether $f(x, y) - f(a, b)$ keeps a fixed sign near $(a, b)$ (using squares/roots) or changes sign along two paths through $(a, b)$.
  4. For absolute extrema on a closed bounded region $R$, sketch $R$ first: Keep only interior critical points strictly inside $R$, substitute every boundary curve to find 1D critical points along each edge, and put all corners into one candidate table.
  5. Read KFUPM MCQ targets carefully: Check whether the question asks for the number of saddles/maxima/minima, the extreme value $M$ or $m$, or a combination like $M + m$.
CONCEPT MASTERCLASS • SECTION 13.9

13.9 Applications of Extrema

Reducing Constrained 3-Variable Optimization to 2 Variables, the $D^2$ Shortest-Distance Trick, Box Volume & Cost Optimization, and Domain Feasibility + Second Partials Verification.

Watch on YouTube ↗
Full topic lecture by Eng. Anas Abu Zahra (video has no chapter/caption index for timestamps).

What You Already Know

In Calculus I, optimization meant writing a quantity as a function of one variable $x$ using a constraint, solving $f'(x) = 0$, and checking endpoints and $f''(x)$. In Section 13.8, you scaled that toolkit up to two variables by solving $f_x(x, y) = 0$ and $f_y(x, y) = 0$ simultaneously.

You also classified interior critical points with the Second Partials Test and compared boundary values on closed bounded domains. Section 13.9 applies that exact machinery to 3D geometry, shortest-distance, box-design, and profit/revenue problems.

Core Concept • §1

1. Reducing Constrained 3-Variable Optimization to 2 Variables

Intuition: Real geometric problems naturally involve three variables $(x, y, z)$, such as length, width, and height of a box, or coordinates on a 3D surface.

Because the Second Partials Test applies to two independent variables, our first move is to solve the constraint equation for one variable (usually $z$) and substitute it into the quantity we want to optimize. That turns a constrained 3D problem into an ordinary 2-variable function $f(x, y)$.

Note (Instructor Notes vs. Book): The textbook covers both Applied Optimization Problems and the Method of Least Squares. In Dr. Alhumaidy’s annotated notes, the Method of Least Squares is crossed out and omitted; coverage focuses exclusively on Applied Optimization word problems, distance minimization, number problems, box problems, and revenue optimization. Dr. Alhumaidy also labels the 3-variable target quantity $M$ (such as $M = x + y + z$ or $M = x^2 + y^2 + z^2$) before substituting the constraint to form $f(x, y)$, and emphasizes symmetry shortcuts ($x = y = z$) to save time on exams. Textbook pp. 948–954; Dr. Alhumaidy Notes
Constraint plane $6x+4y+3z=24$ Inscribed box with volume $V(x,y)$ Closed triangular domain $D$ Interior maximizer $(\tfrac{4}{3}, 2)$

Solving the linear constraint plane equation for z projects the three-dimensional inscribed box problem onto a triangular domain in the xy-plane, where volume is zero on all boundary edges and reaches its maximum at an interior critical point.

3-to-2 Variable Reduction & Plane-Constrained Box Rule

Given an objective $M(x, y, z)$ and a single constraint $g(x, y, z) = C$, solve the constraint for $z = h(x, y)$ (choosing the variable that avoids roots or fractions when possible) and define:

$$f(x, y) = M\big(x, y, h(x, y)\big)$$

Solve the interior critical-point system $f_x(x, y) = 0$ and $f_y(x, y) = 0$ inside the physical domain. For a first-octant rectangular box ($x, y, z > 0$) under a plane $ax + by + cz = K$ with $a, b, c, K > 0$, the maximum volume splits $K$ equally:

$$ax = by = cz = \frac{K}{3}$$

This gives the maximum volume directly:

$$V_{\max} = \frac{K^3}{27abc}$$ Textbook p. 948, Example 1; Dr. Alhumaidy Notes
Example: Minimizing Sum of Squares Under a Fixed Sum
Find three positive integers $x, y, z$ whose sum is $30$ and whose sum of squares is a minimum.
Step 1: Eliminate $z$ to form $f(x, y)$. Write the objective $M = x^2 + y^2 + z^2$ and substitute $z = 30 - x - y$: $$f(x, y) = x^2 + y^2 + (30 - x - y)^2$$
Step 2: Set both first partial derivatives equal to zero. Differentiate with respect to $x$ and $y$: $$\begin{aligned} f_x &= 2x - 2(30 - x - y) = 4x + 2y - 60 = 0 \\ f_y &= 2y - 2(30 - x - y) = 2x + 4y - 60 = 0 \end{aligned}$$
Step 3: Solve the symmetric system. Equating $4x + 2y = 2x + 4y$ gives $2x = 2y$, so $x = y$. Substituting $y = x$ into $4x + 2y = 60$ gives $6x = 60$, so $x = 10$, $y = 10$, and $z = 30 - 10 - 10 = 10$.
Step 4: Verify the result. Compute $f_{xx} = 4 > 0$, $f_{yy} = 4$, and $f_{xy} = 2$, so the Second Partials discriminant is: $$D = f_{xx}f_{yy} - (f_{xy})^2 = (4)(4) - 2^2 = 12 > 0$$ Thus $(10, 10)$ is a strict minimum, and $x + y + z = 30$ with positive integers $10, 10, 10$.
Answer: The three positive integers are $x = 10$, $y = 10$, and $z = 10$, giving minimum sum of squares: $$M_{\min} = 10^2 + 10^2 + 10^2 = 300$$
Textbook p. 953, Exercise 9; Dr. Alhumaidy Notes pp. 953–954
Why It Works: Constrained Surface Reduction

Any point $(x, y, z)$ satisfying the constraint $z = h(x, y)$ has its third coordinate, and therefore its objective value, uniquely fixed by $(x, y)$.

Maximizing or minimizing $M(x, y, z)$ over the constraint surface is therefore identical to optimizing the two-variable function $f(x, y)$ over its allowable domain in the $xy$-plane.

Quick Check 1

Find three positive integers $x, y, z$ whose product is $27$ and whose sum $M = x + y + z$ is a minimum. What is the minimum sum?

(A) $9$
(B) $11$
(C) $13$
(D) $27$
Check Answer & Reason

Answer: (A). Eliminate $z$ using $xyz = 27$ to get:

$$f(x, y) = x + y + \frac{27}{xy}$$

Setting the first partial derivatives to zero yields:

$$\begin{aligned} f_x &= 1 - \frac{27}{x^2 y} = 0 \implies x^2 y = 27 \\ f_y &= 1 - \frac{27}{x y^2} = 0 \implies x y^2 = 27 \end{aligned}$$

Dividing gives $x = y$, so $x^3 = 27$ and $x = y = z = 3$, giving minimum sum $3 + 3 + 3 = 9$.

Textbook p. 953, Exercise 7; Dr. Alhumaidy Notes p. 953
Core Concept • §2

2. The $D^2$ Trick for Shortest Distance to a Surface or Plane

Intuition: Finding the closest point on a plane or curved surface to a fixed point $P_0(x_0, y_0, z_0)$ starts with the 3D Euclidean distance formula:

$$d = \sqrt{(x - x_0)^2 + (y - y_0)^2 + (z - z_0)^2}$$

Differentiating a square root directly wastes time and invites chain-rule algebra errors. Because distance $d \ge 0$ and $u \mapsto u^2$ is strictly increasing on $[0, \infty)$, minimizing $d$ occurs at the exact same point as minimizing the squared distance $D = d^2$.

Surface slice along $x = y$ Shortest orthogonal segment $P_0Q$ Tangent perpendicular to $P_0Q$

Diagonal cross-section showing how minimizing squared distance avoids the outer square root and locates the closest point on the surface along an orthogonal segment.

Squared-Distance ($D^2$) Minimization Formula

To minimize the distance from $P_0(x_0, y_0, z_0)$ to a surface $z = h(x, y)$ or $z^2 = g(x, y)$, minimize:

$$D(x, y) = d^2 = (x - x_0)^2 + (y - y_0)^2 + (z - z_0)^2$$

Substitute $z$ (or $z^2$ directly when $z_0 = 0$), solve $D_x = 0$ and $D_y = 0$, verify the critical point lies in the surface domain, and recover the minimum distance via:

$$d_{\min} = \sqrt{D_{\min}}$$ Textbook p. 953, Exercises 3–6; Dr. Alhumaidy Notes p. 953
Example: Minimum Distance to a Square-Root Surface
Find the minimum distance from the point $(-2, -2, 0)$ to the surface: $$z = \sqrt{1 - 2x - 2y}$$
Step 1: Substitute $z^2$ into the squared distance $D(x, y)$. Since $z_0 = 0$ and $z^2 = 1 - 2x - 2y$ (domain $1 - 2x - 2y \ge 0$), form: $$D(x, y) = (x + 2)^2 + (y + 2)^2 + (1 - 2x - 2y)$$
Step 2: Set $D_x = 0$ and $D_y = 0$. Differentiate and solve for $x$ and $y$: $$\begin{aligned} D_x &= 2(x + 2) - 2 = 2x + 2 = 0 \implies x = -1 \\ D_y &= 2(y + 2) - 2 = 2y + 2 = 0 \implies y = -1 \end{aligned}$$
Step 3: Verify the result. Check domain feasibility: $1 - 2(-1) - 2(-1) = 5 \ge 0$, so the surface height is valid: $$z = \sqrt{5}$$

Expanding and completing the square confirms a global minimum:

$$D(x, y) = (x + 1)^2 + (y + 1)^2 + 7 \ge 7$$

Thus $D_{\min} = 7$ at $(-1, -1)$.

Answer: Taking the square root gives the minimum distance: $$d_{\min} = \sqrt{7}$$
Textbook p. 953, Exercise 5; Dr. Alhumaidy Notes p. 953
Why It Works: Monotonicity and Gradient Alignment of $D = d^2$

Because $d \ge 0$, we have $d(x_1, y_1) < d(x_2, y_2)$ if and only if $[d(x_1, y_1)]^2 < [d(x_2, y_2)]^2$, so both functions share the exact same minimizer.

Differentiating $D = d^2$ by the Chain Rule gives $D_x = 2d\,d_x$ and $D_y = 2d\,d_y$, so whenever $d > 0$, $\nabla D = \mathbf{0}$ holds at the exact same points as $\nabla d = \mathbf{0}$.

Quick Check 2

If $(a, b, c)$, with $c > 0$, is the point on the cone $z^2 = x^2 + y^2$ that is closest to $(1, 2, 0)$, what is $8abc$?

(A) $$4\sqrt{5}$$
(B) $$\sqrt{5}$$
(C) $$5\sqrt{5}$$
(D) $$2\sqrt{5}$$
Check Answer & Reason

Answer: (D). Using $z^2 = x^2 + y^2$, the squared distance to $(1, 2, 0)$ is:

$$D(x, y) = (x - 1)^2 + (y - 2)^2 + x^2 + y^2$$

Setting $D_x = 4x - 2 = 0$ and $D_y = 4y - 4 = 0$ gives $a = \tfrac{1}{2}$ and $b = 1$. Since $c > 0$, we compute:

$$c = \sqrt{\left(\frac{1}{2}\right)^2 + 1^2} = \frac{\sqrt{5}}{2}$$

Therefore:

$$8abc = 8\left(\frac{1}{2}\right)(1)\left(\frac{\sqrt{5}}{2}\right) = 2\sqrt{5}$$
KFUPM Final Term 242, Q12
Core Concept • §3

3. Box Volume, Surface-Area & Cost Optimization

Intuition: Rectangular-box optimization problems test your ability to translate a physical description into the correct area or cost formula before eliminating $z$.

The single biggest distinction is whether the box is closed (two bases plus four walls) or open-top (one base plus four walls), and whether the base material costs more per square unit than the side walls.

Single base face ($xy$) Four vertical side walls ($2xz + 2yz$) Symmetry result when $c_b = 2c_s$

Distinguishing the single rectangular base from the four vertical walls reveals when the base-to-side unit cost ratio creates full symmetry and makes the optimal open-top box a cube.

Box Volume, Surface-Area & Cost Formulas

For a rectangular box with positive dimensions $x, y, z > 0$:

Volume:

$$V = xyz$$

Closed-box surface area (fixed $V$ or $S$ yields a cube $x = y = z$):

$$S = 2xy + 2xz + 2yz$$

Open-top box cost with base unit cost $c_b$ and side unit cost $c_s$:

$$C = c_b(xy) + c_s(2xz + 2yz)$$ Textbook p. 953, Exercises 11–13; KFUPM Final Term 241, Q11
Example: Closed Rectangular Box of Minimum Surface Area
Show that a closed rectangular box of given volume $V = C$ ($C > 0$) and minimum surface area is a cube.
Step 1: Eliminate $z$ using $xyz = C$. Substitute $z = C / (xy)$ into $S = 2xy + 2xz + 2yz$ over $x > 0, y > 0$: $$S(x, y) = 2xy + \frac{2C}{y} + \frac{2C}{x}$$
Step 2: Set $S_x = 0$ and $S_y = 0$. Compute the partial derivatives: $$\begin{aligned} S_x &= 2y - \frac{2C}{x^2} = 0 \implies y = \frac{C}{x^2} \\ S_y &= 2x - \frac{2C}{y^2} = 0 \implies x y^2 = C \end{aligned}$$
Step 3: Solve for $x$, $y$, and $z$. Substitute $y = C / x^2$ into $x y^2 = C$: $$x\left(\frac{C}{x^2}\right)^2 = C \implies \frac{C^2}{x^3} = C \implies x^3 = C \implies x = C^{1/3}$$

Then $y$ and $z$ simplify to the same value:

$$y = \frac{C}{C^{2/3}} = C^{1/3}$$ $$z = \frac{C}{C^{1/3} C^{1/3}} = C^{1/3}$$
Step 4: Verify the result. Evaluate the second partial derivatives at $(C^{1/3}, C^{1/3})$: $$S_{xx} = \frac{4C}{x^3} = 4 > 0$$ $$S_{yy} = \frac{4C}{y^3} = 4$$ $$S_{xy} = 2$$

Thus $S_{xx} > 0$ and the discriminant is positive, confirming a minimum:

$$S_{xx}S_{yy} - (S_{xy})^2 = (4)(4) - 2^2 = 12 > 0$$
Answer: Since all three dimensions are equal ($x = y = z = C^{1/3}$), the closed box of minimum surface area is a cube: $$x = y = z = C^{1/3}$$
Textbook p. 953, Exercise 13; Dr. Alhumaidy Notes p. 953
Why It Works: Boundary Blow-Up on the Open Quadrant

Whenever $x \to 0^+$, $y \to 0^+$, or $x + y \to \infty$ while $xyz = C > 0$, at least one term of $S(x, y)$ grows without bound to $+\infty$.

$$S(x, y) = 2xy + \frac{2C}{y} + \frac{2C}{x} \to +\infty$$

Because $S(x, y)$ is positive and smooth on $(0, \infty) \times (0, \infty)$, its unique interior critical point $(C^{1/3}, C^{1/3})$ must be the global minimum.

Quick Check 3

A company manufactures running shoes ($x_1$ thousand units) and basketball shoes ($x_2$ thousand units) with total revenue given by:

$$R(x_1, x_2) = -5x_1^2 - 8x_2^2 - 2x_1 x_2 + 42x_1 + 102x_2$$

Which production levels $(x_1, x_2)$ maximize revenue?

(A) $(3, 6)$
(B) $(6, 3)$
(C) $(4, 5)$
(D) $(2, 11)$
Check Answer & Reason

Answer: (A). Setting the partial derivatives equal to zero gives a linear system:

$$\begin{aligned} R_{x_1} &= -10x_1 - 2x_2 + 42 = 0 \implies 5x_1 + x_2 = 21 \\ R_{x_2} &= -16x_2 - 2x_1 + 102 = 0 \implies x_1 + 8x_2 = 51 \end{aligned}$$

Substituting $x_2 = 21 - 5x_1$ into the second equation gives $8(21 - 5x_1) + x_1 = 51$, so $-39x_1 = -117$, yielding $x_1 = 3$ and $x_2 = 6$.

Textbook p. 953, Exercise 15; Dr. Alhumaidy Notes pp. 952–953
Core Concept • §4

4. Checking Domain Feasibility, Boundaries & the Second Partials Test

Intuition: Solving $f_x = 0$ and $f_y = 0$ yields candidate points, not a finished proof.

In applied optimization, three checks stand between a candidate point and full credit: confirming the point lies in the physical or square-root domain, rejecting degenerate boundary roots like $x = 0$, and verifying the extremum via the Second Partials Test or completing the square.

Feasible domain & valid critical point Domain boundary ($1 - 2x - 2y = 0$) Infeasible exterior point

Always verify that your critical point satisfies the surface domain (left) and passes either the Second Partials Test or a global completing-the-square bound (right).

Second Partials Test & Closed Bounded Domain Rule

Let $f$ have continuous second partial derivatives on an open region containing $(a, b)$, where $f_x(a, b) = 0$ and $f_y(a, b) = 0$. Define the discriminant:

$$D = f_{xx}(a, b)f_{yy}(a, b) - [f_{xy}(a, b)]^2$$
  • If $D > 0$ and $f_{xx}(a, b) > 0$, then $f(a, b)$ is a relative minimum.
  • If $D > 0$ and $f_{xx}(a, b) < 0$, then $f(a, b)$ is a relative maximum.
  • If $D < 0$, then $\big(a, b, f(a, b)\big)$ is a saddle point (not an extremum).
  • If $D = 0$, the test is inconclusive.

Completing-the-Square Bound: If $D(x, y) = A(x - a)^2 + B(y - b)^2 + k$ with $A, B > 0$, then $(a, b)$ is immediately the strict global minimum with $D_{\min} = k$.

Closed Bounded Domain Remark: When the domain is a closed bounded region (such as a triangle $x \ge 0, y \ge 0, 6x + 4y \le 24$), compare interior critical values against all boundary values.

Textbook p. 948, Remark; Section 13.8 Second Partials Test
Example: Profit Maximization & Second Partials Verification
A manufacturer determines that the profit $P$ (in dollars) obtained by producing and selling $x$ units of Product 1 and $y$ units of Product 2 is approximated by: $$P(x, y) = 8x + 10y - 0.001(x^2 + xy + y^2) - 10{,}000$$ Find the production level that maximizes profit and verify the maximum.
Step 1: Set $P_x = 0$ and $P_y = 0$. Compute the first partial derivatives: $$\begin{aligned} P_x &= 8 - 0.001(2x + y) = 0 \implies 2x + y = 8000 \\ P_y &= 10 - 0.001(x + 2y) = 0 \implies x + 2y = 10{,}000 \end{aligned}$$
Step 2: Solve the linear system. Solving $2x + y = 8000$ and $x + 2y = 10{,}000$ yields $x = 2000$ and $y = 4000$, which are feasible ($x, y > 0$).
Step 3: Verify the result. Compute $P_{xx} = -0.002 < 0$, $P_{yy} = -0.002$, and $P_{xy} = -0.001$. Then: $$D = (-0.002)(-0.002) - (-0.001)^2 = 0.000003 > 0$$ Since $D > 0$ and $P_{xx} < 0$, $(2000, 4000)$ yields the maximum profit.
Answer: Producing $x = 2000$ units and $y = 4000$ units yields the maximum profit: $$P(2000, 4000) = \text{$18,000}$$
Textbook p. 949, Example 2
Why It Works: Hidden Domain Constraints & Hessian Definiteness
