  4. Spot non-elementary integrands immediately: Seeing any of these expressions on the inner integral is your green light to reverse the order of integration rather than forcing an antiderivative: $$e^{\pm y^2},\; \cos(y^2),\; \sin(x^2),\; \sqrt{1+y^3},\; \frac{1}{2+y^3}$$
  5. Exploit rectangle separability and splitting/merging: Over constant rectangular limits, a product $p(x)q(y)$ splits into separate single integrals, and a region split into two integrals in one order often merges into one integral in the reverse order: $$\int_a^b \int_c^d p(x)q(y)\,dy\,dx = \left(\int_a^b p(x)\,dx\right)\left(\int_c^d q(y)\,dy\right)$$
CONCEPT MASTERCLASS • SECTION 14.2

14.2 Double Integrals and Volume

Larson & Edwards & Dr. Alhumaidy Notes — Volume Under and Between Surfaces, Fubini’s Theorem & Reversing Integration Order, Properties, Symmetry & Bounds, and Average Value Over a Region.

Jump to section:
Lecture Video • 14.2 Double Integrals & Volume
14.2 Volumes Under Surfaces (14:43) — Covers computing 3D volumes under and between surfaces by projecting onto the $xy$-plane.
Watch on YouTube ↗
Full topic lecture by Eng. Anas Abu Zahra (video has no chapter/caption index for timestamps).

What You Already Know

In Calculus I and II, the definite integral $\int_a^b f(x)\,dx$ arises as the limit of Riemann sums $\sum f(x_i)\,\Delta x_i$ and measures signed area, volume by cross sections $\int_a^b A(x)\,dx$, and average value:

$$f_{\text{avg}} = \frac{1}{b - a}\int_a^b f(x)\,dx$$

In Section 14.1, you learned how to evaluate iterated integrals over a 2D region $R$ by holding one variable fixed while integrating the other, slicing vertically ($dy\,dx$) or horizontally ($dx\,dy$).

Section 14.2 connects those iterated integrals to true 3D volume, symmetry shortcuts, order reversal on non-elementary integrands, and 2D average value.

Core Concept • §1

1. Double Integrals & Volume Under or Between Surfaces

Intuition: Imagine building a 3D solid standing over a flat floor region $R$ in the $xy$-plane and capped by a roof surface $z = f(x, y) \ge 0$. Cover $R$ with a grid of tiny rectangles inside $R$ (an inner partition $\Delta$ whose norm $\|\Delta\|$ is the longest diagonal).

Above each rectangle of area $\Delta A_i$, erect a vertical rectangular prism of height $f(x_i, y_i)$ and volume $f(x_i, y_i)\,\Delta A_i$. Shrinking the grid ($\|\Delta\| \to 0$) turns the sum of prism volumes into the exact double integral.

When the solid sits between a ceiling $z_{\text{top}}$ and a floor $z_{\text{bottom}}$, each prism has height:

$$\Delta z = z_{\text{top}} - z_{\text{bottom}}$$
Note (Instructor Notes vs. Book): Larson computes the volume between two surfaces as (volume under upper surface) minus (volume under lower surface) and then combines the two double integrals. Dr. Alhumaidy’s notes write $\iint_R \Delta z\,dA$ directly, forming the height $\Delta z$ immediately after setting $z_1 = z_2$ to find the projection shadow $R$ in the $xy$-plane. Textbook p. 985, Example 5; Instructor Notes pp. 983, 988, Ex. 35 & 39
Upper surface $z_{\text{top}} = 4 - x^2 - y^2$ & shadow circle Lower plane $z_{\text{bot}} = 4 - 2x$ Vertical column height $\Delta z = 2x - x^2 - y^2$ Representative slice $dy\,dx$ over $R$

Equating the upper paraboloid height and the lower plane height projects the three-dimensional seam onto a shifted circular disk in the horizontal plane, and integrating the height difference over that shadow disk gives the exact enclosed volume.

Definition: Double Integral & Volume Under One Surface

If $f$ is defined on a closed, bounded region $R$ in the $xy$-plane, then the double integral of $f$ over $R$ is:

$$\iint_R f(x, y)\,dA = \lim_{\|\Delta\| \to 0} \sum_{i=1}^n f(x_i, y_i)\,\Delta A_i$$

The limit exists whenever $f$ is continuous on $R$ and $R$ is a finite union of nonoverlapping vertically or horizontally simple subregions. When $f(x, y) \ge 0$ on $R$, the volume under $z = f(x, y)$ above $R$ is:

$$V = \iint_R f(x, y)\,dA$$ Textbook p. 980
Volume Between Two Surfaces

If $z_{\text{bottom}} \le z_{\text{top}}$ on a shadow region $R$, the volume enclosed between the two surfaces is:

$$V = \iint_R \big(z_{\text{top}}(x, y) - z_{\text{bottom}}(x, y)\big)\,dA$$

When $R$ is not explicitly given, set $z_{\text{top}} = z_{\text{bottom}}$ to find the boundary curve of $R$ in the $xy$-plane, then test an interior point of $R$ to confirm which surface lies on top.

Textbook p. 985, Example 5; Instructor Notes
Example: Volume Under a Plane Over a Rectangle

Find the volume of the solid under the given plane above the rectangle $0 \le x \le 4$ and $0 \le y \le 2$:

$$z = \frac{y}{2}$$
Step 1: Verify nonnegativity and set up the double integral.

On $0 \le y \le 2$, the surface satisfies $z \ge 0$, so the volume is the double integral over $R = [0, 4] \times [0, 2]$:

$$V = \int_0^4 \int_0^2 \frac{y}{2}\,dy\,dx$$
Step 2: Evaluate the inner $y$-integral and outer $x$-integral. $$\begin{aligned} V &= \int_0^4 \left[\frac{y^2}{4}\right]_{y=0}^{y=2} dx \\ &= \int_0^4 1\,dx \\ &= 4 \end{aligned}$$
Step 3: Verify geometrically.

At every $x \in [0, 4]$, the cross section parallel to the $yz$-plane is a right triangle of base $2$ and height $1$, so its area is $1$ and the total prism volume is $1 \times 4 = 4$.

Answer: $$V = 4$$
Textbook p. 987, Ex. 21; Instructor Notes
Why It Works: Cross-Sectional Sweeping

Holding $x$ fixed and integrating with respect to $y$ sweeps a vertical line across the slice to compute the cross-sectional area $A(x)$ parallel to the $yz$-plane:

$$A(x) = \int_{g_1(x)}^{g_2(x)} f(x, y)\,dy$$

Integrating $A(x)$ from $x = a$ to $x = b$ then sweeps that cross section across the base to accumulate the full 3D volume:

$$V = \int_a^b A(x)\,dx$$ Textbook p. 981
Quick Check 1

What is the volume of the solid below $z = 6 - 2y$ and above the rectangle $0 \le x \le 4$ and $0 \le y \le 2$ in the $xy$-plane?

(A) $16$
(B) $24$
(C) $32$
(D) $8$
Check Answer & Reason

Answer: (C) $32$. For $0 \le y \le 2$, we have $6 - 2y \ge 2 > 0$, so integrating over the rectangle gives:

$$\int_0^4 \int_0^2 (6 - 2y)\,dy\,dx = \int_0^4 \Big[6y - y^2\Big]_0^2 dx = \int_0^4 (12 - 4)\,dx = 8(4) = 32$$
Textbook p. 987, Ex. 22
Core Concept • §2

2. Fubini’s Theorem & Reversing the Order of Integration

Intuition: Unlike single integrals, where difficulty depends almost entirely on the integrand $f(x)$, a double integral’s difficulty depends heavily on which direction you slice $R$.

Sometimes slicing horizontally ($dx\,dy$) instead of vertically ($dy\,dx$) avoids splitting $R$ into two pieces. Other times the inner integral has no elementary antiderivative at all until you reverse the order of integration, such as $\int e^{-x^2}\,dx$, $\int e^{y^2}\,dy$, $\int \sin(y^2)\,dy$, or:

$$\int \frac{1}{1 + x^4}\,dx$$
Vertical slice $dy\,dx$: bottom $y=0$ to top $y=x$ Horizontal slice $dx\,dy$: left $x=y$ to right $x=1$ Inner integration sweep direction

Both iterated integrals cover the exact same triangle, yet slicing vertically integrates the exponential integrand cleanly while slicing horizontally gets stuck on a non-elementary inner integral.

Theorem 14.2: Fubini’s Theorem

Let $f$ be continuous on a plane region $R$.

1. Vertically simple ($dy\,dx$): if $R$ is defined by $a \le x \le b$ and $g_1(x) \le y \le g_2(x)$, where $g_1$ and $g_2$ are continuous on $[a, b]$, then:

$$\iint_R f(x, y)\,dA = \int_a^b \int_{g_1(x)}^{g_2(x)} f(x, y)\,dy\,dx$$

2. Horizontally simple ($dx\,dy$): if $R$ is defined by $c \le y \le d$ and $h_1(y) \le x \le h_2(y)$, where $h_1$ and $h_2$ are continuous on $[c, d]$, then:

$$\iint_R f(x, y)\,dA = \int_c^d \int_{h_1(y)}^{h_2(y)} f(x, y)\,dx\,dy$$ Textbook p. 982, Theorem 14.2

3-Step Reversal Recipe (Inside Any General Double Integral):

  1. Read the inequalities from the limits: inner limits give the first variable between two curves; outer limits give the second variable between two constants.
  2. Sketch $R$ and find all corner intersections so you know the global minimum and maximum of both $x$ and $y$.
  3. Re-slice in the perpendicular direction: place constant bounds on the outside and solve the boundary curves for the inner variable (left-to-right for $dx\,dy$, bottom-to-top for $dy\,dx$).
Example: Reversing Order on a Non-Elementary Integral

Sketch the region of integration and evaluate the iterated integral:

$$\int_0^1 \int_{y/2}^{1/2} e^{-x^2}\,dx\,dy$$
Step 1: Sketch $R$ and reverse the slicing direction.

Because $\int e^{-x^2}\,dx$ is non-elementary, we reverse the order. The given limits describe the triangle bounded by $y = 0$, $x = \tfrac{1}{2}$, and $y = 2x$ with vertices $(0, 0)$, $(\tfrac{1}{2}, 0)$, and $(\tfrac{1}{2}, 1)$:

$$0 \le y \le 1$$ $$\frac{y}{2} \le x \le \frac{1}{2}$$

Slicing vertically ($dy\,dx$) gives constant bounds for $x$ and vertical curve bounds for $y$:

$$0 \le x \le \frac{1}{2}$$ $$0 \le y \le 2x$$
Step 2: Evaluate the reversed iterated integral. $$\begin{aligned} \int_0^{1/2} \int_0^{2x} e^{-x^2}\,dy\,dx &= \int_0^{1/2} 2x e^{-x^2}\,dx \\ &= \Big[-e^{-x^2}\Big]_0^{1/2} \\ &= -e^{-1/4} - (-1) \\ &= 1 - e^{-1/4} \end{aligned}$$
Step 3: Verify the antiderivative and limits.

Differentiating $-e^{-x^2}$ with respect to $x$ returns $2xe^{-x^2}$, and at the corner $y = 1$ both descriptions agree on $x = \tfrac{1}{2}$.

Answer: $$1 - e^{-1/4}$$
Textbook p. 988, Ex. 45; Instructor Notes
Why It Works: Slicing the Same Region Two Ways

Both iterated integrals accumulate the same signed volume (or continuous function mass) over the exact same 2D region $R$; only the slicing direction changes.

When $f$ is continuous on $R$, Fubini’s Theorem (Theorem 14.2) guarantees that both orders yield the exact same value:

$$\int_a^b \int_{g_1(x)}^{g_2(x)} f(x, y)\,dy\,dx = \iint_R f(x, y)\,dA = \int_c^d \int_{h_1(y)}^{h_2(y)} f(x, y)\,dx\,dy$$ Textbook p. 982, Theorem 14.2
Quick Check 2

When you reverse the order of integration in the integral below, which iterated integral do you obtain?

$$\int_0^2 \int_{2x}^4 \sin(y^2)\,dy\,dx$$
(A) $$\int_0^4 \int_0^{y/2} \sin(y^2)\,dx\,dy$$
(B) $$\int_0^4 \int_{y/2}^2 \sin(y^2)\,dx\,dy$$
(C) $$\int_0^2 \int_0^{y/2} \sin(y^2)\,dx\,dy$$
(D) $$\int_{2x}^4 \int_0^2 \sin(y^2)\,dx\,dy$$
Check Answer & Reason

Answer: (A). The region $0 \le x \le 2$ and $2x \le y \le 4$ is the triangle with vertices $(0, 0)$, $(0, 4)$, and $(2, 4)$. Slicing horizontally gives $0 \le y \le 4$ and $x$ from $0$ to half of $y$, producing:

$$\int_0^4 \int_0^{y/2} \sin(y^2)\,dx\,dy = \int_0^4 \frac{y}{2}\sin(y^2)\,dy = \frac{1}{4}(1 - \cos 16)$$
Textbook p. 988, Ex. 49
Core Concept • §3

3. Properties of Double Integrals, Symmetry & Bounds

Intuition: Before cranking through an iterated integral, check whether linearity, domain splitting, odd/even symmetry, or a quick upper/lower bound can solve or simplify the problem immediately.

On a region symmetric across an axis, every point $(x, y)$ has a mirror twin $(-x, y)$ or $(x, -y)$. If the integrand flips sign at those twins (odd symmetry), their contributions cancel to zero; if it stays identical (even symmetry), you can integrate over half the region and double the answer.

Symmetric domain $R$ Actual integral $\iint_R f(x,y)\,dA$ Lower bound $m\cdot\text{Area}(R)$ Upper bound $M\cdot\text{Area}(R)$

Symmetry cancels odd terms over symmetric regions, while monotonicity sandwiches any double integral between the flat slabs defined by its minimum and maximum heights.

Theorem 14.1: Properties of Double Integrals

Let $f$ and $g$ be continuous over a closed, bounded plane region $R$, and let $c$ be a constant.

1. Constant multiple:

$$\iint_R c\,f(x, y)\,dA = c\iint_R f(x, y)\,dA$$

2. Sum and difference:

$$\iint_R \big[f(x, y) \pm g(x, y)\big]\,dA = \iint_R f(x, y)\,dA \pm \iint_R g(x, y)\,dA$$

3. Nonnegativity (if $f(x, y) \ge 0$ on $R$):

$$\iint_R f(x, y)\,dA \ge 0$$

4. Monotonicity / comparison (if $f(x, y) \ge g(x, y)$ on $R$):

$$\iint_R f(x, y)\,dA \ge \iint_R g(x, y)\,dA$$

5. Domain additivity (where $R = R_1 \cup R_2$ for nonoverlapping subregions $R_1$ and $R_2$):

$$\iint_R f(x, y)\,dA = \iint_{R_1} f(x, y)\,dA + \iint_{R_2} f(x, y)\,dA$$ Textbook p. 980, Theorem 14.1
Bounding Estimates & Odd/Even Symmetry Rules

For a constant function $k$ on $R$:

$$\iint_R k\,dA = k\cdot\text{Area}(R)$$

If $m \le f(x, y) \le M$ everywhere on $R$, then by monotonicity:

$$m\cdot\text{Area}(R) \le \iint_R f(x, y)\,dA \le M\cdot\text{Area}(R)$$

If $R$ is symmetric about the $y$-axis (so $(x, y) \in R \iff (-x, y) \in R$), then:

$$\iint_R f(x, y)\,dA = \begin{cases} 0 & \text{if } f(-x, y) = -f(x, y) \text{ (odd in } x\text{)}, \\ 2\iint_{R_{x \ge 0}} f(x, y)\,dA & \text{if } f(-x, y) = f(x, y) \text{ (even in } x\text{)}. \end{cases}$$

The exact same odd/even cancellation and doubling rule holds for symmetry about the $x$-axis ($y \mapsto -y$).

Textbook pp. 980, 987, 989, Ex. 11, 59, 65
Example: Zero Integral by Odd Symmetry on a Centered Disk

Evaluate the iterated integral:

$$\int_{-3}^{3} \int_{-\sqrt{9-x^2}}^{\sqrt{9-x^2}} (x + y)\,dy\,dx$$
Step 1: Identify the region $R$ and check symmetry.

The limits describe the centered disk $x^2 + y^2 \le 9$, which is symmetric across both the $y$-axis and the $x$-axis.

Step 2: Split by linearity and apply odd symmetry.

By Theorem 14.1, split the integrand into two terms:

$$\iint_R (x + y)\,dA = \iint_R x\,dA + \iint_R y\,dA$$

Since $x$ is odd in $x$ and $y$ is odd in $y$ over the symmetric disk $R$, both integrals vanish immediately.

Step 3: Verify by pairing mirror points.

Every point $(x, y) \in R$ cancels with $(-x, y) \in R$ for the $x$-term and with $(x, -y) \in R$ for the $y$-term, confirming the net signed volume is $0$.

Answer: $$0$$
Textbook p. 987, Ex. 11
Why It Works: Symmetry Cancellation & Integral Bounds

Domain additivity (Theorem 14.1) lets us split a symmetric region $R$ along an axis into $R_+ \cup R_-$. Substituting $u = -x$ flips the sign of an odd integrand so the two halves cancel exactly:

$$\iint_{R_-} f(x, y)\,dA = -\iint_{R_+} f(x, y)\,dA$$

For bounds, integrating the constant inequalities $m \le f(x, y) \le M$ using monotonicity from Theorem 14.1 produces:

$$m\cdot\text{Area}(R) \le \iint_R f(x, y)\,dA \le M\cdot\text{Area}(R)$$ Textbook p. 980, Theorem 14.1
Quick Check 3

Using symmetry and Theorem 14.1, what is the value of the iterated integral below?

$$\int_{-2}^{2} \int_{-\sqrt{4-x^2}}^{\sqrt{4-x^2}} (5 + x^3 y^2 - 2y)\,dy\,dx$$
(A) $0$
(B) $10\pi$
(C) $20\pi$
(D) $40\pi$
Check Answer & Reason

Answer: (C) $20\pi$. The domain is the disk $x^2 + y^2 \le 4$ of area $\pi(2)^2 = 4\pi$. Since $x^3 y^2$ is odd in $x$ and $-2y$ is odd in $y$, their integrals over the disk are $0$, leaving only the constant term:

$$\iint_R 5\,dA = 5\cdot\text{Area}(R) = 5(4\pi) = 20\pi$$
Core Concept • §4

4. Average Value of a Function Over a Region

Intuition: Imagine melting a sculpted ice block whose roof is $z = f(x, y)$ over a base mold $R$ of area $A$, and letting the water level out inside the exact same mold $R$ until the top is completely flat.

The volume $V = \iint_R f(x, y)\,dA$ has not changed, so the flat water level $f_{\text{avg}}$ satisfies:

$$f_{\text{avg}} \cdot \text{Area}(R) = V$$

Dividing volume by base area gives the average value of $f$ over $R$.

Original solid volume $\iint_R f(x,y)\,dA$ Leveled block over same base $R$ Constant height $f_{\text{avg}}$

The average value of a function over a region equals the constant height of a flat-topped cylinder over the same base whose volume matches the volume under the surface.

Definition: Average Value of a Function Over a Region

If $f$ is integrable over a plane region $R$ of positive area $A = \text{Area}(R) > 0$, then the average value of $f$ over $R$ is:

$$f_{\text{avg}} = \frac{1}{\text{Area}(R)} \iint_R f(x, y)\,dA$$

Here the area of $R$ can be computed geometrically or as:

$$\text{Area}(R) = \iint_R 1\,dA$$ Textbook p. 986; Instructor Notes
Example: Average Value Over a Triangle

Find the average value of the given function over the triangular region $R$ with vertices $(0, 0)$, $(1, 0)$, and $(1, 1)$:

$$f(x, y) = \frac{1}{x + y}$$
Step 1: Compute $\text{Area}(R)$ and describe the triangle.

The triangle has base $1$ and height $1$, so $\text{Area}(R) = \tfrac{1}{2}$, and its bounds are $0 \le x \le 1$ and $0 \le y \le x$.

Step 2: Evaluate the double integral over $R$. $$\begin{aligned} \iint_R \frac{1}{x + y}\,dA &= \int_0^1 \int_0^x \frac{1}{x + y}\,dy\,dx \\ &= \int_0^1 \Big[\ln(x + y)\Big]_{y=0}^{y=x}\,dx \\ &= \int_0^1 \big(\ln(2x) - \ln x\big)\,dx \\ &= \int_0^1 \ln 2\,dx = \ln 2 \end{aligned}$$
Step 3: Divide by $\text{Area}(R)$ and verify bounds.

Dividing by $A = \tfrac{1}{2}$ yields:

$$f_{\text{avg}} = \frac{\ln 2}{1/2} = 2\ln 2$$

Since $x + y \le 2$ on $R$, we have $f(x, y) \ge \tfrac{1}{2}$ everywhere on $R$, and indeed $2\ln 2 \approx 1.386 > \tfrac{1}{2}$.

Answer: $$f_{\text{avg}} = 2\ln 2$$
Textbook p. 988, Ex. 54; Instructor Notes
Why It Works: Continuous Limit of Sample Means

On a discrete grid of $N$ equal subsquares of area $\Delta A = A/N$, the arithmetic mean of the sample heights $f(x_i, y_i)$ rewrites as a Riemann sum divided by total area $A$:

$$\frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^N f(x_i, y_i) = \frac{1}{N\,\Delta A}\sum_{i=1}^N f(x_i, y_i)\,\Delta A = \frac{1}{A}\sum_{i=1}^N f(x_i, y_i)\,\Delta A$$

Taking the limit as the partition norm $\|\Delta\| \to 0$ turns the discrete mean into the integral average:

$$\lim_{\|\Delta\| \to 0} \frac{1}{A}\sum_{i=1}^N f(x_i, y_i)\,\Delta A = \frac{1}{A}\iint_R f(x, y)\,dA$$ Textbook p. 986
Quick Check 4

What is the average value of $f(x, y) = x^2 + y^2$ over the square with vertices $(0, 0)$, $(0, 2)$, $(2, 0)$, and $(2, 2)$?

(A) $$\frac{10}{3}$$
(B) $$\frac{8}{3}$$
(C) $$\frac{16}{3}$$
(D) $$\frac{32}{3}$$
Check Answer & Reason

Answer: (B). Here $R = [0, 2] \times [0, 2]$ has $\text{Area}(R) = 4$, so dividing the double integral by $4$ gives:

$$\begin{aligned} f_{\text{avg}} &= \frac{1}{4}\int_0^2 \int_0^2 (x^2 + y^2)\,dy\,dx \\ &= \frac{1}{4}\int_0^2 \left(2x^2 + \frac{8}{3}\right) dx \\ &= \frac{1}{4}\left(\frac{16}{3} + \frac{16}{3}\right) = \frac{1}{4}\cdot\frac{32}{3} = \frac{8}{3} \end{aligned}$$
KFUPM Final Term 233, Q15; Textbook p. 988, Ex. 53
Master Formulas

Section 14.2 Formula Reference & Edge Cases

Riemann Sum Definition & Integrability Condition

For $f$ defined on a closed, bounded plane region $R$:

$$\iint_R f(x, y)\,dA = \lim_{\|\Delta\| \to 0} \sum_{i=1}^n f(x_i, y_i)\,\Delta A_i$$

Condition: Exists whenever $f$ is continuous on $R$ and $R$ is a finite union of nonoverlapping vertically or horizontally simple subregions.

Textbook p. 980
Volume Under One Surface vs. Between Two Surfaces

Volume under a single surface $z = f(x, y) \ge 0$ over $R$:

$$V = \iint_R f(x, y)\,dA$$

Volume enclosed between an upper surface $z_{\text{top}}$ and a lower surface $z_{\text{bottom}}$ over shadow $R$:

$$V = \iint_R \big(z_{\text{top}}(x, y) - z_{\text{bottom}}(x, y)\big)\,dA$$

Edge case: “First octant” adds $x \ge 0$, $y \ge 0$, and $z \ge 0$ automatically; verify that $z \ge 0$ across all of $R$.

Textbook pp. 980, 985; Instructor Notes
Fubini’s Theorem (Iterated Evaluation Orders)

For continuous $f$ on a vertically simple region $R$ ($a \le x \le b$, $g_1(x) \le y \le g_2(x)$):

$$\iint_R f(x, y)\,dA = \int_a^b \int_{g_1(x)}^{g_2(x)} f(x, y)\,dy\,dx$$

For continuous $f$ on a horizontally simple region $R$ ($c \le y \le d$, $h_1(y) \le x \le h_2(y)$):

$$\iint_R f(x, y)\,dA = \int_c^d \int_{h_1(y)}^{h_2(y)} f(x, y)\,dx\,dy$$

Edge case: If a boundary changes formula midway, split $R = R_1 \cup R_2$ or switch to the order that keeps $R$ in one piece.

Textbook p. 982, Theorem 14.2
Constant Integrals, Bounding Estimates & Odd Symmetry

For a constant height $k$ on $R$:

$$\iint_R k\,dA = k\cdot\text{Area}(R)$$

If $m \le f(x, y) \le M$ on $R$, then:

$$m\cdot\text{Area}(R) \le \iint_R f(x, y)\,dA \le M\cdot\text{Area}(R)$$

Odd symmetry condition: $\iint_R f\,dA = 0$ holds ONLY if BOTH the region $R$ is symmetric across an axis AND $f$ changes sign across that same axis.

Textbook pp. 980, 989, Theorem 14.1, Ex. 59 & 65
Average Value Over a Plane Region

Average value of an integrable function $f$ over a region $R$ with $\text{Area}(R) > 0$:

$$f_{\text{avg}} = \frac{1}{\text{Area}(R)} \iint_R f(x, y)\,dA$$

Area of $R$:

$$\text{Area}(R) = \iint_R 1\,dA$$ Textbook p. 986
Exam Traps

5 Classic Mistakes (WRONG vs. RIGHT)

Trap 1 — Blindly swapping limits when reversing integration order:

WrongRewriting $\int_0^1 \int_0^x f\,dy\,dx$ as $\int_0^x \int_0^1 f\,dx\,dy$ (leaves $x$ in the outer limit!).
RightSketch $R$ first: outer limits are always constants ($0 \le y \le 1$) and inner limits depend only on the outer variable ($y \le x \le 1$).

Trap 2 — Wrong shadow circle or upside-down subtraction $\Delta z$ between two surfaces:

WrongEquating $4 - x^2 - y^2 = 4 - 2x$ to get $x^2 + y^2 = 4$, or writing $(4 - 2x) - (4 - x^2 - y^2)$ without testing a point.
RightComplete the square: $x^2 - 2x + y^2 = 0$ gives $(x - 1)^2 + y^2 = 1$. Testing $(1, 0)$ gives $3 > 2$, so $\Delta z = 2x - x^2 - y^2$.

Trap 3 — Forgetting to divide by $\text{Area}(R)$ (or using $b - a$) in Average Value:

WrongReporting $\iint_R f(x, y)\,dA$ directly as $f_{\text{avg}}$, or dividing by $4 - 0 = 4$ instead of triangle area $\tfrac{1}{2}(2)(4) = 4$.
RightAlways compute $A = \text{Area}(R)$ separately (e.g., $\tfrac{1}{2}bh$ for triangles, $a^2$ for squares) and divide by $A$: $$f_{\text{avg}} = \frac{1}{A}\iint_R f(x, y)\,dA$$

Trap 4 — Claiming an odd integrand gives $0$ on a non-symmetric region:

WrongSaying $\iint_R x\,dA = 0$ on the first-quadrant disk sector $x^2 + y^2 \le 25$ ($x, y \ge 0$) because $x$ is an odd function.
RightOdd symmetry requires $R$ itself to be symmetric across the $y$-axis ($(-x, y) \in R$ whenever $(x, y) \in R$). In Quadrant I, $x \ge 0$ always, so $\iint_R x\,dA > 0$.

Trap 5 — Forgetting the “first octant” walls ($x = 0$, $y = 0$, $z = 0$):

WrongAssuming $z = 4 - y^2$, $y = x$, $y = 1$ needs another wall along $x$, or integrating past $z = 0$.
Right“First octant” supplies $x \ge 0$, $y \ge 0$, and $z \ge 0$, closing the base triangle with $x = 0$ to vertices $(0,0)$, $(0,1)$, and $(1,1)$. KFUPM Final Term 242, Q16
Worked Examples

From Textbook Basics to KFUPM Final Level

Example 1: Volume of a Tetrahedron in the First Octant

Use a double integral to find the volume of the solid in the first octant bounded by the coordinate planes and the plane:

$$2x + 3y + 4z = 12$$
Step 1: Solve for $z$ and find the base triangle $R$.

Solving $2x + 3y + 4z = 12$ for $z$ gives the ceiling surface:

$$z = \frac{12 - 2x - 3y}{4}$$

Setting $z = 0$ locates the trace $2x + 3y = 12$ in the $xy$-plane. Together with $x \ge 0$ and $y \ge 0$, the base $R$ is the triangle with vertices $(0, 0)$, $(6, 0)$, and $(0, 4)$:

$$0 \le x \le 6$$ $$0 \le y \le \frac{12 - 2x}{3}$$
Step 2: Evaluate the inner $y$-integral. $$\begin{aligned} V &= \int_0^6 \int_0^{(12-2x)/3} \frac{12 - 2x - 3y}{4}\,dy\,dx \\ &= \frac{1}{4}\int_0^6 \left[(12 - 2x)y - \frac{3}{2}y^2\right]_{y=0}^{y=(12-2x)/3} dx \\ &= \frac{1}{4}\int_0^6 \left[\frac{(12 - 2x)^2}{3} - \frac{3}{2}\cdot\frac{(12 - 2x)^2}{9}\right] dx \\ &= \frac{1}{4}\int_0^6 \frac{(12 - 2x)^2}{6}\,dx \\ &= \frac{1}{24}\int_0^6 4(6 - x)^2\,dx = \frac{1}{6}\int_0^6 (6 - x)^2\,dx \end{aligned}$$
Step 3: Evaluate the outer $x$-integral. $$\begin{aligned} V &= \frac{1}{6}\left[-\frac{(6 - x)^3}{3}\right]_0^6 \\ &= \frac{1}{18}\big(0 - (-6^3)\big) \\ &= \frac{216}{18} = 12 \end{aligned}$$
Step 4: Verify geometrically.

The solid is a right tetrahedron with intercepts $a = 6$, $b = 4$, and $c = 3$, so its geometric volume matches:

$$V = \frac{1}{3}(\text{base area})(\text{height}) = \frac{1}{3}\left(\frac{1}{2}\cdot 6 \cdot 4\right)(3) = 12$$
Answer: $$V = 12$$
Textbook p. 987, Ex. 23; Instructor Notes
Example 2: Reversing Order to Eliminate a Non-Elementary Integral

Sketch the region of integration and evaluate the iterated integral:

$$\int_0^2 \int_{x^2/2}^{2} \sqrt{y}\cos y\,dy\,dx$$
Step 1: Read the region $R$ and reverse the order.

The given limits describe $0 \le x \le 2$ and $y$ from half of $x^2$ up to $2$:

$$\frac{x^2}{2} \le y \le 2$$

The parabola meets the horizontal line $y = 2$ at $x^2 = 4$, giving $x = 2$ (since $x \ge 0$). Because the inner $y$-integral is not elementary:

$$\int \sqrt{y}\cos y\,dy$$

We slice horizontally ($dx\,dy$) instead:

$$0 \le y \le 2$$ $$0 \le x \le \sqrt{2y}$$
Step 2: Evaluate the inner $x$-integral. $$\int_0^2 \int_0^{\sqrt{2y}} \sqrt{y}\cos y\,dx\,dy = \int_0^2 \sqrt{y}\cos y\Big[x\Big]_{x=0}^{x=\sqrt{2y}}\,dy = \int_0^2 \sqrt{2}\,y\cos y\,dy$$
Step 3: Integrate by parts in $y$.

Let $u = y$ and $dv = \cos y\,dy$, so $du = dy$ and $v = \sin y$:

$$\begin{aligned} \sqrt{2}\int_0^2 y\cos y\,dy &= \sqrt{2}\left(\Big[y\sin y\Big]_0^2 - \int_0^2 \sin y\,dy\right) \\ &= \sqrt{2}\Big[y\sin y + \cos y\Big]_0^2 \\ &= \sqrt{2}\big((2\sin 2 + \cos 2) - (0 + \cos 0)\big) \\ &= \sqrt{2}\big(2\sin 2 + \cos 2 - 1\big) \end{aligned}$$
Step 4: Verify the antiderivative and corner bounds.

Differentiating $y\sin y + \cos y$ confirms the integrand, and at $y = 2$ the reversed upper bound gives $x^2 = 2(2) = 4$, so $x = 2$ matches the original outer upper limit:

$$\frac{d}{dy}(y\sin y + \cos y) = \sin y + y\cos y - \sin y = y\cos y$$
Answer: $$\sqrt{2}\big(2\sin 2 + \cos 2 - 1\big)$$
Textbook p. 988, Ex. 50; Instructor Notes
Example 3: Volume Bounded by a Paraboloid and a Tilted Plane

Set up an iterated double integral in the order $dy\,dx$ for the volume of the solid region bounded by the graphs of:

$$z = 4 - x^2 - y^2$$ $$z = 4 - 2x$$
Step 1: Find the projection $R$ by equating $z$-values. $$\begin{aligned} 4 - x^2 - y^2 &= 4 - 2x \\ x^2 - 2x + y^2 &= 0 \\ (x - 1)^2 + y^2 &= 1 \end{aligned}$$

The shadow $R$ in the $xy$-plane is the disk of radius $1$ centered at $(1, 0)$.

Step 2: Determine $z_{\text{top}} - z_{\text{bottom}}$.

Test the center $(1, 0) \in R$: $z_{\text{paraboloid}}(1, 0) = 3$, whereas $z_{\text{plane}}(1, 0) = 2$. Since $3 > 2$, the paraboloid lies above the plane everywhere on $R$:

$$\Delta z = z_{\text{top}} - z_{\text{bottom}} = (4 - x^2 - y^2) - (4 - 2x) = 2x - x^2 - y^2$$
Step 3: Write the $dy\,dx$ bounds over the disk $R$.

From $(x - 1)^2 + y^2 \le 1$, $x$ runs across the diameter $[0, 2]$, and for each $x \in [0, 2]$, $y$ runs between the lower and upper semicircles:

$$-\sqrt{1 - (x - 1)^2} \le y \le \sqrt{1 - (x - 1)^2}$$

Assembling the volume integral gives:

$$V = \int_0^2 \int_{-\sqrt{1 - (x - 1)^2}}^{\sqrt{1 - (x - 1)^2}} (2x - x^2 - y^2)\,dy\,dx$$
Step 4: Verify positivity of $\Delta z$ on $R$.

Completing the square on the integrand shows it is strictly positive on the interior of the disk and $0$ on the boundary points $(0, 0)$, $(2, 0)$, and $(1, \pm 1)$:

$$\Delta z = 2x - x^2 - y^2 = 1 - \big[(x - 1)^2 + y^2\big] \ge 0$$
Answer: $$V = \int_0^2 \int_{-\sqrt{1 - (x - 1)^2}}^{\sqrt{1 - (x - 1)^2}} (2x - x^2 - y^2)\,dy\,dx$$
KFUPM Final Term 251, Q16 & 243, Q5; Textbook p. 988, Ex. 35
Example 4: Average Value of $4e^{y^2}$ Over a Triangle

Find the average value of $f(x, y) = 4e^{y^2}$ over the plane region $R$ bounded by the curves $y = 2x$, $y = 4$, and $x = 0$.

Step 1: Sketch $R$ and compute $\text{Area}(R)$.

The three lines intersect pairwise at $(0, 0)$, $(0, 4)$, and $(2, 4)$, forming a right triangle with horizontal leg $2$ (along $y = 4$) and vertical leg $4$ (along $x = 0$):

$$\text{Area}(R) = \frac{1}{2}(2)(4) = 4$$
Step 2: Choose $dx\,dy$ to avoid an elementary obstruction in $y$.

Since $e^{y^2}$ has no elementary $y$-antiderivative, slice horizontally with $0 \le y \le 4$ and $x$ from $0$ to half of $y$:

$$0 \le x \le \frac{y}{2}$$

Setting up the average value integral and evaluating the inner $x$-integral gives:

$$\begin{aligned} f_{\text{avg}} &= \frac{1}{4}\int_0^4 \int_0^{y/2} 4e^{y^2}\,dx\,dy \\ &= \int_0^4 \Big[x e^{y^2}\Big]_{x=0}^{x=y/2} dy \\ &= \int_0^4 \frac{y}{2} e^{y^2}\,dy \end{aligned}$$
Step 3: Evaluate by $u$-substitution.

Use $u = y^2$ with transformed limits $u(0) = 0$ and $u(4) = 16$:

$$du = 2y\,dy \implies \frac{y}{2}\,dy = \frac{1}{4}\,du$$

Integrating from $0$ to $16$ gives:

$$f_{\text{avg}} = \frac{1}{4}\int_0^{16} e^u\,du = \frac{1}{4}\Big[e^u\Big]_0^{16} = \frac{e^{16} - 1}{4}$$
Triangle $R$ bounded by $x=0$, $y=4$, $y=2x$ Horizontal slice $0 \le x \le y/2$ Triangle vertices & sweep direction

Drawn to true scale for a line of slope two: slicing horizontally produces the factor of half the vertical coordinate needed for the substitution in the outer integral.

Step 4: Verify the antiderivative and bounding interval.

Differentiating confirms the outer integrand, and since $4 \le 4e^{y^2} \le 4e^{16}$ on $R$, the bounding property guarantees $4 \le f_{\text{avg}} \le 4e^{16}$:

$$\frac{d}{dy}\left(\frac{1}{4}e^{y^2}\right) = \frac{y}{2}e^{y^2}$$
Answer: $$f_{\text{avg}} = \frac{e^{16} - 1}{4}$$
KFUPM Final Term 253, Q16
Example 5: Finding an Unknown Square Side Length $a$ from $f_{\text{avg}}$

Let $f(x, y) = ax^2 + ay^2$, where $a > 0$, over the square region:

$$R = \{(x, y) : 0 \le x \le a,\; 0 \le y \le a\}$$

If the average value of $f$ over $R$ is $18$, find $a$.

Step 1: Set up the average value formula on $R = [0, a]^2$.

The square $R$ has $\text{Area}(R) = a^2$, so:

$$f_{\text{avg}} = \frac{1}{a^2} \int_0^a \int_0^a (ax^2 + ay^2)\,dx\,dy$$
Step 2: Evaluate the double integral in terms of $a$.

First integrate with respect to $x$, holding $y$ fixed:

$$\int_0^a (ax^2 + ay^2)\,dx = \left[\frac{a x^3}{3} + a x y^2\right]_{x=0}^{x=a} = \frac{a^4}{3} + a^2 y^2$$

Now integrate with respect to $y$:

$$\int_0^a \left(\frac{a^4}{3} + a^2 y^2\right) dy = \left[\frac{a^4}{3}y + \frac{a^2 y^3}{3}\right]_{y=0}^{y=a} = \frac{a^5}{3} + \frac{a^5}{3} = \frac{2a^5}{3}$$
Step 3: Solve $f_{\text{avg}} = 18$ for $a > 0$. $$\begin{aligned} f_{\text{avg}} &= \frac{1}{a^2}\cdot\frac{2a^5}{3} = \frac{2}{3}a^3 = 18 \\ a^3 &= 18\cdot\frac{3}{2} = 27 \\ a &= 3 \end{aligned}$$
Step 4: Verify by substituting $a = 3$ back into $f$ and $R$.

With $a = 3$, $f(x, y) = 3x^2 + 3y^2$ on $[0, 3]\times[0, 3]$ ($\text{Area} = 9$), and the average value checks out to $18$:

$$\frac{1}{9}\int_0^3\int_0^3 (3x^2 + 3y^2)\,dx\,dy = \frac{1}{9}\int_0^3 (27 + 9y^2)\,dy = \frac{1}{9}\Big[27y + 3y^3\Big]_0^3 = \frac{162}{9} = 18$$
Answer: $$a = 3$$
KFUPM Final Term 252, Q17
One-Screen Summary

The 5 Things to Know for the Exam

  1. Volume between two surfaces integrates $z_{\text{top}} - z_{\text{bottom}}$ over $R$: Equate $z_1 = z_2$ (completing the square if needed) to find the shadow $R$, and test an interior point of $R$ to confirm which surface is on top.
  2. Always sketch $R$ before reversing the order of integration: Non-elementary inner integrals ($\int e^{-x^2}\,dx$, $\int e^{y^2}\,dy$, $\int \sin(y^2)\,dy$) become elementary once you swap $dy\,dx \leftrightarrow dx\,dy$ correctly from the picture.
  3. Check odd/even symmetry and bounds before integrating: An odd integrand integrates to $0$ only if $R$ is symmetric across that axis; for bounds, $m \le f \le M$ guarantees the integral sits between $m\cdot\text{Area}(R)$ and $M\cdot\text{Area}(R)$.
  4. Average value always divides by $\text{Area}(R)$: Compute $f_{\text{avg}}$ by dividing $\iint_R f(x, y)\,dA$ by $\text{Area}(R)$ — never forget the area denominator, and compute triangle or square areas carefully.
  5. “First octant” supplies $x \ge 0$, $y \ge 0$, and $z \ge 0$: Use $x = 0$ and $y = 0$ as automatic boundary walls of $R$, and verify $z \ge 0$ across all of $R$.

Jump to Timestamp:

What You Already Know

Earlier in polar geometry, you linked rectangular and polar coordinates via the four fundamental conversion equations:

Coordinate definitions:

$$x = r\cos\theta$$ $$y = r\sin\theta$$

Radius and angle relations:

$$r^2 = x^2 + y^2$$ $$\tan\theta = \frac{y}{x}$$

You also learned how to compute the area inside a polar curve $r = g(\theta)$ using Theorem 10.13, and how to evaluate double integrals over rectangular slices.

When a region $R$ is a disk, annulus, cardioid, or sector — or when the integrand features $x^2 + y^2$ — Cartesian slices trap you in messy square roots. Switching to polar sectors turns curved circular boundaries into constant limits.

Theorem 10.13: Area in Polar Coordinates

If $g$ is continuous and nonnegative on the interval $[\alpha, \beta]$ with $0 < \beta - \alpha \le 2\pi$, then the area $A$ of the region bounded by the graph of $r = g(\theta)$ between the radial lines $\theta = \alpha$ and $\theta = \beta$ is given by:

$$A = \frac{1}{2}\int_{\alpha}^{\beta} [g(\theta)]^2\,d\theta = \frac{1}{2}\int_{\alpha}^{\beta} r^2\,d\theta$$ Textbook Section 10.5, Theorem 10.13
Core Concept • §1

1. Polar Sectors & Why $dA = r\,dr\,d\theta$

Intuition: Instead of covering a circular region $R$ with little Cartesian squares of area $\Delta x\,\Delta y$, imagine laying down a spiderweb grid of concentric circles (radii $r_1, r_2, \dots$) and radial rays (angles $\theta_1, \theta_2, \dots$). Each tiny wedge $R_i$ in this grid is a polar sector.

Notice that two wedges with the exact same $\Delta r_i$ and $\Delta\theta_i$ do not have the same area. A wedge far from the origin has a much longer circular arc $r_i \Delta\theta_i$ than one hugging the origin, so the area stretches proportionally to the radius $r_i$.

Note (Instructor Notes vs. Book): The textbook motivates the factor $r$ geometrically via the polar sector area (deferring the formal Jacobian determinant to Section 14.8): $$\Delta A_i = r_i\,\Delta r_i\,\Delta\theta_i$$ $$\frac{\partial(x,y)}{\partial(r,\theta)} = r$$ Dr. Alhumaidy’s notes always write regions directly in explicit set-builder form beside the sketch and treat the extra $r$ in $dA = r\,dr\,d\theta$ as the mandatory first check before integrating: $$R = \big\{(r, \theta) : r_1 \le r \le r_2,\; \theta_1 \le \theta \le \theta_2\big\}$$ Textbook pp. 990–991 & Instructor Notes
Polar sector $R_i$ in the $xy$-plane Corresponding rectangle $S_i$ in the $r\theta$-plane Average sample point $(r_i, \theta_i)$

A rectangle in the r-theta plane maps to a polar sector in the xy-plane whose area is scaled by the average radius, supplying the extra radial factor in the area element.

Theorem 14.3: Change of Variables to Polar Form

Let $R$ be a plane region consisting of all points $(x, y) = (r\cos\theta, r\sin\theta)$ satisfying the bounds:

$$0 \le g_1(\theta) \le r \le g_2(\theta)$$ $$\alpha \le \theta \le \beta \quad (0 \le \beta - \alpha \le 2\pi)$$

If $g_1$ and $g_2$ are continuous on $[\alpha, \beta]$ and $f$ is continuous on $R$, then:

$$\iint_R f(x, y)\,dA = \int_{\alpha}^{\beta} \int_{g_1(\theta)}^{g_2(\theta)} f(r\cos\theta, r\sin\theta)\,r\,dr\,d\theta$$ Textbook p. 992, Theorem 14.3
Example: Quarter-Annulus in Polar Coordinates
Evaluate $\displaystyle\iint_R (x^2 + y^2)\,dA$, where $R$ is the first-quadrant quarter-annulus defined by: $$1 \le x^2 + y^2 \le 9,\quad x \ge 0,\quad y \ge 0$$
Step 1: Describe the region and integrand in polar coordinates. The circular bounds $1 \le r^2 \le 9$ (with $r \ge 0$) give $1 \le r \le 3$, and the first quadrant corresponds to $0 \le \theta \le \tfrac{\pi}{2}$: $$R = \left\{(r, \theta) : 1 \le r \le 3,\; 0 \le \theta \le \frac{\pi}{2}\right\}$$
Step 2: Apply Theorem 14.3 with $x^2 + y^2 = r^2$ and $dA = r\,dr\,d\theta$. Since the limits are constant and the integrand separates, integrate $r$ and $\theta$ independently: $$\begin{aligned} \iint_R (x^2 + y^2)\,dA &= \int_{0}^{\pi/2} \int_{1}^{3} r^2 \cdot r\,dr\,d\theta \\ &= \left(\int_{0}^{\pi/2} d\theta\right)\left(\int_{1}^{3} r^3\,dr\right) \\ &= \frac{\pi}{2}\left[\frac{r^4}{4}\right]_{1}^{3} \\ &= \frac{\pi}{2} \cdot \frac{81 - 1}{4} = 10\pi \end{aligned}$$
Step 3: Verify the magnitude via area bounds. The quarter-annulus has area $\tfrac{1}{4}\pi(3^2 - 1^2) = 2\pi$, and on $R$ the integrand satisfies $1 \le r^2 \le 9$, so the integral must lie between $2\pi$ and $18\pi$: $$2\pi < 10\pi < 18\pi$$
Answer: $$\iint_R (x^2 + y^2)\,dA = 10\pi$$
Adapted from Textbook p. 990, Example 1b
Why It Works: Area of a Polar Sector

The exact area of the polar sector between radii $r_1, r_2$ and angles $\theta_1, \theta_2$ is the difference of two circular sectors:

$$\begin{aligned} \Delta A_i &= \frac{1}{2}r_2^2\Delta\theta_i - \frac{1}{2}r_1^2\Delta\theta_i \\ &= \frac{r_2 + r_1}{2}(r_2 - r_1)\Delta\theta_i \\ &= r_i\,\Delta r_i\,\Delta\theta_i \end{aligned}$$

Here $r_i = \tfrac{1}{2}(r_1 + r_2)$ is the average radius. Summing the sector contributions gives a Riemann sum over the $r\theta$-rectangle $S$ for the integrand $f(r\cos\theta, r\sin\theta)\,r$:

$$\sum_{i=1}^{n} f(r_i\cos\theta_i, r_i\sin\theta_i)\,r_i\,\Delta r_i\,\Delta\theta_i$$ Textbook p. 997, Exercise 68
Quick Check 1

Let $R$ be the first-quadrant quarter-annulus $1 \le x^2 + y^2 \le 4$ with $x \ge 0$ and $y \ge 0$. Which iterated integral equals the double integral below?

$$\iint_R \sqrt{x^2 + y^2}\,dA$$
(A) $$\int_{0}^{\pi/2}\int_{1}^{2} r\,dr\,d\theta$$
(B) $$\int_{0}^{\pi/2}\int_{1}^{2} r^2\,dr\,d\theta$$
(C) $$\int_{0}^{\pi/2}\int_{1}^{4} r^2\,dr\,d\theta$$
(D) $$\int_{0}^{\pi}\int_{1}^{2} r^2\,dr\,d\theta$$
Check Answer & Reason

Answer: (B). Since $x^2 + y^2 = r^2$ and $r \ge 0$, the integrand simplifies to $r$, and multiplying by $dA = r\,dr\,d\theta$ yields $r \cdot r = r^2$.

Also $1 \le r^2 \le 4$ gives $1 \le r \le 2$, and the first quadrant corresponds to $0 \le \theta \le \tfrac{\pi}{2}$.

Core Concept • §2

2. $r$-Simple vs. $\theta$-Simple Regions via Radial Ray Sweep

Intuition: Just as rectangular regions split into vertically simple ($dy\,dx$) and horizontally simple ($dx\,dy$) types, polar regions split into $r$-simple and $\theta$-simple regions.

To set up an $r$-simple region, stand at the origin and fire a radial ray outward at an arbitrary angle $\theta$: the curve where the ray enters $R$ is $r_{\text{in}} = g_1(\theta)$ and the curve where it exits $R$ is $r_{\text{out}} = g_2(\theta)$, while you sweep the ray from $\theta = \alpha$ to $\theta = \beta$.

If a radial ray would exit through two different curves (such as a spiral plus a circle), switch to a $\theta$-simple slice: fix a radius $r \in [r_1, r_2]$ and sweep an arc counterclockwise from $\theta = h_1(r)$ to $\theta = h_2(r)$.

Radial ray sweep ($r$-simple) Circular arc sweep ($\theta$-simple) Spiral boundary $r\theta = \tfrac{\pi}{3}$

For r-simple regions, integrate the radius first along a radial ray between the entry and exit curves; for theta-simple regions, integrate the angle first along a circular arc.

$r$-Simple and $\theta$-Simple Polar Iterated Integrals

$r$-Simple Order ($dr\,d\theta$): Fixed angle bounds $\alpha \le \theta \le \beta$ and radial bounds from $g_1(\theta)$ to $g_2(\theta)$ ($0 \le g_1(\theta) \le r$):

$$\iint_R f(x, y)\,dA = \int_{\alpha}^{\beta} \int_{g_1(\theta)}^{g_2(\theta)} f(r\cos\theta, r\sin\theta)\,r\,dr\,d\theta$$

$\theta$-Simple Order ($d\theta\,dr$): Fixed radius bounds $r_1 \le r \le r_2$ and angular bounds from $h_1(r)$ to $h_2(r)$ ($0 \le h_1(r) \le \theta$):

$$\iint_R f(x, y)\,dA = \int_{r_1}^{r_2} \int_{h_1(r)}^{h_2(r)} f(r\cos\theta, r\sin\theta)\,r\,d\theta\,dr$$ Textbook pp. 992, 994
Example: Integrating Respecting $\theta$ First on a Spiral Region
Find the area of the region $R$ bounded above by the spiral and below by the polar axis $\theta = 0$, between $r = 1$ and $r = 2$: $$r = \frac{\pi}{3\theta}$$
Step 1: Solve for $\theta$ in terms of $r$ to set up $\theta$-simple bounds. Inverting the spiral equation gives $\theta$ as a function of $r$, yielding clean bounds on $1 \le r \le 2$: $$\theta = \frac{\pi}{3r}, \quad 0 \le \theta \le \frac{\pi}{3r}$$
Step 2: Integrate $d\theta\,dr$ with $dA = r\,d\theta\,dr$. Integrating $\theta$ first cancels the factor $r$ immediately: $$\begin{aligned} A &= \int_{1}^{2} \int_{0}^{\pi/(3r)} r\,d\theta\,dr \\ &= \int_{1}^{2} \Big[r\theta\Big]_{0}^{\pi/(3r)} dr \\ &= \int_{1}^{2} r\left(\frac{\pi}{3r}\right) dr \\ &= \int_{1}^{2} \frac{\pi}{3}\,dr = \left[\frac{\pi r}{3}\right]_{1}^{2} = \frac{\pi}{3} \end{aligned}$$
Step 3: Verify by bounding with two annular sectors. On $1 \le r \le 2$, the upper angle satisfies: $$\frac{\pi}{6} \le \frac{\pi}{3r} \le \frac{\pi}{3}$$

Thus $R$ contains the $\tfrac{\pi}{6}$-sector of the annulus and lies inside the $\tfrac{\pi}{3}$-sector, so the area lies between $\tfrac{\pi}{4}$ and $\tfrac{\pi}{2}$:

$$A_{\min} = \frac{1}{2}(2^2 - 1^2)\frac{\pi}{6} = \frac{\pi}{4} < \frac{\pi}{3} < \frac{\pi}{2}$$
Answer: $$A = \frac{\pi}{3}$$
Textbook p. 994, Example 5
Why It Works: Avoiding Split Exit Curves

Look at Diagram 2(b) above: if you tried $dr\,d\theta$ on this spiral region, a radial ray would exit at $r = 2$ for $0 \le \theta \le \pi/6$ and exit at the spiral for $\pi/6 \le \theta \le \pi/3$, forcing two separate integrals.

Instead, circular arcs of constant radius $r \in [1, 2]$ enter cleanly at $\theta = 0$ and exit at the spiral in a single integral:

$$0 \le \theta \le \frac{\pi}{3r}$$
Quick Check 2

Let $R$ be the first-quadrant region bounded by $r = 1$, $r = 3$, $\theta = 0$, and the spiral $r\theta = 1$. Which setup evaluates $\iint_R dA$ as a single iterated integral?

(A) $$\int_{0}^{1}\int_{1}^{3} r\,dr\,d\theta$$
(B) $$\int_{1}^{3}\int_{0}^{1/r} r\,d\theta\,dr$$
(C) $$\int_{0}^{1/3}\int_{1}^{3} r\,dr\,d\theta$$
(D) $$\int_{1}^{3}\int_{0}^{1/r} d\theta\,dr$$
Check Answer & Reason

Answer: (B). Solving $r\theta = 1$ for $\theta$ gives the upper angle bound $\theta = 1/r$ on $1 \le r \le 3$, making $R$ $\theta$-simple.

Do not forget the factor $r$ in $dA = r\,d\theta\,dr$, which eliminates choice (D).

Core Concept • §3

3. Shifted Circles ($r = 2a\cos\theta$, $r = 2a\sin\theta$), Roses, Cardioids & Lines ($x = c$)

Intuition: Circles centered away from the origin — like $(x - a)^2 + y^2 = a^2$ or $x^2 + (y - a)^2 = a^2$ — still pass through $(0,0)$, so a radial ray starting at the origin enters at $r = 0$ and exits on the circle.

The critical exam skill is matching the exact $\theta$-interval where $r(\theta) \ge 0$ so you trace the curve once without entering negative-$r$ territory.

Similarly, vertical lines $x = c$ convert via $r = c\sec\theta$, while roses $r = a\cos(n\theta)$ or $r = a\sin(n\theta)$ require finding consecutive angles where $r = 0$ to isolate a single petal.

Note (Instructor Notes vs. Book): Dr. Alhumaidy’s notes mark shifted circles and rose curves as “important” and emphasize three exam habits:
  1. Complete the square on expressions like $x^2 + y^2 = 2ax$ to spot $(x - a)^2 + y^2 = a^2$, which converts to $r = 2a\cos\theta$.
  2. Build a quick $(\theta, r)$ table to trace one petal and verify $r \ge 0$ rather than guessing limits.
  3. Check whether an inner boundary vanishes before the outer boundary ends (e.g., inside $r = 1+\cos\theta$ and outside $r = 3\cos\theta$, the circle hits $r = 0$ at $\theta = \tfrac{\pi}{2}$ while the cardioid continues to $\theta = \pi$, splitting the integral at $\tfrac{\pi}{2}$).
Textbook pp. 995–996 & Instructor Notes
Horizontal shifted circle $r = 2a\cos\theta$ Vertical shifted circle $r = 2a\sin\theta$ Single petal of rose $r = 2\sin 3\theta$

Shifted circles passing through the origin require half-plane angular intervals so the radius stays nonnegative, while odd-petal roses trace a single petal between consecutive zeros of the radius.

Standard Polar Curves, Shifted Circles, and Line Bounds
  • Horizontal shifted circle $(x - a)^2 + y^2 = a^2$ ($a > 0$): $r = 2a\cos\theta$ on $-\pi/2 \le \theta \le \pi/2$ (upper half: $0 \le \theta \le \pi/2$).
  • Vertical shifted circle $x^2 + (y - a)^2 = a^2$ ($a > 0$): $r = 2a\sin\theta$ on $0 \le \theta \le \pi$ (first-quadrant half: $0 \le \theta \le \pi/2$).
  • Vertical / horizontal lines: $x = c$ converts to $r = c\sec\theta$, and $y = c$ converts to $r = c\csc\theta$.
  • Cardioids $r = a \pm a\cos\theta$ or $r = a \pm a\sin\theta$: $0 \le r \le r(\theta)$ with $0 \le \theta \le 2\pi$ (always $r \ge 0$; for example, $r = 1 + \cos\theta$ has area $\tfrac{3\pi}{2}$).
  • Rose curves $r = a\cos(n\theta)$ or $r = a\sin(n\theta)$: $n$ petals if $n$ is odd; $2n$ petals if $n$ is even. Find one petal by solving $r(\theta) = 0$ for two adjacent roots where $r(\theta) \ge 0$.
Textbook pp. 994–996 & Instructor Notes
Example: Total Area of a Three-Petal Rose
Find the total area enclosed by the 3-petal rose: $$r = 3\cos 3\theta$$
Step 1: Find the angular bounds for one petal. Set $r = 0$ to locate the tangent rays framing the right-hand petal where $\cos 3\theta \ge 0$: $$3\cos 3\theta = 0 \implies 3\theta = \pm\frac{\pi}{2} \implies \theta = \pm\frac{\pi}{6}$$
Step 2: Integrate over one petal and multiply by 3. By symmetry across the three identical petals: $$\begin{aligned} A &= 3\int_{-\pi/6}^{\pi/6}\int_{0}^{3\cos 3\theta} r\,dr\,d\theta \\ &= 3\int_{-\pi/6}^{\pi/6} \frac{9\cos^2 3\theta}{2}\,d\theta \\ &= \frac{27}{4}\int_{-\pi/6}^{\pi/6} (1 + \cos 6\theta)\,d\theta \\ &= \frac{27}{4}\left[\theta + \frac{1}{6}\sin 6\theta\right]_{-\pi/6}^{\pi/6} = \frac{27}{4}\cdot\frac{\pi}{3} = \frac{9\pi}{4} \end{aligned}$$
Step 3: Verify against the circumscribed disk. The rose sits inside the disk $r \le 3$ of area $\pi(3^2) = 9\pi$, and an odd-petal rose $r = a\cos(n\theta)$ covers one-quarter of its circumscribed disk: $$\frac{1}{4}(9\pi) = \frac{9\pi}{4}$$
Answer: $$A = \frac{9\pi}{4}$$
Textbook p. 994, Example 4
Why It Works: Enforcing Nonnegative Radius

Expanding $(x - a)^2 + y^2 = a^2$ gives $x^2 + y^2 = 2ax$, which simplifies in polar form to $r = 2a\cos\theta$.

Because Theorem 14.3 enforces $r \ge 0$, we must restrict $\theta$ so that $\cos\theta \ge 0$:

$$-\frac{\pi}{2} \le \theta \le \frac{\pi}{2}$$

Integrating over $0 \le \theta \le 2\pi$ instead would include Quadrants II and III where $\cos\theta < 0$, re-tracing the circle with negative $r$ and doubling the integral.

Quick Check 3

Which polar bounds describe the upper semicircular disk given below?

$$0 \le x \le 2$$ $$0 \le y \le \sqrt{2x - x^2}$$
(A) $0 \le \theta \le \pi$, $0 \le r \le 2\cos\theta$
(B) $0 \le \theta \le \tfrac{\pi}{2}$, $0 \le r \le 2\cos\theta$
(C) $-\pi/2 \le \theta \le \pi/2$, $0 \le r \le 2\cos\theta$
(D) $0 \le \theta \le \tfrac{\pi}{2}$, $0 \le r \le 2\sin\theta$
Check Answer & Reason

Answer: (B). Squaring the upper boundary gives $(x - 1)^2 + y^2 = 1$ with $y \ge 0$, which is the upper half of $r = 2\cos\theta$.

Because this upper half lies entirely in Quadrant I ($x \ge 0, y \ge 0$), the angle runs over $0 \le \theta \le \tfrac{\pi}{2}$.

Textbook p. 995, Exercises 6 & 23
Core Concept • §4

4. Converting Cartesian Integrals & Volumes to Polar Coordinates

Intuition: Two signals tell you to abandon rectangular $(x, y)$ coordinates and switch to polar: circular boundaries in the limits of integration, and radial expressions such as $x^2 + y^2$ or $e^{-(x^2+y^2)}$ in the integrand.

Common circular boundary radicals include:

$$\sqrt{a^2 - x^2}$$ $$\sqrt{a^2 - y^2}$$ $$\sqrt{2ax - x^2}$$

Even better, a sum of two awkward Cartesian integrals over adjacent triangles and circular caps often glues together into a single circular sector in polar coordinates.

Triangle $R_1$ ($0 \le y \le x$) Circular wedge $R_2$ below $x^2 + y^2 = 8$ Left half-disk ($x \le 0$)

Always sketch the Cartesian limits first: adjacent triangular and circular pieces can merge into a single sector, while a left half-disk spans from one-half pi to three-halves pi.

4-Step Conversion Protocol:

  1. Decode the limits: Sketch the bounding curves ($y \ge 0$ under $x^2 + y^2 = a^2$ is the upper semicircle; $x \ge 0$ is the right semicircle; $y = x$ is $\theta = \pi/4$ in Quadrant I).
  2. Read polar bounds: Use a radial ray sweep to find $g_1(\theta) \le r \le g_2(\theta)$ and $\alpha \le \theta \le \beta$ (remember: $x \ge 0$ gives $-\pi/2 \le \theta \le \pi/2$; $x \le 0$ gives $\pi/2 \le \theta \le 3\pi/2$).
  3. Transform integrand & $dA$: Replace $x = r\cos\theta$, $y = r\sin\theta$, $x^2 + y^2 = r^2$, and $dx\,dy$ or $dy\,dx$ by $r\,dr\,d\theta$.
  4. For Volumes: If a solid lies between $z = z_{\text{bottom}}(x, y)$ and $z = z_{\text{top}}(x, y)$ over a base $R$, convert both the height and $R$ to polar: $$V = \iint_R \big(z_{\text{top}} - z_{\text{bottom}}\big)\,dA$$
Example: Volume Inside a Hemisphere and Outside a Cylinder
Find the volume inside the upper hemisphere $z \ge 0$ and outside the cylinder $x^2 + y^2 = 1$, where the hemisphere surface is: $$z = \sqrt{16 - x^2 - y^2}$$
Step 1: Identify the annular base $R$ and polar height. The hemisphere meets $z = 0$ at $x^2 + y^2 = 16$ ($r = 4$). Outside $x^2 + y^2 = 1$ ($r = 1$), the base $R$ is the annulus $1 \le r \le 4$ with $0 \le \theta \le 2\pi$, and the height is: $$z = \sqrt{16 - r^2}$$
Step 2: Set up and evaluate the polar volume integral using $u = 16 - r^2$. Since $du = -2r\,dr$, the extra factor $r$ in $dA = r\,dr\,d\theta$ gives an immediate antiderivative: $$\begin{aligned} V &= \int_{0}^{2\pi}\int_{1}^{4} \sqrt{16 - r^2}\,r\,dr\,d\theta \\ &= 2\pi\left[-\frac{1}{3}(16 - r^2)^{3/2}\right]_{1}^{4} \\ &= \frac{2\pi}{3}\big(0 - (-15^{3/2})\big) = 10\sqrt{15}\pi \end{aligned}$$
Step 3: Verify against the full hemisphere volume. The entire hemisphere of radius $4$ has volume $\tfrac{128}{3}\pi \approx 134.04$. Removing the central cylindrical core leaves slightly less volume, matching the calculated value: $$10\sqrt{15}\pi \approx 121.67 < \frac{128\pi}{3}$$
Answer: $$V = 10\sqrt{15}\pi$$
Textbook p. 996, Exercise 38 & Instructor Notes
Why It Works: Jacobian Factor Unlocks $u$-Substitution

Notice how the Jacobian factor $r$ in $r\,dr\,d\theta$ is the exact derivative piece needed for $u$-substitution on $u = a^2 - r^2$ or $u = -r^2$ in Gaussian integrals:

$$\int \sqrt{a^2 - r^2}\,r\,dr = -\frac{1}{2}\int u^{1/2}\,du$$

Without that factor $r$, integrating the radical alone would require trigonometric substitution.

Quick Check 4

Which polar iterated integral equals the Cartesian integral below?

$$\int_{-4}^{4} \int_{0}^{\sqrt{16 - x^2}} \cos(x^2 + y^2)\,dy\,dx$$
(A) $$\int_{0}^{\pi} \int_{-4}^{4} r\cos(r^2)\,dr\,d\theta$$
(B) $$\int_{0}^{2\pi} \int_{0}^{4} r\cos(r^2)\,dr\,d\theta$$
(C) $$\int_{0}^{\pi} \int_{0}^{4} r\cos(r^2)\,dr\,d\theta$$
(D) $$\int_{0}^{\pi} \int_{0}^{4} \cos(r^2)\,dr\,d\theta$$
Check Answer & Reason

Answer: (C). Because $-4 \le x \le 4$ and $y$ runs from $0$ to the upper semicircle of $x^2 + y^2 = 16$, $R$ is the upper half-disk of radius $4$.

The upper half-disk spans $0 \le \theta \le \pi$ with nonnegative radius $0 \le r \le 4$ (never $-4$), and $dA = r\,dr\,d\theta$ rules out (D).

KFUPM Final Term 232, Q23
Master Formulas

Section 14.3 Formula Reference & Standard Regions

Core Laws, Bounds & Required Conditions

Coordinate Links & Area Element:

Rectangular-to-polar relations:

$$x = r\cos\theta$$ $$y = r\sin\theta$$ $$r^2 = x^2 + y^2$$ $$\tan\theta = \frac{y}{x}$$

Polar differential area element:

$$dA = r\,dr\,d\theta$$

$r$-Simple vs. $\theta$-Simple Polar Integrals:

For $r$-simple regions ($\alpha \le \theta \le \beta$ with $0 \le \beta - \alpha \le 2\pi$ and $0 \le g_1(\theta) \le r$ up to $g_2(\theta)$):

$$\iint_R f(x, y)\,dA = \int_{\alpha}^{\beta} \int_{g_1(\theta)}^{g_2(\theta)} f(r\cos\theta, r\sin\theta)\,r\,dr\,d\theta$$

For $\theta$-simple regions ($0 \le h_1(r) \le \theta \le h_2(r)$ on $r_1 \le r \le r_2$):

$$\iint_R f(x, y)\,dA = \int_{r_1}^{r_2} \int_{h_1(r)}^{h_2(r)} f(r\cos\theta, r\sin\theta)\,r\,d\theta\,dr$$

Area & Volume via Polar Double Integrals:

Area of a region $R$ (reduces to Theorem 10.13 when $g_1(\theta) = 0$):

$$A = \iint_R 1\,dA = \int_{\alpha}^{\beta} \int_{g_1(\theta)}^{g_2(\theta)} r\,dr\,d\theta$$

Volume between two surfaces $z_{\text{bottom}}(x, y)$ and $z_{\text{top}}(x, y)$ over $R$:

$$V = \iint_R \big(z_{\text{top}} - z_{\text{bottom}}\big)\,dA$$

Essential Half-Plane & Shifted-Circle $\theta$-Intervals ($r \ge 0$):

  • Disk $x^2+y^2 \le a^2$: $0 \le r \le a$, $0 \le \theta \le 2\pi$.
  • Upper half-disk ($y \ge 0$): $0 \le \theta \le \pi$.
  • Right half-disk ($x \ge 0$): $-\pi/2 \le \theta \le \pi/2$.
  • Left half-disk ($x \le 0$): $\pi/2 \le \theta \le 3\pi/2$.
  • Shifted circle $(x-a)^2 + y^2 = a^2$: $r = 2a\cos\theta$, $-\pi/2 \le \theta \le \pi/2$ (upper half: $0 \le \theta \le \pi/2$).
  • Shifted circle $x^2 + (y-a)^2 = a^2$: $r = 2a\sin\theta$, $0 \le \theta \le \pi$ (right half: $0 \le \theta \le \pi/2$).
  • Vertical line $x = c$ converts to $r = c\sec\theta$; horizontal line $y = c$ converts to $r = c\csc\theta$.

Half-Angle Identities & Separability Shortcut:

Cosine squared reduction:

$$\cos^2(k\theta) = \frac{1 + \cos(2k\theta)}{2}$$

Sine squared reduction:

$$\sin^2(k\theta) = \frac{1 - \cos(2k\theta)}{2}$$

If all four limits are constants and the integrand factors as $h(r)k(\theta)$, the double integral separates into a product:

$$\int_{\alpha}^{\beta} \int_{a}^{b} h(r)k(\theta)\,dr\,d\theta = \left(\int_{a}^{b} h(r)\,dr\right)\left(\int_{\alpha}^{\beta} k(\theta)\,d\theta\right)$$ Textbook pp. 990–994 & Instructor Notes
Exam Traps

5 Classic Mistakes (WRONG vs. RIGHT)

Trap 1 — Dropping the polar factor $r$ in $dA = r\,dr\,d\theta$:

WrongWriting: $$\iint_R \sqrt{x^2 + y^2}\,dA = \int_{\alpha}^{\beta} \int_{g_1}^{g_2} r\,dr\,d\theta$$
RightThe integrand itself equals $r$, and $dA = r\,dr\,d\theta$, so the combined integrand is $r \cdot r = r^2$: $$\iint_R \sqrt{x^2 + y^2}\,dA = \int_{\alpha}^{\beta} \int_{g_1}^{g_2} r^2\,dr\,d\theta$$

Trap 2 — Using $0 \le \theta \le 2\pi$ on a shifted circle $r = 2a\cos\theta$ or $r = 2a\sin\theta$:

WrongSetting $0 \le \theta \le 2\pi$ for $r = 2\cos\theta$ or $r = 4\sin\theta$ (double-counts the area or makes $r < 0$).
RightKeep $r \ge 0$: use $-\pi/2 \le \theta \le \pi/2$ for $r = 2a\cos\theta$, and $0 \le \theta \le \pi$ for $r = 2a\sin\theta$.

Trap 3 — Writing negative lower limits for $r$ or confusing a line $x = c$ with a circle:

WrongUsing $-4 \le r \le 4$ for the upper half-disk of radius $4$, or writing $x = 3 \implies r = 3$.
RightRadius is always $r \ge 0$ ($0 \le r \le 4$ for the half-disk), while a vertical line $x = c$ converts to $r = c\sec\theta$.

Trap 4 — Mixing up $\theta$-intervals for half-disks and $y = x$ sectors:

WrongUsing $0 \le \theta \le \pi$ for $x \le 0$ (that is $y \ge 0$), or using $0 \le \theta \le \pi/4$ for $0 \le x \le y$.
Right$x \le 0$ is $\pi/2 \le \theta \le 3\pi/2$; $x \ge 0$ is $-\pi/2 \le \theta \le \pi/2$; $0 \le y \le x$ is $0 \le \theta \le \pi/4$; $0 \le x \le y$ is $\pi/4 \le \theta \le \pi/2$.

Trap 5 — Missing an angular split when the inner curve hits $r = 0$:

WrongFor the region inside $r = 1+\cos\theta$ and outside $r = 3\cos\theta$, integrating without splitting at $\tfrac{\pi}{2}$: $$2\int_{\pi/3}^{\pi} \int_{3\cos\theta}^{1+\cos\theta} r\,dr\,d\theta$$
RightSince $3\cos\theta$ hits $0$ at $\theta = \tfrac{\pi}{2}$, split the integral at $\tfrac{\pi}{2}$: $$2\left[\int_{\pi/3}^{\pi/2}\int_{3\cos\theta}^{1+\cos\theta} r\,dr\,d\theta + \int_{\pi/2}^{\pi}\int_{0}^{1+\cos\theta} r\,dr\,d\theta\right]$$
Textbook p. 996, Exercise 50 & Instructor Notes
Worked Examples

From Textbook Basics to KFUPM Final Level

Example 1: Evaluating a Double Integral Over an Annulus
Let $R$ be the annular region lying between the two circles $x^2 + y^2 = 1$ and $x^2 + y^2 = 5$. Evaluate: $$\iint_R (x^2 + y)\,dA$$
Step 1: Set up polar bounds and transform the integrand. The concentric circles give $1 \le r^2 \le 5$ around $0 \le \theta \le 2\pi$, with $x = r\cos\theta$, $y = r\sin\theta$, and $dA = r\,dr\,d\theta$: $$1 \le r \le \sqrt{5}$$ $$\begin{aligned} \iint_R (x^2 + y)\,dA &= \int_{0}^{2\pi} \int_{1}^{\sqrt{5}} (r^2\cos^2\theta + r\sin\theta)\,r\,dr\,d\theta \\ &= \int_{0}^{2\pi} \int_{1}^{\sqrt{5}} (r^3\cos^2\theta + r^2\sin\theta)\,dr\,d\theta \end{aligned}$$
Step 2: Evaluate the inner $r$-integral. Integrate term by term with respect to $r$: $$\begin{aligned} \int_{1}^{\sqrt{5}} (r^3\cos^2\theta + r^2\sin\theta)\,dr &= \left[\frac{r^4}{4}\cos^2\theta + \frac{r^3}{3}\sin\theta\right]_{1}^{\sqrt{5}} \\ &= \left(\frac{25}{4} - \frac{1}{4}\right)\cos^2\theta + \left(\frac{5\sqrt{5} - 1}{3}\right)\sin\theta \\ &= 6\cos^2\theta + \frac{5\sqrt{5} - 1}{3}\sin\theta \end{aligned}$$
Step 3: Apply the half-angle identity and integrate with respect to $\theta$. Replace $6\cos^2\theta$ with $3 + 3\cos 2\theta$ and integrate over $[0, 2\pi]$: $$\begin{aligned} \int_{0}^{2\pi} \left(3 + 3\cos 2\theta + \frac{5\sqrt{5} - 1}{3}\sin\theta\right) d\theta &= \left[3\theta + \frac{3}{2}\sin 2\theta - \frac{5\sqrt{5} - 1}{3}\cos\theta\right]_{0}^{2\pi} \\ &= \left(6\pi + 0 - \frac{5\sqrt{5} - 1}{3}\right) - \left(0 + 0 - \frac{5\sqrt{5} - 1}{3}\right) \\ &= 6\pi \end{aligned}$$
Step 4: Verify using symmetry. By symmetry across the $x$-axis, $\iint_R y\,dA = 0$, and by rotational symmetry: $$\iint_R x^2\,dA = \frac{1}{2}\iint_R (x^2 + y^2)\,dA = \frac{1}{2}(2\pi)\int_{1}^{\sqrt{5}} r^3\,dr = \pi\left[\frac{r^4}{4}\right]_{1}^{\sqrt{5}} = 6\pi$$
Answer: $$\iint_R (x^2 + y)\,dA = 6\pi$$
Textbook p. 992, Example 2 & Instructor Notes
Example 2: Converting a Shifted-Circle Boundary to $r = 2\cos\theta$
Evaluate the iterated integral by converting to polar coordinates: $$\int_{0}^{2} \int_{0}^{\sqrt{2x - x^2}} xy\,dy\,dx$$
Step 1: Complete the square to identify the shifted circle. The bounds are $0 \le x \le 2$ and $y$ runs from $0$ up to the upper circular boundary: $$0 \le y \le \sqrt{2x - x^2}$$

Squaring this upper boundary (with $y \ge 0$) reveals the upper half of a circle of radius $1$ centered at $(1, 0)$:

$$x^2 - 2x + y^2 = 0 \implies (x - 1)^2 + y^2 = 1$$

In polar coordinates, $x^2 + y^2 = 2x$ becomes $r = 2\cos\theta$, and since $R$ lies entirely in Quadrant I ($x \ge 0, y \ge 0$), a radial ray sweeps $0 \le \theta \le \pi/2$ with $0 \le r \le 2\cos\theta$.

Step 2: Transform the integral and evaluate $r$ first. Substitute $x = r\cos\theta$, $y = r\sin\theta$, and $dy\,dx = r\,dr\,d\theta$: $$\begin{aligned} \int_{0}^{2} \int_{0}^{\sqrt{2x - x^2}} xy\,dy\,dx &= \int_{0}^{\pi/2} \int_{0}^{2\cos\theta} (r\cos\theta)(r\sin\theta)\,r\,dr\,d\theta \\ &= \int_{0}^{\pi/2} \cos\theta\sin\theta \left[\frac{r^4}{4}\right]_{0}^{2\cos\theta} d\theta \\ &= \int_{0}^{\pi/2} \cos\theta\sin\theta \cdot \frac{16\cos^4\theta}{4}\,d\theta \\ &= 4\int_{0}^{\pi/2} \cos^5\theta\,\sin\theta\,d\theta \end{aligned}$$
Step 3: Evaluate the $\theta$-integral via $u = \cos\theta$. With $du = -\sin\theta\,d\theta$, $\theta: 0 \to \tfrac{\pi}{2}$ maps to $u: 1 \to 0$: $$4\int_{1}^{0} u^5(-du) = 4\int_{0}^{1} u^5\,du = 4\left[\frac{u^6}{6}\right]_{0}^{1} = \frac{2}{3}$$
Upper semicircle $(x-1)^2 + y^2 = 1$, $y \ge 0$ Radial ray entering at $r=0$ and exiting at $r = 2\cos\theta$

Exact scale plot of the upper semicircle centered at (1, 0) with radius 1: a radial ray in the first quadrant enters at the origin and exits along the circle.

Step 4: Verify directly in Cartesian coordinates. Evaluating the inner $y$-integral first gives the same result: $$\int_{0}^{2} x \left[\frac{y^2}{2}\right]_{0}^{\sqrt{2x-x^2}} dx = \frac{1}{2}\int_{0}^{2} (2x^2 - x^3)\,dx = \frac{1}{2}\left[\frac{2x^3}{3} - \frac{x^4}{4}\right]_{0}^{2} = \frac{2}{3}$$
Answer: $$\int_{0}^{2} \int_{0}^{\sqrt{2x - x^2}} xy\,dy\,dx = \frac{2}{3}$$
Textbook p. 995, Exercise 23 & Instructor Notes
Example 3: Left Half-Disk Gaussian Integral
Let $R$ be the left half-disk described below, and evaluate the double integral: $$R = \big\{(x, y) : x^2 + y^2 \le 4,\; x \le 0\big\}$$ $$\iint_R e^{-(x^2 + y^2)/2}\,dA$$
Step 1: Convert the region $R$ to polar coordinates. The disk $x^2 + y^2 \le 4$ gives $0 \le r \le 2$, while $x \le 0$ restricts $\theta$ to Quadrants II and III (from the positive $y$-axis to the negative $y$-axis): $$R = \left\{(r, \theta) : 0 \le r \le 2,\; \frac{\pi}{2} \le \theta \le \frac{3\pi}{2}\right\}$$
Step 2: Rewrite the integrand and separate the variables. Substitute $x^2 + y^2 = r^2$ and $dA = r\,dr\,d\theta$, then factor the constant-limit integral: $$\begin{aligned} \iint_R e^{-(x^2 + y^2)/2}\,dA &= \int_{\pi/2}^{3\pi/2} \int_{0}^{2} r e^{-r^2/2}\,dr\,d\theta \\ &= \left(\int_{\pi/2}^{3\pi/2} d\theta\right)\left(\int_{0}^{2} r e^{-r^2/2}\,dr\right) \end{aligned}$$
Step 3: Evaluate using $u = -r^2/2$. Since $du = -r\,dr$, integrating $r$ from $0$ to $2$ and multiplying by the angular span $\pi$ gives: $$\begin{aligned} \left(\frac{3\pi}{2} - \frac{\pi}{2}\right)\left[-e^{-r^2/2}\right]_{0}^{2} &= \pi\big(-e^{-2} - (-1)\big) \\ &= (1 - e^{-2})\pi \end{aligned}$$
Step 4: Verify bounds using area and integrand extrema. The half-disk has area $\tfrac{1}{2}\pi(2^2) = 2\pi$, and on $R$ the integrand satisfies $e^{-2} \le e^{-r^2/2} \le 1$, so the value must lie between $2\pi e^{-2} \approx 0.85$ and $2\pi \approx 6.28$: $$2\pi e^{-2} < (1 - e^{-2})\pi \approx 2.72 < 2\pi$$
Answer: $$\iint_R e^{-(x^2 + y^2)/2}\,dA = (1 - e^{-2})\pi$$
KFUPM Final Term 253, Q17
Example 4: Converting a $dx\,dy$ Sector Bounded by $x = y$
Evaluate the iterated integral: $$\int_{0}^{3/\sqrt{2}} \int_{y}^{\sqrt{9 - y^2}} \sqrt{x^2 + y^2}\,dx\,dy$$
Step 1: Decode the $dx\,dy$ bounds into polar limits. Horizontal slices run from the line $x = y$ ($\theta = \pi/4$) on the left to the circle $x^2 + y^2 = 9$ ($r = 3$) on the right, meeting in Quadrant I at the intersection point above $y = 0$ ($\theta = 0$): $$x = y = \frac{3}{\sqrt{2}}$$

Angular bounds:

$$0 \le \theta \le \frac{\pi}{4}$$

Radial bounds:

$$0 \le r \le 3$$
Step 2: Substitute the polar integrand and area element $dx\,dy = r\,dr\,d\theta$. Since $r \ge 0$, the radial integrand simplifies directly and factors over the constant limits: $$\sqrt{x^2 + y^2} = r$$ $$\int_{0}^{3/\sqrt{2}} \int_{y}^{\sqrt{9 - y^2}} \sqrt{x^2 + y^2}\,dx\,dy = \int_{0}^{\pi/4} \int_{0}^{3} r \cdot r\,dr\,d\theta = \left(\int_{0}^{\pi/4} d\theta\right)\left(\int_{0}^{3} r^2\,dr\right)$$
Step 3: Compute the final value. Evaluate both single integrals: $$\frac{\pi}{4} \cdot \left[\frac{r^3}{3}\right]_{0}^{3} = \frac{\pi}{4} \cdot \frac{27}{3} = \frac{9\pi}{4}$$
Step 4: Verify using sector area and average radius. The $\tfrac{\pi}{4}$-sector of radius $3$ has area $\tfrac{1}{8}\pi(3^2) = \tfrac{9\pi}{8}$, and the average radial distance on a disk or sector of radius $R$ is $\bar{r} = \tfrac{2}{3}R = 2$: $$\text{Area} \times \bar{r} = \frac{9\pi}{8} \cdot 2 = \frac{9\pi}{4}$$
Answer: $$\int_{0}^{3/\sqrt{2}} \int_{y}^{\sqrt{9 - y^2}} \sqrt{x^2 + y^2}\,dx\,dy = \frac{9\pi}{4}$$
KFUPM Final Term 251, Q18
Example 5: Gluing Two Cartesian Regions Into One Polar Sector
Write the sum of the two iterated integrals as a single polar iterated integral and evaluate: $$\int_{0}^{2} \int_{0}^{x} \sqrt{x^2 + y^2}\,dy\,dx + \int_{2}^{2\sqrt{2}} \int_{0}^{\sqrt{8 - x^2}} \sqrt{x^2 + y^2}\,dy\,dx$$
Step 1: Identify $R_1$ and $R_2$ and check their seam at $x = 2$. Region $R_1$ ($0 \le x \le 2$, $0 \le y \le x$) is the triangle below $y = x$ up to $x = 2$, while $R_2$ is bounded above by the circle $x^2 + y^2 = 8$: $$2 \le x \le 2\sqrt{2},\quad 0 \le y \le \sqrt{8 - x^2}$$

As shown in Diagram 4(a), the ray $y = x$ intersects $x^2 + y^2 = 8$ at $2x^2 = 8$, which gives $(2, 2)$ right on the seam $x = 2$, merging $R_1 \cup R_2$ into one sector of radius $R_{\max}$ over $0 \le \theta \le \pi/4$:

$$R_{\max} = \sqrt{8} = 2\sqrt{2}$$
Step 2: Collapse into one polar integral and evaluate. Replacing the radical with $r$ and setting $dA = r\,dr\,d\theta$ merges both integrals into one: $$\begin{aligned} I &= \int_{0}^{\pi/4} \int_{0}^{2\sqrt{2}} r \cdot r\,dr\,d\theta \\ &= \left(\int_{0}^{\pi/4} d\theta\right)\left(\int_{0}^{2\sqrt{2}} r^2\,dr\right) \\ &= \frac{\pi}{4} \cdot \left[\frac{r^3}{3}\right]_{0}^{2\sqrt{2}} \\ &= \frac{\pi}{4} \cdot \frac{16\sqrt{2}}{3} = \frac{4\sqrt{2}\pi}{3} \end{aligned}$$
Step 3: Verify with the sector formula $\tfrac{\pi}{12}R_{\max}^3$. Substituting the outer radius into the $\pi/4$-sector integral checked in Example 4 confirms the value: $$\frac{\pi}{12}(2\sqrt{2})^3 = \frac{\pi}{12}(16\sqrt{2}) = \frac{4\sqrt{2}\pi}{3}$$
Answer: $$\int_{0}^{\pi/4}\int_{0}^{2\sqrt{2}} r^2\,dr\,d\theta = \frac{4\sqrt{2}\pi}{3}$$
KFUPM Final Term 243, Q6 & Textbook p. 995, Exercise 27
One-Screen Summary

The 5 Things to Know for the Exam

  1. Never forget the polar factor $r$ in $dA = r\,dr\,d\theta$: Every Cartesian area element $dx\,dy$ or $dy\,dx$ becomes $r\,dr\,d\theta$ with $r \ge 0$, so integrating a radial integrand gives $r^2$: $$\iint_R \sqrt{x^2 + y^2}\,dA = \iint_R r^2\,dr\,d\theta$$
  2. Sketch first and fire a radial ray from $(0,0)$: Entry curve is $g_1(\theta)$ and exit curve is $g_2(\theta)$; if a ray hits two different exit curves (or the boundary is $r\theta = c$), switch to $\theta$-simple order $r\,d\theta\,dr$.
  3. Lock in shifted-circle and half-plane $\theta$-bounds: Use $-\pi/2 \le \theta \le \pi/2$ for $r = 2a\cos\theta$, use $0 \le \theta \le \pi$ for $r = 2a\sin\theta$, and use $\pi/2 \le \theta \le 3\pi/2$ for the left half-disk ($x \le 0$).
  4. Handle roses and overlapping boundaries with a $(\theta, r)$ table: Solve $r(\theta) = 0$ for one petal of a rose, and split the $\theta$-integral whenever an inner boundary (like $r = 3\cos\theta$) reaches $r = 0$ before the outer curve ends.
  5. Separate constant-limit integrals and merge split Cartesian sectors: When limits are constant and the integrand factors as $h(r)k(\theta)$, evaluate the product of the two 1D integrals, and check whether adjacent Cartesian integrals (triangle + circular arc) combine into one clean sector: $$\int_{\alpha}^{\beta}\int_{a}^{b} h(r)k(\theta)\,dr\,d\theta = \left(\int_{a}^{b} h(r)\,dr\right)\left(\int_{\alpha}^{\beta} k(\theta)\,d\theta\right)$$
