What You Already Know

In Section 14.3, you converted 2D double integrals over disks and shifted circles ($r = 2a\cos\theta$, $r = 2a\sin\theta$) to polar coordinates using $x^2 + y^2 = r^2$ and $dA = r\,dr\,d\theta$. In Section 14.6, you evaluated triple integrals $\iiint_Q f(x, y, z)\,dV$ in rectangular coordinates by projecting $Q$ onto a shadow $R$ and integrating vertically from $z_1(x,y)$ to $z_2(x,y)$.

Back in Section 11.7, you defined cylindrical $(r, \theta, z)$ and spherical $(\rho, \theta, \phi)$ coordinates in $\mathbb{R}^3$. Section 14.7 unites these tools to turn awkward square-root rectangular bounds on cylinders, paraboloids, cones, and spheres into clean iterated integrals.

Core Concept • §1

1. Cylindrical Coordinates ($dV = r\,dz\,dr\,d\theta$) & Choosing the Right System

Intuition: Cylindrical coordinates are simply polar coordinates in the $xy$-plane plus the usual vertical $z$-coordinate. Whenever a 3D solid $Q$ has a circular or polar shadow $R$ in the $xy$-plane and clean vertical floor and ceiling surfaces $z = h_1(r,\theta)$ and $z = h_2(r,\theta)$ — such as vertical cylinders, circular paraboloids, or ellipsoids $ax^2+ay^2+z^2=c$ — cylindrical coordinates collapse $x^2+y^2$ into $r^2$.

By contrast, when $Q$ is bounded by origin-centered spheres and cones (where $x^2+y^2+z^2$ or straight rays from the origin dominate), spherical coordinates usually give constant limits and are simpler to evaluate.

Note (Instructor Notes vs. Book): Larson writes the cylindrical Jacobian as $r$ inside $r\,dz\,dr\,d\theta$ and uses $2\int_0^{\pi/2}$ symmetry on the sphere-and-cylinder volume problem. Dr. Alhumaidy’s notes underline the Jacobian $r$ in red, always solve bounds in the order $z \to r \to \theta$, and explicitly warn what goes wrong if you integrate over $[0, \pi]$ without symmetry and carelessly write $(\cos^2\theta)^{3/2} = \cos^3\theta$ instead of $|\cos\theta|^3$: the $\cos^3\theta$ integral cancels to zero and loses the $-\tfrac{64}{9}$ term! Textbook p. 1025, Example 1; Instructor Notes pp. 1024–1026
Cylindrical block & lower paraboloid $z = 2r^2$ Upper paraboloid $z = 12 - r^2$ Inner vertical $z$-slice ($z$ from $2r^2$ to $12 - r^2$) Intersection radius $r = 2$

(a) Extruding a polar rectangle vertically yields the cylindrical volume element; (b) paraboloid regions slice cleanly along vertical segments over the circular disk of radius two.

Cylindrical Coordinates & Decision Rule

Coordinate conversions between cylindrical $(r, \theta, z)$ and rectangular $(x, y, z)$ coordinates:

$$\begin{aligned} x &= r\cos\theta \\ y &= r\sin\theta \\ z &= z \end{aligned}$$

Polar radius and angle relations:

$$r^2 = x^2 + y^2$$ $$\tan\theta = \frac{y}{x}$$

Iterated triple integral over an $r$-simple base $R$ with $h_1(x,y) \le z \le h_2(x,y)$:

$$\iiint_Q f(x, y, z)\,dV = \int_{\theta_1}^{\theta_2} \int_{g_1(\theta)}^{g_2(\theta)} \int_{h_1(r\cos\theta,\, r\sin\theta)}^{h_2(r\cos\theta,\, r\sin\theta)} f(r\cos\theta,\, r\sin\theta,\, z)\,r\,dz\,dr\,d\theta$$

Cylindrical vs. Spherical Decision Rule: Use cylindrical when $Q$ involves paraboloids ($z = a - r^2$), cylinders ($r = c$ or $r = 2a\cos\theta$), horizontal planes ($z = c$), or integrands with $x^2+y^2$. Use spherical when $Q$ is bounded by origin-centered spheres ($\rho = a$) and cones ($\phi = \alpha$), or integrands with $x^2+y^2+z^2$.

Textbook p. 1024; p. 1030, Ex. 46
Example: Evaluating a Cylindrical Triple Integral
Evaluate the cylindrical triple integral: $$V = \int_0^{2\pi} \int_0^{2\sqrt{2}} \int_{r^2 - 2}^{6} r\,dz\,dr\,d\theta$$
Step 1: Integrate with respect to $z$. Treat $r$ and $\theta$ as constants along the vertical segment: $$\int_{r^2 - 2}^6 r\,dz = r\big(6 - (r^2 - 2)\big) = 8r - r^3$$
Step 2: Integrate with respect to $r$ and $\theta$. Evaluate the radial polynomial over $r \ge 0$ up to the upper limit, then integrate around the full circle: $$\begin{aligned} V &= \int_0^{2\pi} \left[\int_0^{2\sqrt{2}} (8r - r^3)\,dr\right] d\theta \\ &= \int_0^{2\pi} \left[4r^2 - \frac{r^4}{4}\right]_0^{2\sqrt{2}} d\theta \\ &= \int_0^{2\pi} \big(4(8) - 16\big)\,d\theta = \int_0^{2\pi} 16\,d\theta = 32\pi \end{aligned}$$
Step 3: Verify the result. The solid lies between the paraboloid $z = r^2 - 2$ and the plane $z = 6$, which has total height $8$ and squared base radius $8$; a cylinder with those dimensions has volume $\pi(8)(8) = 64\pi$, and a paraboloid occupies exactly half of its bounding cylinder, giving $\tfrac{1}{2}(64\pi) = 32\pi$.
Answer: $$V = 32\pi$$
Textbook p. 1029, Ex. 12; Instructor Notes
Why It Works: Extruding a Polar Area Element

A cylindrical block is a polar rectangle of base area $\Delta A_i$ lifted vertically by height $\Delta z_i$. Multiplying base area by height yields the block volume, which is why the Jacobian factor $r$ always appears even when the integrand is $1$.

$$\Delta V_i = \Delta A_i\,\Delta z_i = r_i\,\Delta r_i\,\Delta\theta_i\,\Delta z_i$$
Quick Check 1

Which coordinate system and iterated integral finds the volume of the solid $Q$ bounded below by the paraboloid $z = x^2 + y^2$ and above by the plane $z = 4$?

(A) Cylindrical: $$\int_0^{2\pi} \int_0^2 \int_{r^2}^4 r\,dz\,dr\,d\theta$$
(B) Cylindrical: $$\int_0^{2\pi} \int_0^4 \int_{r^2}^4 r\,dz\,dr\,d\theta$$
(C) Cylindrical: $$\int_0^{2\pi} \int_0^2 \int_{r^2}^4 dz\,dr\,d\theta$$
(D) Spherical: $$\int_0^{2\pi} \int_0^{\pi/4} \int_0^4 \rho^2\sin\phi\,d\rho\,d\phi\,d\theta$$
Check Answer & Reason

Answer: (A). A paraboloid with a flat plane $z = 4$ favors cylindrical coordinates. Setting $r^2 = 4$ gives the shadow disk $0 \le r \le 2$ and $0 \le \theta \le 2\pi$, with $r^2 \le z \le 4$ and Jacobian $r$ (missing in C).

Textbook p. 1026, Figure 14.67
Core Concept • §2

2. Spherical Coordinates & Geometric Derivation of $dV$

Intuition: Spherical coordinates $(\rho, \theta, \phi)$ locate any point in 3D space like a radar beam from the origin: $\rho \ge 0$ is the straight-line distance from $(0,0,0)$, $\phi \in [0, \pi]$ is the tilt angle down from the positive $z$-axis, and $\theta$ is the horizontal compass angle around the $z$-axis.

Dropping a perpendicular from the point onto the $xy$-plane forms a right triangle with hypotenuse $\rho$, horizontal radius $r = \rho\sin\phi$, and vertical height $z = \rho\cos\phi$.

Note (Instructor Notes vs. Book): Larson’s Remark reminds you that the spherical coordinate $\rho$ is distance from the origin, not mass density (so density problems use $k$ or $\delta$). Dr. Alhumaidy circles $\rho^2\sin\phi$ in red in his notes to stress that the spherical Jacobian has two powers of $\rho$ and $\sin\phi$ — never $\rho\sin\phi$ or $\rho^2\cos\phi$. Textbook p. 1027; Instructor Notes p. 1027
Radial edge $\Delta\rho_i$ Meridian arc $\rho_i\Delta\phi_i$ Latitude arc $(\rho_i\sin\phi_i)\Delta\theta_i$ Horizontal radius $r_i = \rho_i\sin\phi_i$

A spherical block is approximately a tiny rectangular box whose three perpendicular edges are the radial thickness, the meridian arc length, and the latitude arc length, producing the spherical Jacobian factor.

Spherical Coordinate Conversions & Triple Integral

For $\rho \ge 0$, $0 \le \phi \le \pi$, and $\theta_2 - \theta_1 \le 2\pi$, the rectangular conversions are:

$$\begin{aligned} x &= \rho\sin\phi\cos\theta \\ y &= \rho\sin\phi\sin\theta \\ z &= \rho\cos\phi \end{aligned}$$

Distance from the origin:

$$x^2 + y^2 + z^2 = \rho^2$$

Horizontal distance from the $z$-axis (since $\sin\phi \ge 0$ on $[0, \pi]$):

$$\sqrt{x^2 + y^2} = \rho\sin\phi$$

Iterated triple integral in spherical coordinates:

$$\iiint_Q f(x, y, z)\,dV = \int_{\theta_1}^{\theta_2} \int_{\phi_1}^{\phi_2} \int_{\rho_1}^{\rho_2} f(\rho\sin\phi\cos\theta,\, \rho\sin\phi\sin\theta,\, \rho\cos\phi)\,\rho^2\sin\phi\,d\rho\,d\phi\,d\theta$$ Textbook p. 1027
Example: Evaluating a Spherical Iterated Integral
Evaluate the spherical iterated integral: $$\int_0^{2\pi} \int_0^{\pi/2} \int_0^{\sin\phi} \rho\cos\phi\,d\rho\,d\phi\,d\theta$$
Step 1: Integrate with respect to $\rho$. Hold $\phi$ and $\theta$ constant: $$\int_0^{\sin\phi} \rho\cos\phi\,d\rho = \left[\frac{\rho^2}{2}\cos\phi\right]_0^{\sin\phi} = \frac{1}{2}\sin^2\phi\cos\phi$$
Step 2: Integrate with respect to $\phi$ and $\theta$. Use the substitution $u = \sin\phi$, $du = \cos\phi\,d\phi$ for the $\phi$-integral, then integrate in $\theta$: $$\begin{aligned} \int_0^{2\pi} \int_0^{\pi/2} \frac{1}{2}\sin^2\phi\cos\phi\,d\phi\,d\theta &= \int_0^{2\pi} \frac{1}{2}\left[\frac{\sin^3\phi}{3}\right]_0^{\pi/2} d\theta \\ &= \int_0^{2\pi} \frac{1}{6}\,d\theta = \frac{\pi}{3} \end{aligned}$$
Step 3: Verify the result. On $0 \le \phi \le \tfrac{\pi}{2}$ and $0 \le \rho \le \sin\phi \le 1$, the integrand $\rho\cos\phi$ is nonnegative and at most $1$, so the positive result $\tfrac{\pi}{3}$ is consistent with the bounds.
Answer: $$\frac{\pi}{3}$$
Textbook p. 1029, Ex. 7; Instructor Notes
Why It Works: Three Orthogonal Edges of a Spherical Block

Along a fixed ray ($\phi$ and $\theta$ constant), moving outward traces radial length $\Delta\rho$. Varying $\phi$ on a meridian circle of radius $\rho$ traces arc length $\rho\,\Delta\phi$.

Varying $\theta$ on a horizontal latitude circle of radius $r = \rho\sin\phi$ traces arc length $\rho\sin\phi\,\Delta\theta$. Multiplying these three mutually perpendicular edge lengths gives the spherical block volume.

$$\Delta V_i \approx (\Delta\rho_i)(\rho_i\,\Delta\phi_i)(\rho_i\sin\phi_i\,\Delta\theta_i) = \rho_i^2\sin\phi_i\,\Delta\rho_i\,\Delta\phi_i\,\Delta\theta_i$$
Quick Check 2

When converting the triple integral below to spherical coordinates, what does the integrand (including the spherical volume element $dV$) become?

$$\iiint_Q \sqrt{x^2 + y^2}\,dV$$
(A) $$\rho^3\sin\phi\,d\rho\,d\phi\,d\theta$$
(B) $$\rho^3\sin^2\phi\,d\rho\,d\phi\,d\theta$$
(C) $$\rho^2\sin^2\phi\,d\rho\,d\phi\,d\theta$$
(D) $$\rho^4\sin\phi\,d\rho\,d\phi\,d\theta$$
Check Answer & Reason

Answer: (B). Because $0 \le \phi \le \pi$, we have $\sin\phi \ge 0$, so the horizontal radius simplifies cleanly:

$$\sqrt{x^2 + y^2} = r = \rho\sin\phi$$

Multiplying by the spherical volume element yields:

$$(\rho\sin\phi)(\rho^2\sin\phi\,d\rho\,d\phi\,d\theta) = \rho^3\sin^2\phi\,d\rho\,d\phi\,d\theta$$
Core Concept • §3

3. Systematic $\rho, \phi, \theta$ Limits — Upper, Lower & Double Cones

Intuition: Always find spherical limits in three disciplined sweeps. First, shoot a ray straight out from the origin $(0,0,0)$ to read the radial span from $\rho_{\text{in}}$ to $\rho_{\text{out}}$; second, swing a pendulum downward from the $+z$-axis ($\phi = 0$) toward the $-z$-axis ($\phi = \pi$) to read $\phi_1 \le \phi \le \phi_2$.

Third, look down onto the $xy$-plane shadow to read the compass sweep $\theta_1 \le \theta \le \theta_2$. Nearly every exam trap comes from misreading whether a problem refers to the upper cone, the lower cone, or the double cone!

Note (Instructor Notes vs. Book): In the standard ice-cream-cone example, Larson intersects the sphere $x^2+y^2+z^2=9$ with the cone $z^2=x^2+y^2$ to solve for $z$ and then $\cos\phi = z/\rho$ to get $\phi = \tfrac{\pi}{4}$. Dr. Alhumaidy also uses a direct cone-angle shortcut: substitute $z = \rho\cos\phi$ and the horizontal radius $r = \rho\sin\phi$ straight into the cone equation to get $\tan\phi$ immediately, without needing the sphere’s radius first. Textbook p. 1028, Example 4; Instructor Notes p. 1028
Upper cone interior $[0, \tfrac{\pi}{4}]$ Between upper cone & $xy$-plane $[\tfrac{\pi}{4}, \tfrac{\pi}{2}]$ Between $xy$-plane & lower cone $[\tfrac{\pi}{2}, \tfrac{3\pi}{4}]$ Lower cone interior $[\tfrac{3\pi}{4}, \pi]$

Measuring the polar angle downward from the positive vertical axis separates upper-cone, lower-cone, and double-cone regions into exact non-overlapping intervals.

Cone-Angle Formulas in Spherical Coordinates

For an upper cone ($a > 0$), substituting $z = \rho\cos\phi$ and $r = \rho\sin\phi$ gives $\tan\phi = 1/a$:

$$z = a\sqrt{x^2 + y^2}$$

Three standard exam cone angles:

$$\begin{aligned} z = \sqrt{3(x^2 + y^2)} &\implies \phi = \frac{\pi}{6} \\ z = \sqrt{x^2 + y^2} &\implies \phi = \frac{\pi}{4} \\ z = \sqrt{\frac{x^2 + y^2}{3}} &\implies \phi = \frac{\pi}{3} \end{aligned}$$

Lower cone ($a > 0$, where $z < 0$ forces $\phi = \pi - \arctan(1/a)$ in $(\tfrac{\pi}{2}, \pi]$):

$$z = -a\sqrt{x^2 + y^2}$$

Double cone (yields both $\phi = \arctan(1/a)$ and $\phi = \pi - \arctan(1/a)$ unless phrasing restricts to the upper nappe):

$$z^2 = a^2(x^2 + y^2)$$ Instructor Notes; Lecture Video 4
Example: Volume Inside a Sphere, Outside an Upper Cone, Above the $xy$-Plane
Find the volume inside the sphere $x^2 + y^2 + z^2 = 9$, above the $xy$-plane, and outside the upper cone: $$z = \sqrt{x^2 + y^2}$$
Step 1: Determine the spherical bounds. The sphere gives $0 \le \rho \le 3$, and full rotation gives $0 \le \theta \le 2\pi$. Being outside the upper cone ($\phi \ge \tfrac{\pi}{4}$) and above the $xy$-plane ($\phi \le \tfrac{\pi}{2}$) restricts $\phi$ to: $$\frac{\pi}{4} \le \phi \le \frac{\pi}{2}$$
Step 2: Separate and evaluate the volume integral. Since all limits are constants, factor into three 1D integrals: $$\begin{aligned} V &= \left(\int_0^{2\pi} d\theta\right)\left(\int_{\pi/4}^{\pi/2} \sin\phi\,d\phi\right)\left(\int_0^3 \rho^2\,d\rho\right) \\ &= (2\pi)\Big[-\cos\phi\Big]_{\pi/4}^{\pi/2}\left[\frac{\rho^3}{3}\right]_0^3 \\ &= 2\pi\left(\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}\right)(9) = 9\sqrt{2}\pi \end{aligned}$$
Step 3: Verify the result. The upper hemisphere of radius $3$ has volume $18\pi$, and this solid is its outer collar: $$9\sqrt{2}\pi \approx 12.73\pi < 18\pi$$
Answer: $$V = 9\sqrt{2}\pi$$
Textbook p. 1030, Ex. 31; Instructor Notes
Why It Works: Scale Invariance of Cones

Every cone centered on the $z$-axis is scale-invariant from the origin. Scaling $(x, y, z)$ by any $\rho > 0$ leaves the slope ratio $r/z = \tan\phi$ unchanged, so a cone always reduces to a constant $\phi$-equation.

$$\frac{r}{z} = \frac{\rho\sin\phi}{\rho\cos\phi} = \tan\phi$$
Quick Check 3

What are the correct $\phi$-bounds for the solid inside the sphere $x^2 + y^2 + z^2 = 9$ and outside the upper cone below (with no restriction $z \ge 0$)?

$$z = \sqrt{3(x^2 + y^2)}$$
(A) $$0 \le \phi \le \frac{\pi}{6}$$
(B) $$\frac{\pi}{6} \le \phi \le \frac{\pi}{2}$$
(C) $$\frac{\pi}{6} \le \phi \le \pi$$
(D) $$\frac{\pi}{6} \le \phi \le \frac{5\pi}{6}$$
Check Answer & Reason

Answer: (C). For the upper cone, $z = \rho\cos\phi$ and $r = \rho\sin\phi$ give:

$$\tan\phi = \frac{1}{\sqrt{3}} \implies \phi = \frac{\pi}{6}$$

Because no lower cone and no $z \ge 0$ floor are present, the entire lower hemisphere ($\tfrac{\pi}{2} \le \phi \le \pi$) also lies outside the upper cone, giving $\tfrac{\pi}{6} \le \phi \le \pi$.

Core Concept • §4

4. Shifted Spheres ($\rho = 2a\cos\phi$), Ice-Cream Cones & Off-Origin Cylinders

Intuition: Not every sphere on the exam is centered at $(0,0,0)$. A sphere sitting tangent to the $xy$-plane at the origin — such as $x^2 + y^2 + (z - a)^2 = a^2$ or $x^2 + y^2 + z^2 = z$ — lies completely in the upper half-space $z \ge 0$, so every ray from the origin stays inside $0 \le \phi \le \tfrac{\pi}{2}$ and exits the sphere at $\rho = 2a\cos\phi$.

Likewise, in cylindrical coordinates, an off-origin cylinder $(x-a)^2+y^2 = a^2$ becomes $r = 2a\cos\theta$ on $[-\tfrac{\pi}{2}, \tfrac{\pi}{2}]$, while $x^2+(y-a)^2 = a^2$ becomes $r = 2a\sin\theta$ on $[0, \pi]$.

Shifted sphere $x^2+y^2+z^2=z$ ($\rho=\cos\phi$) Cone $z = r$ ($\phi=\tfrac{\pi}{4}$) Ray from origin exiting at $\rho=\cos\phi$ Right triangle with diameter $1$ along $+z$-axis

Cross-section of a shifted sphere tangent to the horizontal plane at the origin intersecting an upper cone: by Thales' theorem on the vertical diameter of length one, an outgoing ray exits the sphere at the cosine of the polar angle, keeping the radius nonnegative only in the upper half-space.

Shifted Spheres & Off-Origin Cylinders

Shifted sphere tangent to the $xy$-plane at the origin ($a > 0$, valid only on $[0, \tfrac{\pi}{2}]$):

$$x^2 + y^2 + (z - a)^2 = a^2 \iff x^2 + y^2 + z^2 = 2az \iff \rho = 2a\cos\phi$$

Off-origin vertical cylinder shifted along the $+x$-axis ($a > 0$, $\theta$ in $[-\tfrac{\pi}{2}, \tfrac{\pi}{2}]$):

$$(x - a)^2 + y^2 = a^2 \iff r = 2a\cos\theta$$

Off-origin vertical cylinder shifted along the $+y$-axis ($a > 0$, $0 \le \theta \le \pi$):

$$x^2 + (y - a)^2 = a^2 \iff r = 2a\sin\theta$$ Textbook p. 1025, Example 1; p. 1030, Ex. 32
Example: Volume of a Shifted Sphere via Spherical Coordinates
Convert $x^2 + y^2 + (z - 2)^2 = 4$ to spherical coordinates and check its volume.
Step 1: Convert the surface to spherical bounds. Expanding gives $x^2 + y^2 + z^2 - 4z = 0$, so $\rho^2 = 4\rho\cos\phi$: $$\rho = 4\cos\phi$$

Since the sphere sits entirely in $z \ge 0$, the bounds are $0 \le \rho \le 4\cos\phi$, $0 \le \phi \le \tfrac{\pi}{2}$, and $0 \le \theta \le 2\pi$.

Step 2: Integrate in spherical coordinates. $$\begin{aligned} V &= \int_0^{2\pi} \int_0^{\pi/2} \int_0^{4\cos\phi} \rho^2\sin\phi\,d\rho\,d\phi\,d\theta \\ &= 2\pi \int_0^{\pi/2} \frac{64}{3}\cos^3\phi\sin\phi\,d\phi \\ &= \frac{128\pi}{3}\left[-\frac{\cos^4\phi}{4}\right]_0^{\pi/2} = \frac{32\pi}{3} \end{aligned}$$
Step 3: Verify the result. A sphere of radius $R = 2$ has geometric volume: $$V = \frac{4}{3}\pi(2)^3 = \frac{32\pi}{3}$$
Answer: $$\rho = 4\cos\phi \quad \left(0 \le \phi \le \frac{\pi}{2}\right)$$ $$V = \frac{32\pi}{3}$$
Lecture Video 3
Why It Works: Thales’ Right Triangle on a Diameter

Any sphere of diameter $2a$ resting on the origin along the $+z$-axis forms a right triangle with any ray from the origin to the sphere surface. By right-triangle trigonometry, $\cos\phi$ equals the chord $\rho$ divided by the diameter $2a$, forcing $\rho = 2a\cos\phi$ and restricting $\phi$ to $[0, \tfrac{\pi}{2}]$ because $\rho \ge 0$.

$$\cos\phi = \frac{\text{adjacent}}{\text{hypotenuse}} = \frac{\rho}{2a} \implies \rho = 2a\cos\phi$$
Quick Check 4

What are the spherical bounds for the solid ball $x^2 + y^2 + (z - 3)^2 \le 9$?

(A) $0 \le \rho \le 3$, $0 \le \phi \le \pi$, $0 \le \theta \le 2\pi$
(B) $0 \le \rho \le 6\cos\phi$, $0 \le \phi \le \pi$, $0 \le \theta \le 2\pi$
(C) $0 \le \rho \le 6\cos\phi$, $0 \le \phi \le \tfrac{\pi}{2}$, $0 \le \theta \le 2\pi$
(D) $0 \le \rho \le 3\cos\phi$, $0 \le \phi \le \tfrac{\pi}{2}$, $0 \le \theta \le 2\pi$
Check Answer & Reason

Answer: (C). Expanding gives $x^2 + y^2 + z^2 \le 6z$, which simplifies to $\rho^2 \le 6\rho\cos\phi$, or $0 \le \rho \le 6\cos\phi$. Since the entire ball lies above the $xy$-plane ($z \ge 0$), $\phi$ runs only over $0 \le \phi \le \tfrac{\pi}{2}$ (otherwise $\cos\phi < 0$).

Core Concept • §5

5. Converting Rectangular Triple Integrals to Cylindrical or Spherical

Intuition: A favorite KFUPM final exam format gives you a rectangular triple integral and asks you to convert or evaluate it:

$$\int_{x_1}^{x_2}\int_{y_1(x)}^{y_2(x)}\int_{z_1(x,y)}^{z_2(x,y)} f(x,y,z)\,dz\,dy\,dx$$

Never guess $\theta$ or $\phi$ from memory! Instead, peel the integral like an onion: the outer two integrals draw the 2D shadow $R$ in the $xy$-plane (fixing $\theta$ and, for cylindrical, $r$), and the innermost $z$-integral tells you the 3D floor and ceiling (fixing $z$ in cylindrical or $\rho, \phi$ in spherical).

Quarter-disk: $0 \le \theta \le \tfrac{\pi}{2}$ Upper half-disk ($y \ge 0$): $0 \le \theta \le \pi$ Right half-disk ($x \ge 0$): $[-\tfrac{\pi}{2}, \tfrac{\pi}{2}]$

Reading the outer two rectangular bounds determines the exact horizontal shadow region and prevents the classic mistake of substituting a full circle interval for a half-disk or quarter-disk.

3-Step Rectangular-to-Curvilinear Conversion Checklist
  1. Decode the $xy$-shadow $R$: Read the outer two bounds ($x, y$) to sketch $R$ and determine $\theta_1 \le \theta \le \theta_2$ (plus $r$-bounds for cylindrical).
  2. Decode the 3D ceiling and floor: Read the inner bounds $z_1(x,y) \le z \le z_2(x,y)$. Paraboloids and planes convert directly to $z(r,\theta)$ in cylindrical, whereas an upper hemisphere $0 \le \phi \le \tfrac{\pi}{2}$, $0 \le \rho \le a$ corresponds to: $$0 \le z \le \sqrt{a^2 - x^2 - y^2}$$
  3. Transform integrand and Jacobian: Convert $f(x, y, z)$ and multiply by $r$ (cylindrical) or $\rho^2\sin\phi$ (spherical).
Textbook p. 1030, Ex. 41–44
Example: Converting & Evaluating a First-Octant Sphere Integral
Convert and evaluate the rectangular triple integral: $$\int_0^3 \int_0^{\sqrt{9-x^2}} \int_0^{\sqrt{9-x^2-y^2}} \sqrt{x^2+y^2+z^2}\,dz\,dy\,dx$$
Step 1: Decode the $xy$-shadow and $z$-bounds. From the outer limits, $R$ is the Quadrant I quarter-disk of radius $3$, giving $0 \le \theta \le \tfrac{\pi}{2}$: $$0 \le x \le 3$$ $$0 \le y \le \sqrt{9 - x^2}$$

The inner limits trace the upper hemisphere of radius $3$, giving $0 \le \rho \le 3$ and $0 \le \phi \le \tfrac{\pi}{2}$:

$$0 \le z \le \sqrt{9 - x^2 - y^2}$$
Step 2: Transform the integrand and evaluate in spherical coordinates. Using the spherical radius $\rho$ and Jacobian $\rho^2\sin\phi\,d\rho\,d\phi\,d\theta$: $$\begin{aligned} \int_0^{\pi/2}\int_0^{\pi/2}\int_0^3 \rho \cdot \rho^2\sin\phi\,d\rho\,d\phi\,d\theta &= \left(\int_0^{\pi/2} d\theta\right)\left(\int_0^{\pi/2} \sin\phi\,d\phi\right)\left(\int_0^3 \rho^3\,d\rho\right) \\ &= \left(\frac{\pi}{2}\right)\Big[-\cos\phi\Big]_0^{\pi/2}\left[\frac{\rho^4}{4}\right]_0^3 \\ &= \frac{\pi}{2}(1)\left(\frac{81}{4}\right) = \frac{81\pi}{8} \end{aligned}$$
Step 3: Verify the result. The first-octant eighth of the ball of radius $3$ has volume $V_{\text{oct}}$ with $0 \le \rho \le 3$, so the integral must lie between $0$ and $3V_{\text{oct}}$: $$V_{\text{oct}} = \frac{1}{8}\cdot\frac{4}{3}\pi(27) = \frac{9\pi}{2} \implies 0 < \frac{81\pi}{8} < \frac{27\pi}{2}$$
Answer: $$\frac{81\pi}{8}$$
Textbook p. 1030, Ex. 44; KFUPM Final Term 251, Q20
Why It Works: Coordinate Independence of Triple Integrals

Fubini’s theorem ensures the value of a triple integral depends only on the geometric solid $Q$ and function $f$, not on the coordinate grid used to slice $Q$. Converting bounds from the outside in preserves the exact 3D region while replacing square roots with clean polar or spherical limits.

$$\iiint_Q f(x, y, z)\,dV_{\text{rect}} = \iiint_Q f\,dV_{\text{cyl}} = \iiint_Q f\,dV_{\text{sph}}$$
Quick Check 5

In cylindrical coordinates, which iterated integral equals the rectangular integral below?

$$\int_0^3 \int_{-\sqrt{9-x^2}}^{\sqrt{9-x^2}} \int_{x^2+y^2}^9 y\,dz\,dy\,dx$$
(A) $$\int_{-\pi/2}^{\pi/2} \int_0^3 \int_{r^2}^9 (r^2\sin\theta)\,dz\,dr\,d\theta$$
(B) $$\int_0^{\pi/2} \int_0^3 \int_{r^2}^9 (r\sin\theta)\,dz\,dr\,d\theta$$
(C) $$\int_0^{\pi} \int_0^3 \int_r^3 (r\sin\theta)\,dz\,dr\,d\theta$$
(D) $$\int_{-\pi/2}^{\pi/2} \int_{-3}^3 \int_{r^2}^9 (r^2\sin\theta)\,dz\,dr\,d\theta$$
Check Answer & Reason

Answer: (A). From $0 \le x \le 3$ and the symmetric $y$-limits, the $xy$-shadow is the right half-disk of radius $3$, so $\theta$ lies in $[-\tfrac{\pi}{2}, \tfrac{\pi}{2}]$ and $0 \le r \le 3$ (always $r \ge 0$). The $z$-limits $x^2+y^2 \le z \le 9$ become $r^2 \le z \le 9$, and:

$$y\,dV = (r\sin\theta)(r\,dz\,dr\,d\theta) = r^2\sin\theta\,dz\,dr\,d\theta$$
KFUPM Final Term 253, Q20
Master Formulas

Section 14.7 Formula Reference & Boundary Dictionary

Core Coordinate Conversions, Volume Elements & Applications

Cylindrical Coordinates ($r \ge 0$, $\theta_2 - \theta_1 \le 2\pi$):

$$\begin{aligned} x &= r\cos\theta \\ y &= r\sin\theta \\ z &= z \\ r^2 &= x^2 + y^2 \end{aligned}$$

Cylindrical differential of volume (6 possible orders):

$$dV = r\,dz\,dr\,d\theta$$

Spherical Coordinates ($\rho \ge 0$, $0 \le \phi \le \pi$, $\theta_2 - \theta_1 \le 2\pi$):

$$\begin{aligned} x &= \rho\sin\phi\cos\theta \\ y &= \rho\sin\phi\sin\theta \\ z &= \rho\cos\phi \end{aligned}$$

Spherical radius and horizontal radius identities:

$$\rho^2 = x^2 + y^2 + z^2$$ $$\sqrt{x^2 + y^2} = \rho\sin\phi$$

Spherical differential of volume (note $\sin\phi \ge 0$ on $[0, \pi]$):

$$dV = \rho^2\sin\phi\,d\rho\,d\phi\,d\theta$$

Shifted Surfaces & Edge Cases:

Shifted sphere tangent to the $xy$-plane at the origin ($0 \le \phi \le \tfrac{\pi}{2}$):

$$x^2 + y^2 + (z - a)^2 = a^2 \iff \rho = 2a\cos\phi$$

Shifted cylinder along the $+x$-axis ($\theta$ in $[-\tfrac{\pi}{2}, \tfrac{\pi}{2}]$):

$$(x - a)^2 + y^2 = a^2 \iff r = 2a\cos\theta$$

Shifted cylinder along the $+y$-axis ($0 \le \theta \le \pi$):

$$x^2 + (y - a)^2 = a^2 \iff r = 2a\sin\theta$$

Physical Integrals: Using density $\delta(x, y, z)$ (or $k$) so it does not clash with spherical $\rho$:

Volume:

$$V = \iiint_Q dV$$

Mass:

$$m = \iiint_Q \delta(x, y, z)\,dV$$

Center of mass $z$-coordinate:

$$\bar{z} = \frac{M_{xy}}{m} = \frac{1}{m}\iiint_Q z\,\delta\,dV$$

Moment of inertia about the $z$-axis:

$$I_z = \iiint_Q (x^2 + y^2)\,\delta\,dV$$

Constant-Limit Separability Rule: If all limits are constants and $F(\rho, \phi, \theta)$ factors as $g(\theta)h(\phi)k(\rho)$:

$$\int_{\theta_1}^{\theta_2}\int_{\phi_1}^{\phi_2}\int_{\rho_1}^{\rho_2} g(\theta)h(\phi)k(\rho)\,d\rho\,d\phi\,d\theta = \left(\int_{\theta_1}^{\theta_2} g(\theta)\,d\theta\right)\left(\int_{\phi_1}^{\phi_2} h(\phi)\,d\phi\right)\left(\int_{\rho_1}^{\rho_2} k(\rho)\,d\rho\right)$$ Textbook pp. 1024–1028
Exam Traps

5 Classic Mistakes (WRONG vs. RIGHT)

Trap 1 — Dropping or corrupting the Jacobian factor ($r$ or $\rho^2\sin\phi$):

WrongWriting $dV = dz\,dr\,d\theta$ or using $\rho\sin\phi\,d\rho\,d\phi\,d\theta$ or $\rho^2\,d\rho\,d\phi\,d\theta$.
RightAlways insert $r$ in cylindrical ($r\,dz\,dr\,d\theta$) and $\rho^2\sin\phi$ in spherical ($\rho^2\sin\phi\,d\rho\,d\phi\,d\theta$).

Trap 2 — Replacing $(\cos^2\theta)^{1/2}$ or $(\sin^2\theta)^{1/2}$ without absolute value:

WrongAssuming $\cos\theta \ge 0$ on $[0, \pi]$ and writing: $$\int_0^{\pi} (4 - 4\sin^2\theta)^{3/2}\,d\theta = \int_0^\pi 8\cos^3\theta\,d\theta = 0$$ Instructor Notes p. 1026
RightUse absolute values or fold by symmetry to $2\int_0^{\pi/2}$ where $\cos\theta \ge 0$ and $\sin\theta \ge 0$: $$(4\cos^2\theta)^{3/2} = 8|\cos\theta|^3$$

Trap 3 — Mixing up upper cone, $xy$-plane cutoff, and double cone $\phi$-intervals:

WrongUsing $[\tfrac{\pi}{4}, \tfrac{\pi}{2}]$ for “outside the upper cone $z = r$”, or forgetting the lower nappe in $z^2 = x^2+y^2$.
Right“Outside the upper cone $z = r$” alone is $[\tfrac{\pi}{4}, \pi]$; adding “above $xy$-plane” stops at $\tfrac{\pi}{2}$; “outside double cone” is $[\tfrac{\pi}{4}, \tfrac{3\pi}{4}]$.

Trap 4 — Sweeping $\theta \in [0, 2\pi]$ on shifted circles or half-disk shadows:

WrongIntegrating $r = 2\sin\theta$ over $[0, 2\pi]$ (traces twice and allows $r < 0$), or setting $-3 \le r \le 3$ for a disk.
RightAlways keep $r \ge 0$: $r = 2a\sin\theta$ uses $0 \le \theta \le \pi$; $r = 2a\cos\theta$ uses $\theta$ in $[-\tfrac{\pi}{2}, \tfrac{\pi}{2}]$.

Trap 5 — Letting $\phi$ exceed $\tfrac{\pi}{2}$ on shifted spheres $\rho = 2a\cos\phi$:

WrongSetting $0 \le \phi \le \pi$ for $x^2+y^2+z^2 = z$ (causes $\rho = \cos\phi < 0$ and cancels volume to $0$!).
RightBecause $z = x^2+y^2+z^2 \ge 0$, the entire shifted sphere sits in $z \ge 0$, so $0 \le \phi \le \tfrac{\pi}{2}$.
Worked Examples

From Textbook Basics to KFUPM Final Level

Example 1: Volume Between Two Circular Paraboloids
Find the volume of the solid $Q$ bounded above by the paraboloid $z = 12 - x^2 - y^2$ and below by the paraboloid $z = 2x^2 + 2y^2$.
Step 1: Choose cylindrical coordinates and intersect the paraboloids. Both surfaces depend only on $x^2 + y^2 = r^2$: the ceiling is $z = 12 - r^2$ and the floor is $z = 2r^2$. Set them equal to find the shadow radius: $$12 - r^2 = 2r^2 \implies 3r^2 = 12 \implies r^2 = 4 \implies r = 2$$

Since the solid wraps fully around the $z$-axis, the cylindrical bounds are $0 \le \theta \le 2\pi$, $0 \le r \le 2$, and $2r^2 \le z \le 12 - r^2$.

Step 2: Integrate in the order $dz\,dr\,d\theta$. $$\begin{aligned} V &= \int_0^{2\pi} \int_0^2 \int_{2r^2}^{12 - r^2} r\,dz\,dr\,d\theta \\ &= \int_0^{2\pi} \int_0^2 r\big[(12 - r^2) - 2r^2\big]\,dr\,d\theta \\ &= \left(\int_0^{2\pi} d\theta\right) \int_0^2 (12r - 3r^3)\,dr \\ &= 2\pi \left[6r^2 - \frac{3}{4}r^4\right]_0^2 = 2\pi\left(24 - 12\right) = 24\pi \end{aligned}$$
Step 3: Verify the result. A cylinder of radius $2$ and full height $12$ has volume $\pi(2^2)(12) = 48\pi$; because each paraboloid occupies half of its bounding cylinder, the lens between them has half that volume, $\tfrac{1}{2}(48\pi) = 24\pi$.
Answer: $$V = 24\pi$$
KFUPM Final Term 252, Q19; Lecture Video 1
Example 2: Solid Cut from a Sphere by a Shifted Cylinder (Symmetry & Sign Trap)
Find the volume of the solid $Q$ cut from the sphere $x^2 + y^2 + z^2 = 4$ by the cylinder $x^2 + y^2 - 2y = 0$ (i.e., $r = 2\sin\theta$). Also determine the setup constants $a, b, c$ when the volume is written as: $$V = \int_0^{a\pi}\int_0^{b\sin\theta}\int_{-\sqrt{c-r^2}}^{\sqrt{c-r^2}} r\,dz\,dr\,d\theta$$
Step 1: Convert both surfaces to cylindrical bounds. Substituting $x^2 + y^2 = r^2$ into the sphere equation $r^2 + z^2 = 4$ gives $c = 4$ and the vertical limits: $$-\sqrt{4 - r^2} \le z \le \sqrt{4 - r^2}$$

For the cylinder $x^2 + y^2 - 2y = 0$, substituting $x^2+y^2=r^2$ and $y=r\sin\theta$ gives $r^2 = 2r\sin\theta$, or $r = 2\sin\theta$ ($b = 2$). Completing the square gives $x^2 + (y - 1)^2 = 1$ in the upper half-plane $y \ge 0$, traced once for $0 \le \theta \le \pi$ ($a = 1$).

Step 2: Apply symmetry to avoid the $(\cos^2\theta)^{3/2}$ sign trap. The solid is symmetric across both $z = 0$ and the $yz$-plane ($\theta = \tfrac{\pi}{2}$). Folding onto $0 \le \theta \le \tfrac{\pi}{2}$ guarantees $\cos\theta \ge 0$: $$\begin{aligned} V &= \int_0^{\pi} \int_0^{2\sin\theta} \int_{-\sqrt{4-r^2}}^{\sqrt{4-r^2}} r\,dz\,dr\,d\theta \\ &= 4 \int_0^{\pi/2} \int_0^{2\sin\theta} \int_0^{\sqrt{4-r^2}} r\,dz\,dr\,d\theta \\ &= 4 \int_0^{\pi/2} \int_0^{2\sin\theta} r\sqrt{4 - r^2}\,dr\,d\theta \end{aligned}$$
Step 3: Substitute $u = 4 - r^2$ and integrate in $\theta$. Evaluate the inner radial integral first: $$\int_0^{2\sin\theta} r\sqrt{4 - r^2}\,dr = \left[-\frac{1}{3}(4 - r^2)^{3/2}\right]_0^{2\sin\theta} = \frac{1}{3}\Big(8 - (4\cos^2\theta)^{3/2}\Big) = \frac{8}{3}(1 - \cos^3\theta)$$

Using the identity $\cos^2\theta = 1 - \sin^2\theta$, integrate $\cos^3\theta$ over $[0, \tfrac{\pi}{2}]$:

$$\begin{aligned} V &= \frac{32}{3} \int_0^{\pi/2} \big[1 - \cos\theta(1 - \sin^2\theta)\big]\,d\theta \\ &= \frac{32}{3} \left[\theta - \sin\theta + \frac{\sin^3\theta}{3}\right]_0^{\pi/2} = \frac{32}{3}\left(\frac{\pi}{2} - 1 + \frac{1}{3}\right) = \frac{32}{3}\left(\frac{3\pi - 4}{6}\right) = \frac{16}{9}(3\pi - 4) \end{aligned}$$
Step 4: Verify the result. Numerically, this volume is approximately $9.644$, which is safely less than the bounding cylinder volume $\pi(1)^2(4) = 4\pi \approx 12.566$ because the sphere curves inward at top and bottom.
Answer: $$V = \frac{16}{9}(3\pi - 4)$$

Setup parameters: $a = 1$, $b = 2$, $c = 4$ (so $a + b + c = 7$).

Textbook p. 1025, Example 1; Instructor Notes p. 1026; KFUPM Final Term 241, Q20 & Term 243, Q8
Example 3: Volume Inside a Sphere and Outside the Upper Cone
Find the volume of the solid $Q$ inside the sphere $x^2 + y^2 + z^2 = 16$ and outside the upper cone: $$z = \sqrt{x^2 + y^2}$$
Step 1: Convert the surfaces to spherical bounds.
  • Sphere: $x^2 + y^2 + z^2 = 16$ gives $\rho^2 = 16$, so $0 \le \rho \le 4$.
  • Upper cone: Substituting $z = \rho\cos\phi$ and $r = \rho\sin\phi$ gives $\tan\phi = 1$, so $\phi = \tfrac{\pi}{4}$.
  • Outside the upper cone (all $z$): Since there is no $z \ge 0$ cutoff, $\phi$ sweeps from $\tfrac{\pi}{4}$ all the way to the $-z$-axis ($\pi$), giving $\tfrac{\pi}{4} \le \phi \le \pi$ and $0 \le \theta \le 2\pi$.
Step 2: Factor and evaluate the constant-limit spherical integral. $$\begin{aligned} V &= \int_0^{2\pi} \int_{\pi/4}^{\pi} \int_0^4 \rho^2\sin\phi\,d\rho\,d\phi\,d\theta \\ &= \left(\int_0^{2\pi} d\theta\right)\left(\int_{\pi/4}^{\pi} \sin\phi\,d\phi\right)\left(\int_0^4 \rho^2\,d\rho\right) \\ &= (2\pi) \Big[-\cos\phi\Big]_{\pi/4}^{\pi} \left[\frac{\rho^3}{3}\right]_0^4 \\ &= 2\pi\left(-\cos\pi + \cos\frac{\pi}{4}\right)\left(\frac{64}{3}\right) \\ &= 2\pi\left(1 + \frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}\right)\left(\frac{64}{3}\right) = \frac{64\pi}{3}(2 + \sqrt{2}) \end{aligned}$$
Step 3: Verify the result. The complementary ice-cream cone inside the upper cone ($0 \le \phi \le \tfrac{\pi}{4}$) has volume: $$V_{\text{inside}} = 2\pi\left(1 - \frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}\right)\left(\frac{64}{3}\right) = \frac{64\pi}{3}(2 - \sqrt{2})$$

Adding inside and outside volumes gives the exact full sphere volume:

$$\frac{64\pi}{3}(4) = \frac{256\pi}{3} = \frac{4}{3}\pi(4)^3$$
Answer: $$V = \frac{64\pi}{3}(2 + \sqrt{2})$$
KFUPM Final Term 241, Q19; cf. Textbook p. 1028, Example 4
Example 4: Volume Bounded by $x^2 + y^2 + z^2 = z$ and $z = r$
Use spherical coordinates to find the volume of the solid $Q$ bounded above by the shifted sphere $x^2 + y^2 + z^2 = z$ and below by the upper cone: $$z = \sqrt{x^2 + y^2}$$
Step 1: Find the spherical equations and limits.
  • Shifted sphere: $\rho^2 = \rho\cos\phi$ gives $\rho = \cos\phi$, so rays from the origin run over $0 \le \rho \le \cos\phi$.
  • Upper cone floor: $\rho\cos\phi = \rho\sin\phi$ gives $\phi = \tfrac{\pi}{4}$. Since the solid lies above the cone (inside the ice-cream cap), $0 \le \phi \le \tfrac{\pi}{4}$ (where $\cos\phi > 0$) and $0 \le \theta \le 2\pi$.
Step 2: Evaluate in the order $d\rho\,d\phi\,d\theta$. First integrate with respect to $\rho$: $$\begin{aligned} V &= \int_0^{2\pi} \int_0^{\pi/4} \int_0^{\cos\phi} \rho^2\sin\phi\,d\rho\,d\phi\,d\theta \\ &= \int_0^{2\pi} \int_0^{\pi/4} \left[\frac{\rho^3}{3}\right]_0^{\cos\phi} \sin\phi\,d\phi\,d\theta \\ &= \frac{1}{3} \left(\int_0^{2\pi} d\theta\right) \int_0^{\pi/4} \cos^3\phi\sin\phi\,d\phi \end{aligned}$$

Substitute $u = \cos\phi$, $du = -\sin\phi\,d\phi$:

$$V = \frac{2\pi}{3} \left[-\frac{\cos^4\phi}{4}\right]_0^{\pi/4} = \frac{\pi}{6}\left(1 - \left(\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}\right)^4\right) = \frac{\pi}{6}\left(1 - \frac{1}{4}\right) = \frac{\pi}{6} \cdot \frac{3}{4} = \frac{\pi}{8}$$
Step 3: Verify the result geometrically. Completing the square gives a sphere of radius $\tfrac{1}{2}$ and volume $\tfrac{\pi}{6}$: $$x^2 + y^2 + \left(z - \frac{1}{2}\right)^2 = \frac{1}{4}$$

Because the cone $z = r$ cuts through the sphere’s equator $z = \tfrac{1}{2}$, the solid is the upper hemisphere plus a lower inverted cone of radius $\tfrac{1}{2}$ and height $\tfrac{1}{2}$:

$$V = \frac{1}{2}\left(\frac{\pi}{6}\right) + \frac{1}{3}\pi\left(\frac{1}{2}\right)^2\left(\frac{1}{2}\right) = \frac{\pi}{12} + \frac{\pi}{24} = \frac{\pi}{8}$$
Answer: $$V = \frac{\pi}{8}$$
Textbook p. 1030, Ex. 32; Instructor Notes
Example 5: Converting & Evaluating a Hemisphere Triple Integral
Evaluate the rectangular triple integral by converting to spherical coordinates: $$\int_{-1}^{1} \int_{0}^{\sqrt{1 - x^2}} \int_{0}^{\sqrt{1 - x^2 - y^2}} (8x^2 + 8y^2 + 8z^2)^{2/3}\,dz\,dy\,dx$$
Step 1: Identify the 3D solid $Q$ from rectangular inequalities. The outer bounds describe the upper half-disk of radius $1$ in the $xy$-plane ($y \ge 0$, Quadrants I and II), so $0 \le \theta \le \pi$: $$-1 \le x \le 1$$ $$0 \le y \le \sqrt{1 - x^2}$$

The inner bounds sweep the upper hemisphere of the unit ball $x^2 + y^2 + z^2 \le 1$ ($z \ge 0$), giving $0 \le \rho \le 1$ and $0 \le \phi \le \tfrac{\pi}{2}$:

$$0 \le z \le \sqrt{1 - x^2 - y^2}$$
Step 2: Convert the integrand and include $\rho^2\sin\phi$. Using $x^2 + y^2 + z^2 = \rho^2$: $$(8x^2 + 8y^2 + 8z^2)^{2/3} = (8\rho^2)^{2/3} = 8^{2/3}\rho^{4/3} = 4\rho^{4/3}$$

Multiplying by the spherical Jacobian $\rho^2\sin\phi\,d\rho\,d\phi\,d\theta$ yields:

$$(4\rho^{4/3})(\rho^2\sin\phi)\,d\rho\,d\phi\,d\theta = 4\rho^{10/3}\sin\phi\,d\rho\,d\phi\,d\theta$$
Step 3: Separate and evaluate each 1D factor. $$\begin{aligned} \iiint_Q (8x^2+8y^2+8z^2)^{2/3}\,dV &= \int_0^{\pi} \int_0^{\pi/2} \int_0^1 4\rho^{10/3}\sin\phi\,d\rho\,d\phi\,d\theta \\ &= \left(\int_0^{\pi} d\theta\right)\left(\int_0^{\pi/2} \sin\phi\,d\phi\right)\left(\int_0^1 4\rho^{10/3}\,d\rho\right) \\ &= (\pi)\Big[-\cos\phi\Big]_0^{\pi/2}\left[4 \cdot \frac{3}{13}\rho^{13/3}\right]_0^1 \\ &= \pi \cdot 1 \cdot \frac{12}{13} = \frac{12\pi}{13} \end{aligned}$$
Step 4: Verify the result. The quarter-ball $Q$ has volume $\tfrac{\pi}{3}$, and on $Q$ the integrand $4\rho^{4/3}$ satisfies $0 \le 4\rho^{4/3} \le 4$. Thus the integral must lie strictly between $0$ and $4(\tfrac{\pi}{3}) = \tfrac{4\pi}{3}$, which $\tfrac{12\pi}{13} < \tfrac{4\pi}{3}$ satisfies.
Answer: $$\frac{12\pi}{13}$$
KFUPM Final Term 253, Q21
One-Screen Summary

The 5 Things to Know for the Exam

  1. Never forget the Jacobian: Cylindrical uses $dV = r\,dz\,dr\,d\theta$ (with $x^2+y^2 = r^2$); Spherical uses $\rho^2\sin\phi\,d\rho\,d\phi\,d\theta$ (with $x^2+y^2+z^2 = \rho^2$ and horizontal radius $r = \rho\sin\phi$).
  2. Pick Cylindrical for paraboloids/cylinders, Spherical for origin spheres/cones: Paraboloids ($z = a - r^2$) and off-origin cylinders ($r = 2a\cos\theta$ on $[-\tfrac{\pi}{2}, \tfrac{\pi}{2}]$, $r = 2a\sin\theta$ on $[0, \pi]$) belong in cylindrical; cones ($\phi = \alpha$) and spheres ($\rho = a$ or $\rho = 2a\cos\phi$) belong in spherical.
  3. Read $\phi \in [0, \pi]$ carefully from the $+z$-axis for cones: Inside the upper cone $z = r$ is $[0, \tfrac{\pi}{4}]$; outside and above the $xy$-plane is $[\tfrac{\pi}{4}, \tfrac{\pi}{2}]$; outside the upper cone (all $z$) is $[\tfrac{\pi}{4}, \pi]$; outside the double cone $z^2 = r^2$ is $[\tfrac{\pi}{4}, \tfrac{3\pi}{4}]$.
  4. Always use symmetry or $|\cos\theta|$ before simplifying $(a^2\cos^2\theta)^{3/2}$: Fold symmetric integrals to $[0, \tfrac{\pi}{2}]$ so $\cos\theta \ge 0$ and $\sin\theta \ge 0$, avoiding the sign-cancellation trap.
  5. Convert rectangular triple integrals from outside in: Outer two bounds fix the $xy$-shadow $R$ (Quadrant I $\implies$ $[0, \tfrac{\pi}{2}]$, upper half $\implies$ $[0, \pi]$, right half $\implies$ $[-\tfrac{\pi}{2}, \tfrac{\pi}{2}]$), while the inner $z$-bounds fix ceiling, floor, and $\phi$.
